itemVerdicts.item: (a) ICI: index domestic equity MFs+ETFs = 19% of US stock market value at YE2025; active 11%; other 69%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the 2026 Investment Company Fact Book ch.2 (re-downloaded from https://www.icifactbook.org/pdf/2026-factbook-ch2.pdf; the icifactbook.org host without www returns 403 to curl): "index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs remain relatively small investors in the US stock markets, holding 19% of the value of US stocks at year-end 2025 (Figure 2.6). Actively managed domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs held another 11%, while other investors—including hedge funds, pension funds, life insurance companies, and individuals—held the majority (69%)." Figure 2.6 is labeled "Percentage of US stock market capitalization, year-end"; sources line reads "Investment Company Institute and World Federation of Exchanges."

Each of the four cited points verified by extracting per-word bounding boxes from Figure 2.6 (pdftotext -bbox, file page 8) and matching x-centers to the year-axis labels, because flat text extraction interleaves the three stacked rows. Full index row 2015-2025 = 11, 12, 13, 13, 16, 15, 17, 18, 18, 18, 19. Note the series is NOT monotonic: it dips from 16 (2019) to 15 (2020) before resuming. Active row = 18, 17, 16, 15, 16, 15, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11; other row = 71, 71, 71, 71, 68, 69, 68, 69, 68, 70, 69.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Vanguard Aug 2025 "Setting the record straight": US 23% as of Dec 31 2024, broader numerator over CRSP Total Market denominator; Australia 13%, Canada 12%, Europe 13%, UK 12%
itemVerdicts.note: Re-downloaded the PDF from the cited corporate.vanguard.com URL (HTTP 200, 565,725 bytes) and re-extracted. Header line 1 reads "Vanguard research   August 2025"; title "Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing"; authors Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green. Figure 2, "Index fund assets as a percentage of market capitalization", column order United States / Australia / Canada / Europe / United Kingdom with values 23% / 13% / 12% / 13% / 12% — all five country figures match the claim exactly. Notes: "Data are as of December 31, 2024. U.S. equity fund market share is represented by assets of equity funds worldwide allocated to U.S. equities, plus assets of funds in a Morningstar global category containing 'U.S. Equity' in U.S. dollars. U.S. equity market capitalization is represented by the CRSP Total Market Index in U.S. dollars." Body text on p.4: "Figure 2 on page 5 shows the percentage of equity market capitalization held by equity index funds in several countries or regions." One drafting caution: the figure title and body say INDEX funds, but the methodology note itself says only "equity funds worldwide" without the word index — quote the title/body, not the note, when attributing the 23% to index funds.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fed staff paper (Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela, FEDS 2018-060r1, May 2020 draft): passive MFs+ETFs ~14% of domestic equity market as of March 2020, up from <4% in 2005; passive = 41% of fund AUM; 97% of ETF assets passive
itemVerdicts.note: Re-downloaded https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2018060r1pap.pdf (HTTP 200, 418,439 bytes). Cover: cite as FEDS 2018-060r1 (2020); title page "First draft: August 27, 2018 / This draft: May 15, 2020" — the r1/May-2020 attribution is correct. Verbatim: "As of March 2020, U.S. stocks held in passive MFs and ETFs accounted for about 14 percent of the domestic equity market, up from less than four percent in 2005." / "As of March 2020, passive funds accounted for 41 percent of combined U.S. MF and ETF assets under management (AUM), up from three percent in 1995 and 14 percent in 2005." / "As of March 2020, 97 percent of ETF assets were in passive funds (see Figure 1). Source: Morningstar, Inc." Two precision points: the 41% denominator is specifically combined U.S. MF and ETF AUM (not "fund AUM" generally), and the paper's very next sentences undercut any use of 14% as a ceiling — "The aggregate passive share, including passively managed holdings outside of MFs and ETFs, is still larger. For example, BlackRock (2017) estimated that passive investors owned 18 percent of all global equity at the end of 2016, with most of the holdings outside the MF and ETF sectors."

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Fed paper concentration stat: top ten passive managers ≈ 90% of passive AUM since 2004
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote 27, verbatim: "The high concentration for passive funds is also reflected in the combined market share of the ten largest passive-fund asset managers, which has averaged about 90 percent of total passive-fund industry AUM since 2004." Caliber is "has averaged about 90 percent ... since 2004" (a time-series average), not "has been 90% since 2004"; and the base is passive-fund industry AUM, not all fund AUM.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The Fed paper's four-channel risk taxonomy contains NO "price discovery / index bubble" channel
itemVerdicts.note: Half right, half wrong. RIGHT: there is no price-discovery / price-informativeness channel. The abstract lists exactly four: "(i) funds' liquidity and redemption risks, (ii) asset-market volatility, (iii) asset-management industry concentration, and (iv) comovement of asset returns and liquidity," and the intro's four are "(1) effects on funds' liquidity transformation and redemption risk...; (2) growth of passive investing strategies that amplify volatility; (3) increased asset-management industry concentration; and (4) changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement." Price discovery appears only in a survey sentence about other people's claims ("including claims about effects on industry concentration, asset prices, volatility, price discovery, market liquidity, competition, and corporate governance") — not as a channel the paper analyzes. WRONG: saying the taxonomy contains no "index bubble" channel. Channel 4 is titled "Changes in asset VALUATIONS, volatility, and comovement" (Section 4, p.21, and Table 1 row 4), and the index bubble is explicitly taken up inside it, verbatim: "First, in theory, rising prices can lead to more indexed investing, and the resulting 'index bubble' eventually could burst. However, the scope of such bubbles is probably limited insofar as index-inclusion effects on valuations are largely cross-sectional. That is, documented effects suggest that stock valuations become distorted relative to one another, not necessarily that broader aggregate valuations are distorted relative to fundamentals." Table 1 grades channel 4's financial-stability sign as "Uncertain." So the paper does not omit the index bubble — it addresses and largely deflates it, which is a stronger fact for the article than the false omission claim.

corrections: Sub-claim (d) must be split. Correct version: the Fed paper's four channels are (1) funds' liquidity transformation and redemption risk, (2) passive strategies that amplify volatility, (3) asset-management industry concentration, and (4) changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement — none of which is a price-discovery / price-informativeness channel. Do NOT write that the taxonomy has no 'index bubble' channel: the index bubble is discussed inside channel (4), where the paper concludes 'the scope of such bubbles is probably limited insofar as index-inclusion effects on valuations are largely cross-sectional' and Table 1 grades the channel's financial-stability sign as 'Uncertain.'

Sub-claim (c): the 41% figure is 'passive funds accounted for 41 percent of combined U.S. MF and ETF assets under management (AUM)' as of March 2020 — write 'combined US mutual fund and ETF AUM', not the looser 'fund AUM'. Also date-stamp the 97% ETF figure as March 2020.

Sub-claim (c) must carry the Fed's own caveat or it misrepresents the source: immediately after the 14% figure the paper writes 'The aggregate passive share, including passively managed holdings outside of MFs and ETFs, is still larger,' citing BlackRock (2017)'s estimate that passive investors owned 18 percent of all global equity at end-2016 'with most of the holdings outside the MF and ETF sectors.' The 14% cannot be presented as the Fed's estimate of total passive ownership.

Sub-claim (b) must carry Vanguard's own footnote 2, or the 23% is presented more confidently than Vanguard presents it: 'We recognize an alternative estimate of the proportion of equity market capitalization held by passive equity strategies attributed to Chinco and Sammon (2024). Our estimate considers only mutual fund and ETF assets, as it allows us to provide a consistent estimate for markets outside the U.S.'

Sub-claim (a): specify that ICI's numerator is index DOMESTIC EQUITY mutual funds and ETFs only (US-equity sleeves of global, international, allocation and target-date index funds are excluded), and that the denominator is US stock market capitalization sourced from the World Federation of Exchanges. Without those qualifiers the 19% reads as total passive ownership, which ICI does not claim.

If the article prints the ICI series, either print it in full (2015-2025 = 11, 12, 13, 13, 16, 15, 17, 18, 18, 18, 19) or avoid describing it as steadily rising — it dips from 16% in 2019 to 15% in 2020.

Attribution hygiene: cite the Vanguard piece as Rowley, Lawrence and Ryder-Green, 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing,' Vanguard research, August 2025. Cite the Fed paper as FEDS 2018-060r1 (draft of May 15, 2020) and note it was published as Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe and Osambela, 'The Shift from Active to Passive Investing: Risks to Financial Stability?', Financial Analysts Journal 76(4), 23-39 (2020) — the article should not imply it is only an unpublished working paper.
newContradictions: Chinco and Sammon, 'The passive ownership share is double what you think it is,' Journal of Financial Economics 157 (2024) 103860 — peer-reviewed and published, and the headline number did NOT change from the April 7, 2024 working paper. Verbatim from the published PDF: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%,' and 'Our 33.5% estimate for the US passive ownership share is more than double the ICI's index-fund ownership share of 16%.' They further state that adding $2.25t of internally indexed assets they lack data on would take 33.5% to 38.5%. Any passage presenting ICI's 19% / Vanguard's 23% / the Fed's 14% as THE market-cap caliber must acknowledge this published rival estimate on the same market-cap caliber, or it is cherry-picking the low end of a live dispute. Note the year mismatch: C-S is 2021, ICI's 19% is YE2025.

All three low-caliber sources self-identify as lower bounds — the Fed paper ('the aggregate passive share ... is still larger'), Vanguard (footnote 2 conceding Chinco-Sammon and limiting itself to 'only mutual fund and ETF assets'), and ICI implicitly via its domestic-equity-fund-only numerator. The article cannot use them as a refutation of 'passive owns half the market' without conceding that none of them measures total passive ownership.

Supporting find that strengthens the article's central point: ICI Figure 2.5 is the source of the '52%' that gets misreported as 'passive owns half the market' — 'At year-end 2025, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for the majority (52%) of assets in long-term funds, up from 19% at year-end 2010,' on a base of $36.6 trillion in long-term fund total net assets. That is share of FUND ASSETS, not share of market cap. Chinco-Sammon's 33.5-38.5% is still well short of half, so the article's core distinction survives even on the high caliber.
reasoning: I re-downloaded all three cited primary documents rather than relying on the local extractions, and verified every load-bearing string in the freshly extracted text: the 2026 ICI Fact Book chapter 2 (via www.icifactbook.org — the bare host 403s), the Vanguard August 2025 paper, and FEDS 2018-060r1. For the ICI series I did not trust flat text extraction, because pdftotext interleaves the three stacked-bar label rows of Figure 2.6 at overlapping y-positions; I instead ran pdftotext -bbox on file page 8 and matched each label's x-center to the year-axis label x-centers, which pins the index row to 11, 12, 13, 13, 16, 15, 17, 18, 18, 18, 19 for 2015-2025 and independently confirms 2015=11, 2019=16, 2023=18, 2024=18, 2025=19. Everything in (a), (b), (c) and the concentration stat in (d) checks out verbatim, including all five Vanguard country figures, the Dec 31 2024 as-of date, the CRSP Total Market denominator, the May 15 2020 draft date, and the four Fed numbers. The one substantive failure is the taxonomy half of (d): I grepped the Fed paper for 'bubble' and found an explicit 'index bubble' discussion on p.21 inside channel 4, whose body-and-Table-1 title is 'changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement' (the abstract compresses this to 'comovement of asset returns and liquidity', which is what makes the omission claim look plausible). The paper does not omit the index bubble; it addresses and largely deflates it. Separately I checked working-paper-vs-published status on both sides of the dispute: the Fed paper was published in Financial Analysts Journal 76(4) 23-39 (2020), and Chinco-Sammon was published in JFE 157 (2024) 103860 with the 33.5%/38.5% figures unchanged from the April 2024 draft — I fetched the JFE PDF from alexchinco.com and read the abstract and introduction directly rather than accepting a search summary. Residual uncertainty: I did not obtain the paywalled Elsevier or Taylor & Francis typeset copies, only the authors'/Fed-hosted PDFs of the same articles, so I cannot rule out copy-edit-level differences in the published texts; and I did not attempt to reconcile why Chinco-Sammon cite ICI's 2021 index share as 16% while the 2026 Fact Book's Figure 2.6 now shows 17% for 2021 — most likely an ICI revision across fact-book vintages, but I did not confirm that against the 2022 or 2023 fact books.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ICI: index domestic equity MFs+ETFs held 19% of US stock market value at YE2025; series 2015=11, 2019=16, 2023=18, 2024=18, 2025=19; active another 11%; other investors 69%
itemVerdicts.note: Re-fetched https://icifactbook.org/pdf/2026-factbook-ch2.pdf today (1,203,257 bytes) and extracted with pdftotext -layout. Body text verbatim: "index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs remain relatively small investors in the US stock markets, holding 19% of the value of US stocks at year-end 2025 (Figure 2.6). Actively managed domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs held another 11%, while other investors—including hedge funds, pension funds, life insurance companies, and individuals—held the majority (69%)." I parsed Figure 2.6 by character column against the year axis to avoid misreading the stacked bars: index row = 2015:11, 2016:12, 2017:13, 2018:13, 2019:16, 2020:15, 2021:17, 2022:18, 2023:18, 2024:18, 2025:19. Active row = 18,17,16,15,16,15,15,14,13,12,11. Other = 71,71,71,71,68,69,68,69,68,70,69. Every value in the claim matches. Cross-checked the 2025 Fact Book ch2 (fetched separately) — it shows 2014=10 and the identical 2015-2024 series plus text "holding only 18 percent of the value of US stocks at year-end 2024... another 12 percent... the majority (70 percent)", so ICI has not restated. Figure sources line: "Investment Company Institute and World Federation of Exchanges" (i.e., WFE market cap is the denominator). CALIBER NOTE, not an error: the numerator is index DOMESTIC equity MFs+ETFs only — it excludes the US-equity sleeves of index global/international and balanced/target-date funds, and excludes all non-fund index vehicles (CITs, index separate accounts, direct indexing). That is precisely why Vanguard gets 23% and Chinco-Sammon 33.5%.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Vanguard Aug 2025 "Setting the record straight": 23% US as of Dec 31 2024, numerator = worldwide funds' US-equity allocations, denominator = CRSP Total Market; Australia 13%, Canada 12%, Europe 13%, UK 12%
itemVerdicts.note: Re-fetched the Vanguard PDF today (565,856 bytes). Header line verbatim: "Vanguard research    August 2025" / "Setting the record straight: / The truths about index fund investing" (doc code ISGTAI 082025). Figure 2, titled "Index fund assets as a percentage of market capitalization", shows United States 23%, Australia 13%, Canada 12%, Europe 13%, United Kingdom 12% — all five match. Notes verbatim: "Data are as of December 31, 2024. U.S. equity fund market share is represented by assets of equity funds worldwide allocated to U.S. equities, plus assets of funds in a Morningstar global category containing "U.S. Equity" in U.S. dollars. U.S. equity market capitalization is represented by the CRSP Total Market Index in U.S. dollars." and "Registered fund assets are as represented by Morningstar and exclude funds of funds." The claim's description of the broader numerator and CRSP denominator is exact. IMPORTANT CAVEAT the article must carry: Vanguard's own footnote 2 reads verbatim "We recognize an alternative estimate of the proportion of equity market capitalization held by passive equity strategies attributed to Chinco and Sammon (2024). Our estimate considers only mutual fund and ETF assets, as it allows us to provide a consistent estimate for markets outside the U.S." So 23% is registered-fund-only by Vanguard's own admission and is not an upper bound on passive ownership.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fed staff paper (Anadu et al., FEDS 2018-060r1): passive MFs+ETFs ~14% of domestic equity market as of March 2020, up from <4% in 2005; passive = 41% of fund AUM; 97% of ETF assets passive
itemVerdicts.note: Re-fetched https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2018060r1pap.pdf today (418,439 bytes) rather than trusting the local anadu.txt; the local extraction matched the fresh one on all three strings. Verbatim: "As of March 2020, U.S. stocks held in passive MFs and ETFs accounted for about 14 percent of the domestic equity market, up from less than four percent in 2005." Footnote 4 to that sentence: "These figures are based on the authors' calculations using Bloomberg, Morningstar, Inc., and Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA) data." Verbatim: "passive funds accounted for 41 percent of combined U.S. MF and ETF assets under management (AUM), up from three percent in 1995 and 14 percent in 2005" — note the denominator is combined US MF+ETF AUM across ALL asset classes, not equity funds only. Verbatim (Figure 1 note): "As of March 2020, 97 percent of ETF assets were in passive funds (see Figure 1). Source: Morningstar, Inc." Cover/draft dates: "First draft: August 27, 2018 / This draft: May 15, 2020", cite-as line gives FEDS 2018-060r1, DOI 10.17016/FEDS.2018.060r1. One attribution wrinkle: the Fed's own landing page dates the revision "August 2018 (Revised June 2020)" even though the PDF's internal draft date is May 15, 2020; and a published version exists — Financial Analysts Journal Vol. 76, No. 4 (2020), "The Shift from Active to Passive Investing: Risks to Financial Stability?" I could not read the FAJ text (paywalled), so I cannot confirm the published version carries the same 14/41/97 figures.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) The Fed paper's four-channel taxonomy contains NO price discovery / index bubble channel; top ten passive managers ≈90% of passive AUM since 2004
itemVerdicts.note: The concentration stat is exact — verbatim from the fresh PDF: "The high concentration for passive funds is also reflected in the combined market share of the ten largest passive-fund asset managers, which has averaged about 90 percent of total passive-fund industry AUM since 2004." (it is a footnote to the Figure 4 concentration discussion, and it is an AVERAGE since 2004, not a point-in-time 2020 figure). The taxonomy claim is where caliber slips. WRONG as stated: implying the taxonomy has no channel touching prices/valuations. RIGHT: no channel is named "price discovery" or "index bubble", but channel 4 is explicitly a VALUATION channel. The paper states its four channels twice with slightly different wording. Abstract verbatim: "(i) funds' liquidity and redemption risks, (ii) asset-market volatility, (iii) asset-management industry concentration, and (iv) comovement of asset returns and liquidity." Introduction verbatim: "(1) effects on funds' liquidity transformation and redemption risk, particularly in the MF and ETF sectors; (2) growth of passive investing strategies that amplify volatility; (3) increased asset-management industry concentration; and (4) changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement." Section 4 is headed "4. Changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement" and its Table 4 has a row literally labeled "Valuation" — "Price of asset increases (decreases) when it is added to (removed from) index" — with the evidence column reading "For equities, valuation effects have declined significantly since 2000; for bonds, little research to date". Table 1 scores channel 4's impact on financial stability as "Uncertain" (vs Reduces / Increases / Increases for channels 1-3). Also, the paper's intro explicitly acknowledges price discovery as part of the surrounding literature: "The shift to passive investing has sparked wide-ranging research and commentary, including claims about effects on industry concentration, asset prices, volatility, price discovery, market liquidity, competition, and corporate governance."

corrections: Fix (d): do not say the Fed paper's taxonomy has no channel touching prices. Say instead: the four channels are (1) liquidity transformation and redemption risk, (2) passive strategies that amplify volatility, (3) asset-management industry concentration, and (4) 'changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement' — none of which is framed as price discovery or an index bubble. Channel 4 is a valuation channel: its Table 4 'Valuation' row covers index-inclusion price effects and reports that 'For equities, valuation effects have declined significantly since 2000', and Table 1 scores channel 4's net financial-stability impact as 'Uncertain'.

Qualify the Fed 90% stat as an average, not a level: 'the combined market share of the ten largest passive-fund asset managers ... has averaged about 90 percent of total passive-fund industry AUM since 2004' — and note it appears in a footnote to the paper's concentration figure, not as a headline finding.
Specify the Fed 41% denominator: passive = 41% of combined U.S. mutual fund AND ETF AUM across all asset classes as of March 2020 (up from 3% in 1995 and 14% in 2005) — not 41% of equity fund assets.

Spell out the ICI numerator so the 19% is not read as total passive ownership: it counts index DOMESTIC equity mutual funds and ETFs only, over World Federation of Exchanges US market cap. It excludes the US-equity sleeves of index global/international and balanced/target-date funds and all non-fund index vehicles (collective investment trusts, index separate accounts, internally managed institutional index portfolios, direct indexing).

Whenever citing Vanguard's 23%, carry Vanguard's own footnote 2 verbatim or in substance: 'We recognize an alternative estimate of the proportion of equity market capitalization held by passive equity strategies attributed to Chinco and Sammon (2024). Our estimate considers only mutual fund and ETF assets, as it allows us to provide a consistent estimate for markets outside the U.S.' Presenting 23% as a ceiling on passive ownership misrepresents the source that produced it.

Do not let 19% / 23% / 14% stand as the sole rebuttal to 'passive owns half the market'. Chinco and Sammon (April 7, 2024, 'The Passive Ownership Share Is Double What You Think It Is') state verbatim: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%', rising to 38.5% if less popular indexes are included. The fund-based and strategy-based numerators measure different things; the honest framing is a range (roughly 19-23% in registered funds vs ~33-38% including internal indexing and closet indexing), not a single refuting number.

Attribution precision on the Fed paper: the PDF's internal date line is 'First draft: August 27, 2018 / This draft: May 15, 2020', but the Federal Reserve's own landing page dates it 'August 2018 (Revised June 2020)'. Safest wording is 'FEDS 2018-060r1, revised 2020'. Also acknowledge the published version: Financial Analysts Journal 76(4), 2020, 'The Shift from Active to Passive Investing: Risks to Financial Stability?' (I could not verify whether the published version carries the same 14%/41%/97% figures — it is paywalled).
newContradictions: Chinco and Sammon (2024), 'The Passive Ownership Share Is Double What You Think It Is', abstract verbatim: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%. Our headline number is twice as large because it reflects index funds as well as other kinds of passive investors, such as institutional investors with internally managed index portfolios and active managers who are closet indexing.' Body adds that including less popular indexes would raise 33.5% to 38.5%. This does not falsify the ICI/Vanguard/Fed numbers but it directly contradicts using them as the passive ownership share.

Vanguard itself concedes the point in footnote 2 of the very paper being cited for 23%, stating its estimate 'considers only mutual fund and ETF assets'. The article cannot cite Vanguard's 23% as a debunk while omitting Vanguard's own acknowledgement of the Chinco-Sammon alternative.

The Fed paper does contain a valuation/index-inclusion analysis (Section 4, Table 4), so it cannot be cited as evidence that regulators never examined whether indexing distorts prices. What it can support is the narrower and better-documented point that the Fed found equity index-inclusion valuation effects have 'declined significantly since 2000' and rated the overall valuation/comovement channel 'Uncertain'.

The three headline shares are not comparable and must not be presented as a converging series: ICI 19% = index domestic equity MFs+ETFs / WFE US market cap at YE2025; Vanguard 23% = worldwide equity funds' US-equity allocations / CRSP Total Market at 12/31/2024; Fed 14% = US stocks in passive MFs+ETFs / SIFMA domestic equity market at March 2020 (authors' calculations from Bloomberg, Morningstar and SIFMA data). Different numerators, different denominators, different dates.
reasoning: I refused to rely on the pre-extracted local files for the load-bearing numbers and re-downloaded all three primary PDFs today, extracting with pdftotext -layout: the ICI 2026 Fact Book chapter 2 (1,203,257 bytes), the Vanguard August 2025 white paper (565,856 bytes), and FEDS 2018-060r1 (418,439 bytes). For the ICI stacked bar chart I did not eyeball the extracted digits — I parsed each row's character offsets in Python and aligned them to the year-axis offsets, because a stacked bar in a text dump is exactly where a year-to-value mis-mapping would hide. All eleven index-share values, all eleven active values and all eleven other-investor values reconcile to ~100 per year, and the 2025 Fact Book (fetched separately) reproduces the overlapping 2015-2024 series and its own YE2024 text (18/12/70), so there is no restatement. Every quoted string in my item notes is one I saw byte-for-byte in a freshly fetched document; I quoted nothing from a web-fetch summary. Three sub-claims survive verbatim with no slippage. The one that fails is (d): the assertion that the taxonomy contains no price-discovery/index-bubble channel is defensible only as a statement about channel NAMES. Channel 4 is titled 'Changes in asset valuations, volatility, and comovement', Section 4 is devoted to index-inclusion effects, and Table 4's first row is labeled 'Valuation' and describes prices rising on index addition. The paper's actual finding there — equity valuation effects 'have declined significantly since 2000', net stability impact 'Uncertain' — supports the article's thesis better than the overstated version does, so the fix costs nothing and removes an attack surface. Two further caliber problems that the claim group as written does not flag: the three percentages are constructed from three different numerators, denominators and dates and cannot be strung together as one series; and both ICI's 19% and Vanguard's 23% are registered-fund-only measures, which Vanguard concedes in footnote 2 while pointing at Chinco-Sammon's 33.5% (38.5% including less popular indexes). Presenting 19-23% as the refutation of 'passive owns half' without that range invites a well-sourced rebuttal. Remaining uncertainty: I could not read the paywalled Financial Analysts Journal 76(4) 2020 version of the Anadu et al. paper, so I cannot confirm the 14%/41%/97% figures survived into print — the article should cite the FEDS working paper explicitly, as it currently does, rather than the FAJ article. I also did not attempt to reconcile ICI's visible 2018→2019 jump (13→16) in the index share; it appears identically in both the 2025 and 2026 Fact Books, so it is ICI's own series behavior and not an extraction artifact, but I have no ICI methodology note explaining it.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ICI 2026 Fact Book ch.2: index domestic equity MFs+ETFs held 19% of US stock market value at YE2025; active 11%; other 69%; series 2015=11, 2019=16, 2023=18, 2024=18, 2025=19
itemVerdicts.note: I re-downloaded https://icifactbook.org/pdf/2026-factbook-ch2.pdf myself and read the sentence verbatim: 'index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs remain relatively small investors in the US stock markets, holding 19% of the value of US stocks at year-end 2025 (Figure 2.6). Figure 2.6 is titled 'Index Domestic Equity Fund Share of US Stock Market Is Small / Percentage of US stock market capitalization, year-end'; sources line: 'Investment Company Institute and World Federation of Exchanges'. Plain pdftotext scrambles stacked-bar labels, so I parsed the chart with pdftotext -bbox-layout and matched each label to its year by x-coordinate. Index row: 2015=11, 2016=12, 2017=13, 2018=13, 2019=16, 2020=15, 2021=17, 2022=18, 2023=18, 2024=18, 2025=19. Active row: 18,17,16,15,16,15,15,14,13,12,11. Other row: 71,71,71,71,68,69,68,69,68,70,69. Every year the article cites matches. Cross-checked against the 2025 Fact Book chapter 2 (same figure, series 2014-2024): 2014=10, 2015=11, ..., 2019=16, 2020=15, ..., 2024=18, with text 'holding only 18 percent of the value of US stocks at year-end 2024 ... another 12 percent ... (70 percent)'. So the counterintuitive 2019=16 then 2020=15 dip is ICI's own series, not an extraction artifact.
