itemVerdicts.item: (a) Vanguard (Aug 2025): index fund portfolio-management trading = 1.2% of total US exchange dollar volume in 2024, up from 0.3% in 2006; active funds 2-5%
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the Vanguard PDF (local extraction vg.txt / v_vg.txt / vanguard2025.txt, all byte-identical, 69,905 bytes; header line 1: 'Vanguard research   August 2025'; title 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing'; authors Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green). Body text: 'Trading volume has slowly increased from about $38 trillion in 2006 to about $153 trillion in 2024. During that period, active fund volume remained between 2% and 5% of total trading volume, while index fund trading volume slowly grew from about 0.3% of total volume to 1.2%.' Note for the article: the SAME paragraph gives the current active figure as 2%, not 2-5% ('Although active fund trading volume is higher (2% of total volume)'); 2-5% is the 2006-2024 RANGE, not a current level. Also the prose rounds index funds to 'just over 1% of total trading activity'; 1.2% is the 2024 chart endpoint.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont) Definition = cash-flow-adjusted turnover / Cboe total volume
itemVerdicts.note: Figure 6 note verbatim: 'Data are as of December 31, 2024. The percentage of total trading volume is cash-flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume. Data include all available equity open-end funds and ETFs with U.S. equity exposure from January 1, 2006, through December 31, 2024, in each category as defined by Morningstar. Data include net assets, turnover ratio, net flow, and U.S. equity exposure data from Morningstar, along with total trading volume on U.S. exchanges from Cboe Exchange. Sources: Vanguard calculations, using data from Morningstar, Inc., and Cboe Exchange, Inc.; originally published in Rowley, Zorina, and Zhu (2019).' Numerator/denominator as claimed.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont) The 1.2% metric EXCLUDES ETF secondary-market trading, index derivatives, and indexed separate accounts
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG to attribute this exclusion list to the Vanguard PDF: the PDF never states it. RIGHT: it is an inference from the stated methodology — the body says Figure 6 shows volume 'attributable to the portfolio management of index and active funds' and the note defines the metric as fund-level cash-flow-adjusted TURNOVER of Morningstar open-end funds and ETFs, which is portfolio (primary-market) trading only. The exclusions are separately corroborated by Vanguard's own statement in the Institutional Investor piece: 'Even after accounting for indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds and removing trading volume due to [high-frequency trading] and shares of ETFs, we estimate that indexing represents less than 5 percent...' — i.e. Vanguard itself treats indexed separate accounts and ETF share trading as outside the base-case number. Present the exclusions as inference/corroboration, not as a Vanguard statement in the PDF.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont) Verbatim conclusion: 'the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false.'
itemVerdicts.note: Exact, verified in vg.txt (text is line-wrapped in the two-column PDF but reads continuously): 'Index funds are an important source of ownership, but the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false. Index fund investing leaves ample room for price discovery.' The section heading is 'The growth of index fund investing doesn't inhibit price discovery' and the figure title is 'Index fund trading volume is a drop in the bucket.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) ICI 2026 Fact Book: ETF secondary-market trading averaged 28% of total US stock market trading in 2025; series 25-32% since 2016
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers CONFIRMED by fresh independent download of the exact cited URL (re-extracted with pdftotext -layout from a 4,051,734-byte PDF, matching the pre-existing local ici2026qf.txt). Chart title verbatim: 'ETF Secondary Market Trading Averaged 28% of Daily US Stock Trading in 2025'; subtitle 'Average daily ETF share of total US stock market trading, percentage, annual'; yearly values 2016-2025 = 27, 25, 27, 27, 26, 25, 32, 30, 27, 28 — so the 25-32% range is right. TWO caliber corrections: (1) WRONG 'ICI 2026 Fact Book'; RIGHT '2026 Investment Company Fact Book: Quick Facts Guide' — that is the document at the cited URL and where this chart appears. (2) The series is ALL ETFs, not passive/index ETFs; the accompanying text is generic ('Retail investors access ETFs through the secondary market... ETFs' share of trading volume increased somewhat, which was likely related to elevated market volatility'). Filing 28% under 'passive's share of trading' silently includes active, leveraged and inverse ETFs.

itemVerdicts.item: (b-cont) Denominator comparability with (a)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG to present 1.2% and 28% as points on one continuous scale without noting the denominators differ. ICI's text says ETF secondary trading 'is a substantial share of total trading on US stock exchanges AND OTHER VENUES' and the chart denominator is 'total US stock market trading' (exchange + off-exchange). Vanguard's denominator is 'total U.S. exchange trading volume' from Cboe. RIGHT: state that the low end uses an exchange-only denominator and the high end an all-venue denominator, so the spread is partly a denominator artifact on top of the numerator-definition artifact.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) SSGA (Jan 23, 2026, 'Closing time'): US MOC volume rose from 8.40% (Jan 2018) to 15.39% (Dec 2025)
itemVerdicts.note: Date, title and byline CONFIRMED (page header: 'Closing time: How passive investing is reshaping equity market microstructure', 'January 23, 2026', Elise Ryan). The two numbers exist and I re-fetched the page a second time independently to confirm the table. BUT the date basis is WRONG. The figure is titled 'Figure 2: Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume – USA versus Developed Europe versus APAC' and its row labels are 'From Jan 2018', 'From Jan 2019', '1 Year', 'Q4 2025', '25-Dec'. US Close% by row: 8.40 / 9.24 / 12.11 / 13.10 / 15.39. So WRONG: '8.40% of total volume in January 2018'. RIGHT: 8.40% is the daily-average US closing-auction share over the whole window SINCE January 2018; 15.39% is the December 2025 average. Source line: 'Instinet as of December 31, 2025. Last two hours figures exclude closing auction.' The article's own prose confirms the endpoint: 'Developed Europe allocates roughly 34.82 percent of daily volume to the closing auction, compared with 15.39 percent in the United States and 16.78 percent in Asia ex Japan.' Safest fix: quote SSGA's label rather than inventing a start-date reading.

itemVerdicts.item: (c-cont) The SSGA piece gives NO passive share of MOC volume
itemVerdicts.note: Correct — I read the full page text end to end. Every quantitative figure is a regional close/open/last-two-hours share of total volume; no figure decomposes MOC volume into passive vs active. The passive linkage is asserted causally and hedged ('likely driven in large part by the expansion of indexing'; 'If the rise of Market-on-Close volume is best viewed as a structural response to the growth of indexing...'). The piece in fact argues active managers migrate to the close too, which further inflates MOC without being passive.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Institutional Investor (Jan 3, 2025): Green estimates passive direct trading 20% + index derivatives 8% + passive market making 36% vs active managers 10%, down from 80% in 1995
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the article (local ii.txt, headline 'Why Michael Green Is Known as the Cassandra of Passive Investing', by Michelle Celarier, January 3, 2025): 'Using statistics compiled from various market and academic sources, Green estimates that passive direct trading now accounts for about 20 percent of all trading, passive index derivatives make up 8 percent, and passive market making contributes a further 36 percent. By contrast, trading by active managers totals only 10 percent, down from 80 percent in 1995.' No later retraction or revision found in searches up to 2026-08.

itemVerdicts.item: (d-cont) Vanguard's statement in the same article: index funds ~1% and all-in indexing <5% of volume
itemVerdicts.note: Quote CONFIRMED verbatim: 'Our base case estimates that index funds account for approximately 1 percent of overall trading volume on U.S. exchanges, well below the more widely quoted 5 percent to 7 percent. Even after accounting for indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds and removing trading volume due to [high-frequency trading] and shares of ETFs, we estimate that indexing represents less than 5 percent of overall U.S. trading volume.' CORRECTION to how it is used: the <5% is NOT an all-in figure on a common denominator — Vanguard adds indexed separate accounts to the numerator while STRIPPING HFT and ETF share trading out of the denominator. Green's 64% keeps HFT/market-making inside the denominator (indeed 36 of his 64 points ARE market making). So the '1% vs 64%' contrast is not apples-to-apples in either direction and must be labeled as such.

itemVerdicts.item: Umbrella framing: passive's share of trading spans 1.2% to 64% depending on definition
itemVerdicts.note: The 1.2% and the components of 64% are all real and sourced. But 64% appears nowhere as a figure — it is the article's own sum of Green's three components (20+8+36). WRONG: attributing '64%' to Green as a stated estimate. RIGHT: 'Green's components sum to 64%.' Also flag that his largest component, 'passive market making' at 36%, is not passive investors trading at all — it is intermediary volume Green attributes to passive-driven flow — so the top of the range is a causal attribution, not a measurement of passive orders.

corrections: SSGA date basis (most important): do not write '8.40% of total volume in January 2018'. SSGA's Figure 2 is titled 'Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume' and the row is labeled 'From Jan 2018'. Write: US closing-auction volume averaged 8.40% of daily volume over the period since January 2018 and reached 15.39% in December 2025 (Instinet data as of December 31, 2025). The actual January-2018 level is not disclosed.

Attribute the exclusion list correctly: the Vanguard PDF never states that its 1.2% excludes ETF secondary-market trading, index derivatives and indexed separate accounts. It states only that the metric is 'cash flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume' for Morningstar open-end funds and ETFs, described in the body as volume 'attributable to the portfolio management of index and active funds'. Present the exclusions as an inference, corroborated by Vanguard's separate statement to Institutional Investor about 'removing trading volume due to [HFT] and shares of ETFs'.

Active-fund figure: '2-5%' is Vanguard's 2006-2024 range, not a current level. The same paragraph puts active fund trading at 2% of total volume currently. Say 'active funds ran 2%-5% over 2006-2024 and sit at about 2% today.'
Source name for (b): the cited URL is the '2026 Investment Company Fact Book: Quick Facts Guide', not the Fact Book proper. Cite it by that name.
ICI's 28% covers ALL ETFs — including active, leveraged and inverse ETFs — not index ETFs. Do not present it as a passive share without that qualifier.

Denominator mismatch: Vanguard's 1.2% is over Cboe US EXCHANGE volume; ICI's 28% is over 'total US stock market trading' on 'US stock exchanges and other venues' (exchange plus off-exchange). Note this when placing them on one range, or the spread is partly an artifact of the denominator, not just the definition.

64% is the article's arithmetic sum of Green's three components (20+8+36), not a figure Green states in the piece. Say so. And note that his largest component — 'passive market making', 36% — is intermediary volume attributed to passive flow, not passive investors' own orders.

Vanguard's '<5%' from the II article is not a like-for-like all-in number: it adds indexed portfolio management outside registered funds to the numerator while removing HFT and ETF share trading from the denominator. State the adjustment, otherwise the 1%-vs-64% contrast reads as a measurement dispute when it is largely a definitional one.
newContradictions: SSGA's 'Closing time' undercuts the implied passive-drives-the-close story in a way the article should not suppress: it explicitly says active managers migrate to the close too and that 'This migration by active managers further amplifies MOC volumes, reinforcing the trend.' So rising MOC share is not a clean proxy for passive share.

ICI's own explanation for the peak year cuts against a passive-growth reading of its series: the 2022 jump to 32% is attributed to 'elevated market volatility, as investors often turn to ETFs to quickly transfer or hedge investment risk', and the share then DECLINED to 27-28% while passive AUM kept growing. The series is roughly flat 2016-2025 (25-28% outside the 2022-23 bulge), which is evidence against ETF trading share tracking passive asset growth.

The Vanguard PDF's own Figure 6 shows total US exchange volume quadrupling ($38T in 2006 to $153T in 2024) alongside the index share rising 0.3%->1.2%. A rising share of a quadrupled base means index-fund portfolio trading grew roughly 16x in dollars — the 'drop in the bucket' framing is a share statement only, and the article should not let it imply flat absolute activity.
reasoning: Reached all four primary documents. (a) Vanguard 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing', August 2025 — read the full price-discovery section and Figure 6 note verbatim from the local pdftotext extraction (four byte-identical copies: vg.txt, v_vg.txt, vg_v.txt, vanguard2025.txt). Confirmed 0.3%->1.2%, active 2-5% over the window (2% currently), $38T->$153T, 'cash flow adjusted turnover / total U.S. exchange trading volume', Cboe source, and the 'demonstrably false' sentence exactly. Also checked the other '1.2%' occurrence in the file (line 208) — it is an unrelated y-axis label on Figure 1 (expense ratios), not a duplicate of the trading figure. (b) ICI — I did not rely on the pre-existing local extraction alone: I re-downloaded the exact cited URL (direct curl was blocked with a 457-byte stub, but WebFetch retrieved the real 4,051,734-byte PDF, which I then ran through pdftotext -layout myself) and read the chart region as document text, not as a fetch summary. Chart title, subtitle, the 'averaged 28% in 2025' sentence and all ten annual values reproduced identically to the local file. (c) SSGA — read the full page text; re-fetched the page a second time through an independent path and confirmed the Figure 2 table byte-for-byte before concluding the row-label issue. The row labels 'From Jan 2018 / From Jan 2019 / 1 Year / Q4 2025 / 25-Dec' under a figure titled 'Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume' are period averages of decreasing length; a 'January 2018 point value' reading would require one mixed row type among four averages and is not what the label says. Confirmed no passive share of MOC volume appears anywhere in the piece. (d) Institutional Investor — read the actual paragraphs; both the Green decomposition and the Vanguard statement are verbatim. Searched for post-publication revisions to Green's estimates and for competing 2026 trading-share measurements; found none that alter these figures (the only Green update surfaced concerns passive OWNERSHIP share, ~53-54% of market cap, not trading share). Residual uncertainty: the SSGA row-label reading is a strong inference from the label plus the figure title, not from an explicit methodology note — SSGA publishes no note defining 'From Jan 2018', so the safe fix is to reproduce SSGA's label rather than assert either reading. I could not locate a source note under the ICI chart in the layout extraction, so the precise venue coverage of its denominator rests on the body sentence 'total trading on US stock exchanges and other venues'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Morningstar: passive US long-term fund+ETF assets passed active at END-2023, $13.29T vs $13.23T; $60bn margin, ~0.2% of a $26.5T base; money market funds excluded; Morningstar editorial classification
itemVerdicts.note: Date and pair both reach primary/citable confirmation. Morningstar's own article (published 2024-01-17, 'It's Official: Passive Funds Overtake Active Funds', morningstar.com/funds/recovery-us-fund-flows-was-weak-2023) says verbatim: 'After steadily encroaching on active funds' turf for years, passive funds closed 2023 with more assets.' The article TEXT does not print the dollar pair — it lives in the embedded chart (cloudfront .../ZY3STRQTZNHPLBHE6DFJMGE46I.png, 'A line chart of active assets versus passive assets from 1993 through 2023'), which I downloaded and read: axis in $Bil, green Passive crosses above orange Active only at the very right edge at roughly 13,300 — consistent, but unlabeled. The numeric pair is confirmed by CNBC 2024-01-18 (Jeff Cox) verbatim: 'The total assets under management in exchange-traded funds and notes along with passively managed mutual funds reached a combined $13.29 trillion at the end of December, nudging above the $13.23 trillion held in active assets, according to Morningstar.' Morningstar re-affirms the year twice more: its Jan-2025 piece 'After overtaking active fund assets for the first time ever in 2023...', and its Dec-2025 monthly report 'Since passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023...'. Arithmetic checks: 13.29-13.23 = $60bn; base 26.52T; 60/26,520 = 0.226%, so '~0.2%' is fair. MMF exclusion confirmed verbatim in the Morningstar report footnote: '1 Long-term funds exclude money market funds.' MISSING QUALIFIER (see corrections): Morningstar ALSO excludes funds of funds — disclosure page: 'This report includes both mutual funds and exchange-traded funds but not funds of funds unless specifically stated. It does not include collective investment trusts or separate accounts.' That exclusion is what makes Morningstar's crossover date differ from ICI's.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The equity-only crossover was earlier, ~August 2019 ($4.27T vs $4.25T, US equity funds only)
itemVerdicts.note: Reached the primary document: Morningstar Direct Fund Flows Commentary: United States, August 2019 (www.morningstar.com/content/dam/marketing/shared/pdfs/Research/Fund_Flows_August2019_Final.pdf), page 2, verbatim: 'Preliminary numbers show that passive U.S. equity assets passed active U.S. equity assets by about $25 billion. (At the time of publication, we were still waiting for 70 or so funds, including all of Artisan's funds, to report their total net assets as of month-end.) If this result holds, passive share of U.S. equity open-end and ETF assets would be 50.15% versus 49.85% for active funds.' Exhibit 1 on the same page gives US Equity category-group assets = $8,517 Bil at Aug. 31, 2019. 50.15% x 8,517 = $4,271B and 49.85% x 8,517 = $4,246B — i.e. exactly the $4.27T / $4.25T pair reported contemporaneously by Citywire ('By the end of August, passive US funds had total net assets of $4.27 trillion, compared with $4.25 trillion in active US equity funds, according to data provided by Morningstar') and ThinkAdvisor 2019-09-20 ('As of Aug. 31, the assets of mutual funds and ETFs invested in U.S. equity index funds totaled $4.27 trillion, more than the $4.25 trillion invested in actively managed U.S. equity funds'). So the pair is Morningstar's, internally consistent, and the scope 'US equity funds only' is right. TRAP AVOIDED: the rounded pair implies a $20bn gap; Morningstar's stated gap is 'about $25 billion' (rounding artifact of 4.271 vs 4.246). Also: Morningstar had prematurely called parity in May 2019 — its April-2019 commentary says 'Passive U.S. equity funds had assets of $4.305 trillion by month-end, just $6 billion shy of active U.S. equity funds' $4.311 trillion,' and Aug-2019 was labelled PRELIMINARY.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Morningstar Dec-2025 US Fund Flows report: passive 'over 55%' of net assets at YE2025 ($19.42T vs ~$16.02T), internally inconsistent because 19.42/(19.42+16.02)=54.8%
itemVerdicts.note: Verified from the cited PDF itself. Note the contentstack PDF has a broken ToUnicode map that silently DELETES the digits 3, 6, 8 and the capitals A/N/F/O from text extraction (that is why any grep of the extracted text shows '$1 .02T' and 'back in 202 '); I rendered page 5 to PNG and read the page image. Verbatim on page 5: 'Since passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023, they've continued to gain market share of the US funds universe. As of year-end 2025, passively managed funds made up over 55% of net assets, increasing from 53% the year prior.' Chart legend labels: 'Passively Managed $19.42T' and 'Actively Managed $16.02T', source line 'Morningstar Direct Asset Flows. Data as of Dec. 31, 2025.' Key Takeaway bullet on page 1: 'Passive funds continued their streak of taking market share from active funds, especially with equity funds, reaching a 55% market share in total.' The inconsistency is real and as stated: 19.42/(19.42+16.02) = 54.80%; you would need active <= $15.88T to clear 55%. The '53% the year prior' also checks against Morningstar's own Jan-2025 article: 'About 53% of assets in long-term open-end funds and exchange-traded funds are now in indexed strategies.' Minor: the claim's '~$16.02T' should drop the tilde — $16.02T is the printed label, not an estimate.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) ICI 2026 Fact Book: index MFs+ETFs = 52% of long-term fund assets at YE2025 ($19.1T of $36.6T; excludes MMFs and commodity ETFs; series 2010=19%, 2015=28%, 2020=40%)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified against the fetched PDF (icifactbook.org/pdf/2026-factbook-ch2.pdf), verbatim: 'By year-end 2025, total net assets in these two index fund categories had grown to $19.1 trillion... At year-end 2025, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for the majority (52%) of assets in long-term funds, up from 19% at year-end 2010 (Figure 2.5).' Figure 2.5 stack labels read 19%, 28%, 40%, 52% over 2010/2015/2020/2025, with the Total net assets row $9.9 / $14.9 / $24.8 / $36.6 trillions. Figure note verbatim: 'Note: Data exclude money market funds. Data for ETFs exclude commodity ETFs.' Cross-check: 52% x 36.6 = 19.03, consistent with $19.1T. CAVEAT worth carrying (see newContradictions): ICI's own Research Perspective Vol. 32 No. 1 (March 2026) reprints the identical figure for the identical YE2025 snapshot but states '$19.3 trillion' with the note 'Data for ETFs exclude non-1940 Act ETFs' — same 52%, same $36.6T, $0.2T different index total.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ICI monthly release: index $21.88T vs active $18.83T in June 2026 = 53.7%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the ICI page (title 'Release: Active and Index Investing, June 2026'): 'Washington, DC; July 31, 2026 — The combined assets of the nation's active mutual funds and ETFs increased by $85.12 billion, or 0.5%, to $18.83 trillion in June while the combined assets of the nation's indexed mutual funds and ETFs increased by $59.04 billion, or 0.3%, to $21.88 trillion in June according to the Investment Company Institute's official survey of the mutual fund and ETF industry.' Table 'Total Net Assets Long-Term Mutual Funds and ETFs', billions: Domestic equity 8,615.8 / 15,215.3 / 63.8; World equity 3,297.1 / 3,414.8 / 50.9; Hybrid 1,799.4 / 87.9 / 4.7; Bond 5,117.9 / 3,162.3 / 38.2; Total 18,830.2 / 21,880.3 / 53.7. Components sum exactly. Footnote verbatim: '* Data for funds that invest primarily in other mutual funds were excluded from the series.' TWO CITATION HAZARDS: (1) the cited slug .../combined_active_index_0526 is NOT a month-stable permalink — I fetched _0426, _0526 and _0626 and all three return the identical June-2026 release, so the URL will silently show a different month once ICI posts July; (2) this monthly series excludes funds of funds, unlike Fact Book Figure 2.5, so 53.7% here and 52% at YE2025 there are not on the same universe.

corrections: (a) Add the second exclusion. Morningstar's universe excludes funds of funds as well as money market funds. Disclosure page of the Morningstar report, verbatim: 'This report includes both mutual funds and exchange-traded funds but not funds of funds unless specifically stated. It does not include collective investment trusts or separate accounts.' Do not write 'money market funds excluded' alone — the funds-of-funds exclusion is precisely what produces the crossover-date disagreement with ICI, so it must be named.

The $13.29T/$13.23T pair does NOT appear in the text of the Morningstar article at morningstar.com/funds/recovery-us-fund-flows-was-weak-2023 — that article only says 'passive funds closed 2023 with more assets' and puts the numbers in an unlabeled chart image. Cite it as 'Morningstar data as reported by CNBC (Jan. 18, 2024)', not as a quotation from Morningstar's own text.

CNBC calls it 'exchange-traded funds and notes, along with passively managed mutual funds,' which read literally would fold active ETFs (~$0.5T at YE2023) into passive and would by itself more than erase the $60bn margin. That is a journalist's gloss, not Morningstar's classification: Morningstar classifies by index/active regardless of vehicle, and its YE2023 passive total ($13.29T) matches ICI's index total ($13.3T) rather than exceeding it by the size of the active-ETF book. Describe the bucket as 'index-tracking mutual funds and ETFs'.

(b) Add the caliber Morningstar itself used, and the preliminary flag. Wrong: presenting Aug-2019 as a settled $20bn margin. Right: Morningstar's August 2019 commentary says 'Preliminary numbers show that passive U.S. equity assets passed active U.S. equity assets by about $25 billion,' with '70 or so funds, including all of Artisan's funds' not yet reported, and 'If this result holds, passive share of U.S. equity open-end and ETF assets would be 50.15% versus 49.85% for active funds.' Figure 2.5 excludes money market funds and commodity ETFs but INCLUDES funds of funds; the monthly Active-and-Index release excludes 'funds that invest primarily in other mutual funds'. Say which universe each number is on.

(e) Replace or annotate the URL. www.ici.org/research/stats/combined_active_index_0526 is not month-stable — the 0426, 0526 and 0626 slugs all currently serve the identical June-2026 release (issued July 31, 2026). Cite it as 'ICI, Active and Index Investing, June 2026 (released July 31, 2026)' and expect the link to drift.

Adjudication of 2023 vs 2024 — state it this way, do not just pick a year. On Morningstar's own data the answer is unambiguously END-2023: Morningstar says so in three separate publications ('passive funds closed 2023 with more assets', Jan 2024; 'After overtaking active fund assets for the first time ever in 2023', Jan 2025; 'Since passive funds surpassed active funds in total net assets back in 2023', Dec 2025). But 'the crossover' is provider-dependent, not a fact of nature: on ICI's data active was still the majority at YE2023 and the 50% line was crossed in 2024. The article must attribute the date to a provider rather than assert it flatly.
newContradictions: ICI's own data contradict a provider-neutral 'passive crossed 50% at end-2023'. ICI 2024 Fact Book, chapter 2, verbatim: 'By year-end 2023, total net assets in these two index fund categories had grown to $13.3 trillion... At year-end 2023, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for 48 percent of assets in long-term funds, up from 19 percent at year-end 2010 (Figure 2.5). Nevertheless, actively managed funds still accounted for more than half of long-term fund assets (52 percent) at year-end 2023.' Figure 2.5 total net assets for 2023 = $27.6 trillion. ICI 2025 Fact Book then gives YE2024: '$16.2 trillion' index and 'the majority (51 percent) of assets in long-term funds'. So ICI's crossover is 2024, Morningstar's is 2023. Note the index side agrees almost exactly ($13.3T ICI vs $13.29T Morningstar); the whole disagreement is in the ACTIVE denominator ($14.35T ICI vs $13.23T Morningstar, ~$1.1T apart), which is consistent with Morningstar excluding funds of funds (mostly active target-date/allocation vehicles) while Fact Book Figure 2.5 does not. This is a strong, checkable point the article should make rather than a problem to hide.

SSGA's '2024' is not a competing claim about US fund assets and carries no citation. State Street Global Advisors, 'Closing time: How passive investing is reshaping equity market microstructure', verbatim: 'Indexing has expanded its footprint within global AUM. In 2024, the AUM of passive funds surpassed that of active funds, and its market share continues to climb.' The subject is GLOBAL AUM, the sentence has no footnote (the piece's three footnotes are Instinet Dec-31-2025, BofA Jun-2024, Instinet Dec-31-2025 — none attached to it), and the piece's own data tables run to Q4 2025 / Dec 2025. Treat SSGA as a loose global-scope assertion, not evidence against Morningstar's US end-2023 date. Its coincidence with ICI's US 2024 crossover is worth one sentence, not a correction.

Two ICI publications weeks apart disagree on the YE2025 index total. ICI 2026 Fact Book ch.2: '$19.1 trillion', note 'Data for ETFs exclude commodity ETFs.' ICI Research Perspective Vol. 32, No. 1 (March 2026), same figure and same 52%/$36.6T: '$19.3 trillion', note 'Data for ETFs exclude non-1940 Act ETFs.' If the article quotes a dollar level for ICI's index total, cite which ICI publication — the two differ by $0.2T on the same date.

Morningstar's own Dec-2025 report carries a stale disclosure line: 'The figures in this report were compiled on Jan. 12, 2025' in a report whose every source line reads 'Data as of Dec. 31, 2025.' Almost certainly a template typo for Jan. 12, 2026, but do not quote that disclosure sentence as a date.

Fabrication discipline: every quoted string above was read either from a rendered page image or from a document-text conversion I inspected line by line. itemVerdicts.item: (a) Headline: index funds held 16% of the US market in 2021 but total passive ownership ≈33.5%, using reconstitution-day CLOSING-volume spikes across five indexes (S&P 500, S&P 400, R1000, R2000, NDX)
itemVerdicts.note: The 16% / 33.5% pair and the five indexes are verbatim correct. JFE abstract (cs_jfe.txt L37): 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%.' Indexes (L461-462): 'the S&P 500, the S&P MidCap 400, the Russell 1000, the Russell 2000, and the Nasdaq 100.' WRONG: 'closing-volume spikes.' RIGHT: the headline 33.5% is built from TOTAL reconstitution-day volume (their variable DailyVolume), not closing volume. Fig. 2 caption (L219-220): 'Calculation is based on total volume experienced by index additions and deletions on reconstitution day.' Table 3 caption (L1191): 'when using DailyVolume to proxy for passive rebalancing volume.' The closing/after-hours-restricted variant is what produces the 24.6% number, not 33.5%. The 'closing volumes' phrasing belongs to the July 2022 working paper ('This estimate is based on the closing volumes of index additions and deletions on reconstitution days'), not the published version. Minor: the index is 'S&P MidCap 400', not 'S&P 400'.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Honest range 24.6% (after-hours-volume-only proxy) to 38.5% (adding Vanguard's $2.25T CRSP-tracking assets, in which case ICI's 16% falls to 11%); 'double' is a choice of which pair to divide
itemVerdicts.note: All four numbers are verbatim in the paper, and the paper's own §3.3 is titled 'Range of estimates', so the framing is fair. L1106-1107: 'When using Volume1600to2359 instead of DailyVolume, we still put the US passive ownership share at 24.6% in 2021.' L1115-1118: 'In December 2021 Vanguard had roughly $2.25t tracking CRSP indexes. If we were to remove this $2.25t from ICI's asset base, their 16% would fall to 11%. If we were to include this $2.25t, our 33.5% would climb to 38.5%.' WRONG: the article's 'in which case' makes 38.5% and 11% simultaneous. RIGHT: they are two mutually exclusive alignments — you either strip CRSP assets out of ICI's base (16%→11%, compared against 33.5%, a 3.0x gap) OR add them to Chinco-Sammon's numerator (33.5%→38.5%, compared against 16%, a 2.4x gap). Applying both would double-count the same $2.25t adjustment. Two supporting details the article omits and should use: (i) the paper's own apples-to-apples benchmark is ~6%, not 16% — L179-181: 'Using fund holdings, we estimate that if all passive investing was index-fund investing, we would have estimated a value of around 6% not 16%' (Appendix B derives it as 0.16 × 33.5% ≈ 6% from a regression slope), which is the strongest version of the 'which pair to divide' point; (ii) Table 4 column (2), volume net of average daily volume, gives 28.65% for 2021, and the paper concedes (L1518-1520) the headline 'might be overestimating the true passive ownership share by somewhere between 2%pt and 5%pt.' Caveat: the 24.6% series only runs 2004-2021 (TAQ availability), not 2000-2021; and Volume1600to2359 is 4:00pm-11:59pm, which includes the closing cross, so 'after-hours-only' is slightly loose.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) On their own measure passive share was already 13.4% in 2000 — 2.5x rise vs 5.3x for the fund-based measure (3%→16%)
itemVerdicts.note: Both ratios check out and both endpoints are the paper's own words. Table 3 'Total' column, 2000 = 13.39 (s.e. 1.35), 2021 = 33.50 (s.e. 2.91) → 2.50x; the text rounds it itself at L2398-2399: 'the overall passive ownership share has grown from 13.4% to 33.5% during this same period', and L2069: 'the US passive ownership share in 2000, 13.4%.' Fund-based endpoints are verbatim at L44-47: 'Index funds had combined assets under management (AUM) of just $0.4t in 2000, roughly 3% of the value of the US stock market. By 2021, these funds had $7.2t in AUM, which represented 16% of the market's value.' 16/3 = 5.33x. Two caveats worth carrying: pre-2009 index weights are interpolated rather than obtained from the provider (L2076-2078), though the authors say the interpolation is deliberately conservative and biases the estimate DOWN — which if anything shrinks the 2.5x further; and the series is non-monotonic (2009 = 31.85%, above 2016's 25.92%), so it is not a smooth ramp in either direction.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Index add/delete returns 'steadily converged to nearly zero' while passive doubled; Tesla Dec-18-2020 reconstitution-day return +5.96%
itemVerdicts.note: Both strings verify verbatim but one qualifier is dropped. L2395-2399: 'the returns to buying index additions and the returns to selling index deletions have steadily converged to nearly zero. This has happened in spite of the fact that the overall passive ownership share has grown from 13.4% to 33.5% during this same period.' L2407-2409: 'Tesla's addition to the S&P 500 on December 18th 2020 was an exception to this rule... so Tesla realized a 5.96% reconstitution-day return in Fig. 13' (Fig. 13 caption confirms these are realized, i.e. raw, returns; announcement was November 17th 2020). WRONG: 'index add/delete returns... converged to nearly zero' without qualification. RIGHT: it is specifically RECONSTITUTION-DAY returns that converged to zero; the paper immediately and explicitly denies the general reading, L2396-2401: 'To be clear: index inclusion does affect prices. The effect just does not come by way of passive rebalancing demand on reconstitution days. Greenwood and Sammon (2024) document that, even in the modern era there are announcement-day returns associated with direct additions and deletions.' If the article uses this to argue index inclusion no longer moves prices, that is the opposite of what the paper says. Useful adjacent numbers: excluding Tesla, other 2020 S&P 500 additions had abnormal reconstitution-day returns of just 1.20%; including Tesla, 2020 S&P 500 additions were 5.14pp above the market.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) The method concedes it counts ANY close-of-reconstitution-day rebalancing as passive (active managers forced to trade on index changes included)
itemVerdicts.note: The core concession is verbatim, the parenthetical is not. L189-191: 'Our procedure counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive holdings; it does not matter who actually owns these assets. As such, our numbers likely includes passive investments made by people who would not consider themselves to be passive investors.' WRONG: attributing to the authors a concession that active managers forced to trade on index changes are swept in. RIGHT: the authors raise that objection and reject it — L2065-2069: 'DailyVolume and Volume1600to2359 could be capturing reconstitution-day volume coming from active investors. This would lead us to overestimate the true passive ownership share. However, the data are not consistent with active investors delaying trades to take advantage of the high liquidity...' What they DO quantify is the counterfactual in Table 4 col (2): 'if other investors kept on trading index additions and deletions in the exact same way on reconstitution days, then column (2) suggests that our headline numbers might be overestimating the true passive ownership share by somewhere between 2%pt and 5%pt.' Also note the headline is stronger than the quoted concession implies: the 33.5% attributes the WHOLE reconstitution-day volume (not just the close) to passive rebalancing.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Earlier drafts' 2020 value was ~37.8% vs published 32.19% — the number moved between versions
itemVerdicts.note: Directionally right and the two numbers are exact, but the reason is understated. July 19 2022 draft abstract, verbatim: 'We estimate that passive investors held at least 37.8% of the US stock market in 2020... 37.8% is more than double the widely accepted previous value of 15%'; its Table 6 row reads '2020  25.53  11.36  0.87  37.77  15  22.77'. Published JFE Table 3 'Total' for 2020 = 32.19 (s.e. 3.26). WRONG to imply the same estimator drifted. RIGHT: the 2022 draft covered only THREE indexes (S&P 500, Russell 1000, Russell 2000) over 2011-2021, was benchmarked against ICI's 15% for 2020, and was framed as a lower bound on 'strict end-of-day indexers'; the published version covers FIVE indexes over 2000-2021. The S&P 500 component alone fell from 25.53% (2022 draft, 2020) to 15.77% (published, 2020) — so the estimator itself was rebuilt, and adding two indexes still produced a lower total. There is also an intermediate May 19 2023 draft: headline 33.3% for 2021, 2000 value 12.8% (vs published 13.4%), and the Vanguard adjustment there used $4.4t of total Vanguard equity holdings to reach 39.8% (vs the published $2.25t of CRSP-tracked holdings reaching 38.5%). The article should cite the published pair or state which draft it means.

corrections: Change 'reconstitution-day closing-volume spikes' to 'reconstitution-day total (all-day) volume spikes'. The headline 33.5% uses total reconstitution-day volume (their DailyVolume variable); Fig. 2's caption reads 'Calculation is based on total volume experienced by index additions and deletions on reconstitution day.' Restricting to 4:00pm-onward volume is what yields the lower 24.6% figure. 'Closing volumes' is the July 2022 working paper's language, not the published paper's.

Do not present 38.5% and 11% as a single adjustment. The paper offers them as two mutually exclusive alignments of the same $2.25T of Vanguard CRSP-tracked assets: remove it from ICI's base and ICI's 16% falls to 11% (against an unchanged 33.5%), OR add it to Chinco-Sammon's numerator and 33.5% rises to 38.5% (against an unchanged 16%). Applying both would double-count. Verbatim: 'If we were to remove this $2.25t from ICI's asset base, their 16% would fall to 11%. If we were to include this $2.25t, our 33.5% would climb to 38.5%.'

Strengthen the 'which pair to divide' point with the paper's own apples-to-apples number: 'Using fund holdings, we estimate that if all passive investing was index-fund investing, we would have estimated a value of around 6% not 16%' (Appendix B derives it as 0.16 x 33.5% ~ 6%). The authors add that 'The ICI's 16% figure is not a lower bound because it is based on more indexes.'

Add the paper's own quantified overestimate band to the range discussion: Table 4 column (2) uses reconstitution-day volume net of average daily volume and gives 28.65% for 2021, with the text conceding the headline 'might be overestimating the true passive ownership share by somewhere between 2%pt and 5%pt.'

Note that the 24.6% series only exists for 2004-2021 (TAQ intraday data availability), not the full 2000-2021 window of the 33.5% series, and that the 4:00pm-11:59pm window includes the closing cross, so describe it as 'volume from 4:00pm onward' rather than 'after-hours only'.

Restore the dropped qualifier on the convergence finding: it is RECONSTITUTION-DAY returns to index additions and deletions that 'have steadily converged to nearly zero'. The paper immediately states the opposite of the general reading: 'To be clear: index inclusion does affect prices. The effect just does not come by way of passive rebalancing demand on reconstitution days,' citing Greenwood and Sammon (2024) on persistent announcement-day returns. Do not use this passage to claim index inclusion no longer moves prices.

Drop or rewrite the parenthetical that the authors concede active managers forced to trade on index changes are counted as passive. They raise that objection and reject it: 'the data are not consistent with active investors delaying trades to take advantage of the high liquidity experienced by index additions and deletions at market close on reconstitution day.' The concession they actually make is the broader one: 'Our procedure counts any holdings that get rebalanced at this one point in time as passive holdings; it does not matter who actually owns these assets.'

When citing the version drift, say why the number moved rather than implying estimator drift: the 37.8% (37.77 in the table) was a 2020 figure from only three indexes (S&P 500 25.53 + Russell 1000 11.36 + Russell 2000 0.87), sample 2011-2021, benchmarked to ICI's 15%; the published 32.19% for 2020 comes from five indexes over 2000-2021. The S&P 500 component alone fell from 25.53% to 15.77% for the same year between versions. An intermediate May 2023 draft had 33.3% for 2021, 12.8% for 2000, and a $4.4T Vanguard adjustment to 39.8%.
Cite the index by its proper name, 'S&P MidCap 400', not 'S&P 400'.

Bibliographic details check out and can be stated precisely: Journal of Financial Economics, Vol. 157 (July 2024), article 103860, doi 10.1016/j.jfineco.2024.103860; received 19 May 2023, revised 29 April 2024, accepted 1 May 2024. The PDF at alexchinco.com (dated April 7, 2024) matches the published version on every number checked (33.5, 24.6, 38.5, 11, 13.4, 32.19, 5.96).
newContradictions: The paper explicitly contradicts a common downstream use of its convergence result: 'To be clear: index inclusion does affect prices. The effect just does not come by way of passive rebalancing demand on reconstitution days.' Any article passage using Chinco-Sammon to argue index inclusion has stopped moving prices is contradicted by the source.

The paper's own apples-to-apples benchmark undercuts the word 'double' more sharply than the article does: if all passive investing were index-fund investing, their method would have produced ~6%, not 16%. Against that benchmark the gap is ~5.6x, not 2x. Conversely, against the most conservative proxy (24.6%) versus ICI's 16%, the gap is only ~1.5x. The 'double' headline sits in the middle of a 1.5x-to-5.6x spread depending on which pair is divided.

The authors' pre-2009 estimates rest on interpolated index weights, which they say is 'an extremely conservative approach' biasing estimates downward — so the 13.4% for 2000 may itself be understated, which would shrink the 2.5x growth ratio further and reinforce (not weaken) the article's anti-regime-change point.

No corrigendum, erratum, published comment, or replication challenging the paper was found as of 2026-08. The Mendeley replication package (data.mendeley.com/datasets/x4vzjxkhtv/1) is the authors' own.
reasoning:
I worked from primary text throughout. Local extractions in the scratchpad gave me three distinct versions of the paper, which I confirmed are genuinely different documents by reading their title pages: cs_jfe.txt (published Journal of Financial Economics 157 (2024) 103860, with the running header, doi, and 'Received 19 May 2023; Received in revised form 29 April 2024; Accepted 1 May 2024'), cs_live.txt / chinco_sammon.txt (the April 7 2024 PDF posted at alexchinco.com — the exact URL the article cites), cs_may23.txt (May 19 2023 draft), and cs_2022.txt (July 19 2022 draft).

For (a) I read the abstract, the introduction, the Fig. 2 caption, and §2.1, confirming the 16%/33.5% pair and the five named indexes, but the Fig. 2 and Table 3 captions both say the calculation rests on total/DailyVolume, not closing volume — that is where the article slipped, and I traced the 'closing volumes' phrasing to the superseded 2022 abstract.

For (b) I read §3.3 'Range of estimates' and the Fig. 5 discussion, which contain 24.6%, 11%, 38.5% and $2.25t verbatim. Reading the two sentences in sequence made clear they are alternative alignments, not one compound adjustment. I also pulled Table 4 in full and mapped its columns by year: for 2021, col (1) all-day = 33.50, col (2) minus ADV = 28.65, col (3) 4:00pm-11:59pm = 24.62. And I found the Appendix B passage deriving the ~6% apples-to-apples figure from a 0.16 regression slope.

For (c) I extracted all of Table 3 and mapped the column-major extraction carefully — this was the main trap, since a naive grep for '13.4' hits the S&P 500 column's 2008 value (13.40), not the 2000 total. The 'Total' column runs 13.39 (2000) ... 32.19 (2020), 33.50 (2021), and the text independently rounds 2000 to 13.4%. The 3%/16% fund-based endpoints are in the paper's opening paragraph verbatim.

For (d) and (e) I read the surrounding paragraphs rather than the grep hits alone, which is what surfaced the two caliber problems: the convergence sentence is scoped to reconstitution-day returns and is immediately followed by an explicit denial of the general claim; and the active-investor objection is raised and rejected rather than conceded.

For (f) I read the 2022 draft's abstract, its Table 6 header and 2020 row, and its intro, establishing that 37.8% came from three indexes over 2011-2021 against an ICI benchmark of 15%, and that its S&P 500 component for 2020 (25.53) is far above the published one (15.77). I also captured the intermediate May 2023 draft's numbers (33.3%, 12.8% for 2000, $4.4t/39.8%).

Web work was limited to metadata and post-publication checks: ScienceDirect returned 403, so I confirmed volume/issue via RePEc plus a search establishing JFE Vol 157 is the July 2024 issue, and the article number and dates independently from the published PDF's own header. Searches for a corrigendum, erratum, comment, or replication returned nothing through 2026-08.

Two search summaries returned figures I did NOT accept as evidence and did not use: one asserted '33.6%' (the paper says 33.5%) and one quoted the superseded 37.8% as if it were current. Consistent with the fabrication warning, every number and quoted string in this verdict comes from text I read directly in the extracted PDFs.

Residual uncertainty: I could not independently verify Tesla's 12/18/2020 close-to-close return against a market data source — the local tsla.csv is a bot-challenge page, not data — so 5.96% rests on the paper's own Fig. 13 and text, which is the correct primary source for a claim attributed to the paper but is not an external cross-check. I also did not open the Mendeley replication package to re-derive Table 3.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Vanguard Aug 2025: index fund portfolio-management trading = 1.2% of total US exchange dollar volume in 2024 (from 0.3% in 2006); active funds 2-5%; verbatim 'the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the local extraction of the Vanguard Aug 2025 paper 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing' (Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green), p.9 body text: 'Trading volume has slowly increased from about $38 trillion in 2006 to about $153 trillion in 2024. During that period, active fund volume remained between 2% and 5% of total trading volume, while index fund trading volume slowly grew from about 0.3% of total volume to 1.2%. Index funds are an important source of ownership, but the claim that they are becoming the primary driver of market dynamics is demonstrably false.' Figure 6 notes verbatim: 'The percentage of total trading volume is cash-flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume... all available equity open-end funds and ETFs with U.S. equity exposure from January 1, 2006, through December 31, 2024... total trading volume on U.S. exchanges from Cboe Exchange. Sources: Vanguard calculations, using data from Morningstar, Inc., and Cboe Exchange, Inc.; originally published in Rowley, Zorina, and Zhu (2019).' TWO CAVEATS the article should not overstate: (i) the exclusion list (ETF secondary-market trading, index derivatives, indexed separate accounts) is NOT stated in the PDF — it is an inference from 'cash-flow adjusted turnover' of a Morningstar open-end/ETF universe; the explicit authority for those exclusions is Vanguard's own statement in the Institutional Investor piece, which separately names 'indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds' and 'shares of ETFs'. Cite II for the exclusions, not the PDF. (ii) Vanguard labels the denominator 'U.S. exchanges,' but $153T for 2024 is consolidated-tape scale (on- plus off-exchange); exchange-only 2024 dollar volume is roughly half that, which would roughly double the ratio. Repeat Vanguard's label but do not add precision Vanguard does not have.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) ICI 2026 Fact Book: ETF secondary-market trading averaged 28% of total US stock market trading in 2025; series 25-32% since 2016; trading in ETF shares not underlyings
itemVerdicts.note: Independently re-fetched the live PDF (https://www.ici.org/system/files/2026-04/2026-factbook-quick-facts-guide.pdf, 3.9MB) and ran pdftotext -layout myself rather than trusting the pre-existing local extraction. Chart title verbatim: 'ETF Secondary Market Trading Averaged 28% of Daily US Stock Trading in 2025'; subtitle 'Average daily ETF share of total US stock market trading, percentage, annual'. Annual values 2016-2025: 27, 25, 27, 27, 26, 25, 32, 30, 27, 28 — so min 25% (2017, 2021), max 32% (2022): the '25-32% since 2016' range is exact. Body text verbatim: 'While ETF secondary market trading is a substantial share of total trading on US stock exchanges and other venues, the average remained relatively flat through 2021... This share declined from its 2022 peak as market volatility eased and averaged 28% in 2025.' Note ICI's denominator is 'US stock exchanges and other venues' (i.e. includes off-exchange), and the numerator is ALL ETFs — active as well as index — so 28% is not a passive figure; the article must not let it read as one.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) SSGA 'Closing time' (Jan 23, 2026): US market-on-close volume rose from 8.40% of total volume (Jan 2018) to 15.39% (Dec 2025); piece gives no passive share of MOC volume
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers are real but the BASELINE IS MISLABELED. Re-fetched the live SSGA page and read the raw Figure 2 table markup. WRONG: '8.40% of total volume in January 2018.' RIGHT: 8.40% is the daily-average US closing-auction share for the whole window running FROM January 2018 through December 31, 2025 — the row label is 'From Jan 2018' under the figure heading 'Figure 2: Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume – USA versus Developed Europe versus APAC'. The rows are nested trailing windows (From Jan 2018 8.40% / From Jan 2019 9.24% / 1 Year 12.11% / Q4 2025 13.10% / 25-Dec 15.39%), not point observations. The 15.39% figure IS a single month (December 2025) and is confirmed in prose: 'December 2025 data shows that Developed Europe allocates roughly 34.82 percent of daily volume to the closing auction, compared with 15.39 percent in the United States and 16.78 percent in Asia ex Japan.' Source line: 'Instinet as of December 31, 2025. Last two hours figures exclude closing auction.' Also: the metric is the CLOSING AUCTION share of daily volume, not 'MOC orders' as such. CONFIRMED sub-claim: the piece gives no passive share of MOC volume — I read the full article plus both embedded chart datasets; Figure 1 is 'Figure 1: Active versus passive AUM ($T)' (Morningstar, as of June 30, 2025), an AUM series, and Figure 2 is the session-split table. No figure anywhere attributes a share of closing-auction volume to passive. The causal link ('likely driven in large part by the expansion of indexing') is asserted, never quantified — and the piece is a State Street marketing communication.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Institutional Investor (Jan 3, 2025): Green estimates passive direct trading 20% + index derivatives 8% + passive market making 36% vs active managers 10% (down from 80% in 1995); Vanguard statement in same article says index funds ~1% and all-in indexing <5%
itemVerdicts.note: Green's figures confirmed verbatim from the local capture of the article (dated 'January 3, 2025'; HTML publishDate 1735925725684 = Jan 3, 2025): 'Using statistics compiled from various market and academic sources, Green estimates that passive direct trading now accounts for about 20 percent of all trading, passive index derivatives make up 8 percent, and passive market making contributes a further 36 percent. By contrast, trading by active managers totals only 10 percent, down from 80 percent in 1995.' Vanguard statement confirmed verbatim: 'Our base case estimates that index funds account for approximately 1 percent of overall trading volume on U.S. exchanges, well below the more widely quoted 5 percent to 7 percent. Even after accounting for indexed portfolio management outside of registered funds and removing trading volume due to [high-frequency trading] and shares of ETFs, we estimate that indexing represents less than 5 percent of overall U.S. trading volume.' CORRECTION: 'all-in indexing < 5%' mischaracterizes the second figure. WRONG: '<5% is indexing all-in.' RIGHT: the <5% figure ADDS indexed portfolio management outside registered funds but explicitly REMOVES high-frequency trading and ETF-share trading — i.e. it strips out precisely the ~28% ETF secondary-market bucket in item (b), so it is the opposite of 'all-in'. Second correction: '64%' appears nowhere in the article; it is the article author's sum of 20+8+36, and Green is not quoted giving a combined total.

corrections: SSGA baseline: replace 'US market-on-close volume rose from 8.40% of total volume (Jan 2018) to 15.39% (Dec 2025)' with 'the US closing auction took a daily-average 8.40% of volume over the whole period since January 2018, versus 15.39% in December 2025 alone' — the SSGA table row is labeled 'From Jan 2018' in a figure titled 'Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume', and the rows are nested trailing windows (From Jan 2018 8.40% / From Jan 2019 9.24% / 1 Year 12.11% / Q4 2025 13.10% / Dec 2025 15.39%), not point-in-time observations. 8.40% is NOT January 2018's value.

Vanguard's second figure in Institutional Investor is not 'all-in indexing'. Replace 'all-in indexing < 5% of volume' with wording that carries Vanguard's own qualifiers: 'even after adding indexed portfolio management outside registered funds and removing high-frequency trading and ETF-share volume, Vanguard estimates indexing at under 5% of overall US trading volume.' The <5% figure explicitly strips out ETF secondary-market trading — the very bucket the ICI 28% measures — so calling it 'all-in' inverts its meaning.

Do not present '64%' as Green's or Institutional Investor's number. The article prints only the components (20% direct + 8% index derivatives + 36% passive market making, vs 10% active); 64% is an arithmetic sum the writer is performing. Label it as such ('summing his components gives roughly 64%').

Attribute the definitional exclusions for Vanguard's 1.2% (ETF secondary-market trading, index derivatives, indexed separate accounts) to Vanguard's statement in Institutional Investor, not to the August 2025 PDF. The PDF says only that the metric is 'cash-flow adjusted turnover as a percentage of total U.S. exchange trading volume' over 'equity open-end funds and ETFs'; it never enumerates what is excluded.

When quoting Vanguard's denominator, keep Vanguard's own label ('total U.S. exchange trading volume', Cboe) without upgrading it to a claim about exchange-only volume: the $38T (2006) to $153T (2024) magnitudes correspond to consolidated on- plus off-exchange US equity dollar volume, so 'exchange' in Vanguard's note is loose. If the article contrasts the ICI 28% (explicitly 'US stock exchanges and other venues') with Vanguard's 1.2%, note the denominators are broadly comparable rather than implying Vanguard used a narrower one.
When citing the ICI 28%, state that the numerator is all ETFs — active as well as index — so it is a ceiling on ETF-share trading, not a measure of passive trading.
newContradictions: The article stacks ICI's 28% (ETF secondary-market trading) next to Vanguard's 1.2% as if they were rival estimates of the same quantity, but Vanguard's own Institutional Investor statement says its broader (<5%) estimate is computed with ETF-share trading REMOVED. So the two numbers are not merely different definitions of one thing — Vanguard's methodology treats ETF secondary trading as categorically not indexing activity, while the 28% headline treats it as the numerator. The article should state that disagreement explicitly rather than presenting a smooth 'range depending on definition'.

Green's 36% 'passive market making' bucket has no primary source: Institutional Investor attributes it only to 'statistics compiled from various market and academic sources' with no citation, and it is the single largest component of the 64%. It is also conceptually double-countable against his 20% 'passive direct trading' (a market maker's hedge of an index-fund order is the same economic trade seen from the other side). The article should not present 64% as a measured quantity comparable to Vanguard's Morningstar/Cboe computation or ICI's tape-based share.

SSGA's 'Closing time' is a marketing communication by the third-largest index manager, and it asserts the indexing-to-MOC causal link ('likely driven in large part by the expansion of indexing') without quantifying passive's share of the auction — the only quantified series in the piece are total closing-auction share of volume and a total active-vs-passive AUM chart. It cannot support any sentence of the form 'passive is X% of closing-auction volume'.
reasoning: I verified all four sub-claims against primary text, treating each as false until read. Sources reached verbatim: (1) Vanguard, "Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing", August 2025 (Rowley/Lawrence/Ryder-Green) — read the full p.9 price-discovery section and the Figure 6 note block from the local extraction at /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/vg.txt; I also confirmed the standalone "1.2%" appearing earlier in the file (line 208) is the y-axis of Figure 1 (expense ratios), not the trading figure, so the body sentence is the sole source. (2) ICI 2026 Fact Book Quick Facts Guide — I did NOT trust the pre-existing local extraction; a direct curl was blocked (457-byte stub), so I fetched the live 3.9MB PDF via WebFetch, copied it to /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/v3_qf.pdf, and ran pdftotext -layout myself, reading the chart axis labels directly (values 2016-2025: 27/25/27/27/26/25/32/30/27/28). The extraction's leading "30%" on the data row is the y-axis gridline label, not a data point — I checked the column alignment before accepting the series. (3) SSGA "Closing time" — I re-fetched the live page (143KB) and read the raw Figure 2 table markup rather than the flattened text, which is how I caught the baseline error: the row labels are "From Jan 2018 / From Jan 2019 / 1 Year / Q4 2025 / 25-Dec" under a figure titled "Daily Average Comparison of Trade Volume", a nested-trailing-window structure, so 8.40% is a period average since Jan 2018, not January 2018's reading. I also dumped both embedded chart JSON payloads to confirm Figure 1 is "Figure 1: Active versus passive AUM ($T)" (AUM, not volume) and that no passive share of closing-auction volume appears anywhere in the piece. (4) Institutional Investor, "Why Michael Green Is Known as the Cassandra of Passive Investing" — stripped the local HTML capture to text and read both the Green estimate sentence and the full Vanguard statement verbatim; publication date confirmed two ways (visible "January 3, 2025" and HTML publishDate epoch 1735925725684). Two web searches for later corrections/replications through 2026-08 turned up none for either the Vanguard paper or the II article. Verdict CORRECTED rather than HOLDS because of two real caliber slips: the SSGA 8.40% baseline is a multi-year average mislabeled as a January 2018 point, and Vanguard's <5% is described as "all-in" when the quote says it is computed with HFT and ETF-share volume removed. Remaining uncertainty: Vanguard's denominator label "U.S. exchanges" is imprecise — the $38T/$153T magnitudes look like consolidated on- plus off-exchange dollar volume, and Vanguard does not disclose the Cboe series used, so I could not pin the denominator to a specific published Cboe aggregate; I flagged this rather than asserting an error. Green's 36% market-making figure is unsourced in II and I found no primary document behind it, so it is unverifiable in principle, not merely unreached.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) verbatim 'I view the markets as fundamentally broken'; mechanism = passive has no opinion about value + value-manager redemption spiral; 'almost the best way to get your stock to go up is to start by being overvalued.'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim against both the local extraction (einhorn_transcript.txt, line 84-87) and a live WebFetch of ritholtz.com/2024/02/transcript-david-einhorn/. Exact quotes present: 'I view the markets as fundamentally broken' (~00:22:53); 'Passive investors have no opinion about value. They're gonna assume everybody else's done the work'; redemption-spiral stated explicitly: 'when that happens, the value managers get redeemed, the value stocks go down more, it causes more redemptions of the value managers, it caused those stocks to go down more'; and 'almost the best way to get your stock to go up is to start by being overvalued' appears verbatim (~00:23:58). Air date: transcript page posted 2024-02-12, but the underlying Bloomberg Masters in Business episode URL slug is dated 2024-02-08, matching the claim's stated air date.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) SAME interview: buying at 'four times earnings, five times earnings' with '15, 20% cash flow' returned via buybacks; concession that opportunity set is 'as good or better than it's ever been' because 'the competitors have essentially left the field.'
itemVerdicts.note: All four phrases verified verbatim in the same transcript (local file + live WebFetch): 'We're buying things at four times earnings, five times earnings' (~00:21:48), repeated 'at four times earnings and at five times earnings' (~00:28:18); 'So we need 15, 20% cash flow type of type of numbers' (~00:21:48), in context of companies with 'huge buybacks'; 'I just think the opportunity is actually probably as good or better than, than it's ever been' (~00:30:41); 'the competitors have essentially left the field' (~00:31:41). No caliber slippage.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) At the Robin Hood conference Oct 2024 he used the weaker phrase 'a bit of a broken market' (per Institutional Investor)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: claim attributes 'a bit of a broken market' to the Robin Hood Investors Conference (Oct 23, 2024). RIGHT: that quote is from CNBC's 14th Delivering Alpha Investor Summit in New York, where Einhorn was interviewed on-stage by CNBC's Leslie Picker on Nov 13, 2024 (CNBC article by Bob Pisani published Nov 14, 2024: 'Greenlight's David Einhorn says the markets are broken and getting worse'). Fetched the CNBC article directly via curl (WebFetch got a 403) and it contains the exact quote verbatim, with photo caption confirming venue/date: 'David Einhorn ... speaking at the 14th CNBC Delivering Alpha Investor Summit in New York City on Nov. 13, 2024.' Full quote: '...we have a structurally dysfunctional market, a bit of a broken market, and essentially a perpetual erosion of value as a strategy, as you would.' The Institutional Investor article itself does NOT name Robin Hood or October — it only says the remark was made 'at a recent conference,' unspecified. Einhorn did separately speak at the actual Robin Hood conference on Oct 23, 2024 (confirmed via search of hedgefundalpha.com coverage), but that appearance was about stock picks (e.g., CNH Industrial); no primary source found tying the 'broken market' quote to that event.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Einhorn credits Michael Green for the framework (per II) — downstream of Green, not independent corroboration
itemVerdicts.note: Verified via direct WebFetch extraction of verbatim sentences from the Institutional Investor 'Cassandra of Passive Investing' article: 'Meanwhile, Greenlight Capital's David Einhorn credits Green with helping him understand why the value investing playbook he ran didn't work for many years as investors yanked money from active managers and put it into index funds.' Directly supports the claim that II frames Einhorn as downstream of Green's framework.

corrections: Item (c): the 'a bit of a broken market' remark is NOT from the Robin Hood conference (Oct 23, 2024). It is from CNBC's Delivering Alpha Investor Summit, where Einhorn was interviewed by Leslie Picker on Nov 13, 2024 (article published Nov 14, 2024). The Institutional Investor piece quoting this line does not itself name any conference — it just says 'at a recent conference' — so the specific Robin Hood/October attribution in the claim is unsupported, and the identifiable primary source (CNBC) contradicts it. Correct citation: 'at CNBC's Delivering Alpha Investor Summit, Nov 13, 2024 (per CNBC), quoted in Institutional Investor,' not 'Robin Hood conference Oct 2024.'
reasoning: Checked local extraction /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/einhorn_transcript.txt against a live WebFetch of ritholtz.com/2024/02/transcript-david-einhorn/ — both matched verbatim on all quoted phrases in (a) and (b), including the redemption-spiral mechanism description and the 'competitors have essentially left the field' / 'as good or better than it's ever been' concession. Confirmed the Bloomberg podcast air date of 2024-02-08 embedded in the transcript page (distinct from the blog post's Feb 12 publish date), matching the claim. For (c)/(d), fetched the Institutional Investor 'Cassandra of Passive Investing' article directly and extracted verbatim sentences: it confirms Einhorn credits Michael Green (item d, HOLDS) and does quote 'a bit of a broken market,' but only attributes it to 'a recent conference' without naming Robin Hood. I then located and fetched (via curl with a browser UA, since WebFetch returned a 403) the CNBC article 'Greenlight's David Einhorn says the markets are broken and getting worse' (published Nov 14, 2024), which contains the identical quote verbatim and identifies the venue/date explicitly via a photo caption: 'David Einhorn ... speaking at the 14th CNBC Delivering Alpha Investor Summit in New York City on Nov. 13, 2024,' interviewed by Leslie Picker. This directly contradicts the claim's 'Robin Hood conference Oct 2024' attribution. Einhorn did separately appear at the actual Robin Hood Investors Conference on Oct 23, 2024 (confirmed via search result titles from hedgefundalpha.com), but that appearance concerned stock picks (e.g., CNH Industrial), and no primary-source confirmation was found that the 'broken market' quote was uttered there. Net: three of four sub-claims (a, b, d) HOLD verbatim; sub-claim (c) is CORRECTED on venue and exact date.

itemVerdicts.item: Sept 2019 Bloomberg interview was conducted by EMAIL
itemVerdicts.note: CNBC (2019-09-04, Yun Li) states verbatim: 'Burry told Bloomberg News in an email.' The Bloomberg excerpt reproduced on acquirersmultiple reads: 'One of his most provocative views from a lengthy email interview with Bloomberg News on Tuesday'. Bloomberg article URL confirms publication date 2019-09-04 (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-09-04/michael-burry-explains-why-index-funds-are-like-subprime-cdos). Note the interview itself was 'on Tuesday' = 2019-09-03; publication 2019-09-04 (a Wednesday).

itemVerdicts.item: Quote: 'And now passive investing has removed price discovery from the equity markets... This is very much like the bubble in synthetic asset-backed CDOs before the Great Financial Crisis'
itemVerdicts.note: Both fragments are verbatim and the mid-quote ellipsis is correctly placed (one sentence elided: 'The simple theses and the models that get people into sectors, factors, indexes, or ETFs and mutual funds mimicking those strategies -- these do not require the security-level analysis that is required for true price discovery.'). WRONG: ending the quotation at 'Great Financial Crisis' with no trailing ellipsis, which presents a mid-sentence cut as the end of Burry's sentence. RIGHT: the sentence continues '...before the Great Financial Crisis in that price-setting in that market was not done by fundamental security-level analysis, but by massive capital flows based on Nobel-approved models of risk that proved to be untrue.' Add a trailing ellipsis or quote the full sentence.

itemVerdicts.item: Liquidity counts: 1,049 Russell 2000 stocks traded <$5m that day, 456 <$1m, 266 S&P 500 stocks <$150m
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the Yahoo/GuruFocus reproduction: 'Today I counted 1,049 stocks that traded less than $5 million in value during the day. That is over half, and almost half of those -- 456 stocks -- traded less than $1 million during the day.' and 'The S&P 500 is no different -- the index contains the world's largest stocks, but still, 266 stocks -- over half -- traded under $150 million today.' All three numbers, both thresholds, and both index attributions are exact. Burry's own 'over half' framing for both indexes is worth preserving.

itemVerdicts.item: Quote: 'The theater keeps getting more crowded, but the exit door is the same as it always was'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, and independently corroborated by CNBC 2019-09-04 which quotes the same sentence. In the source it sits at the end of the liquidity paragraph, immediately after 'trillions of dollars in assets globally are indexed to these stocks', and is followed by 'All this gets worse as you get into even less liquid equity and bond markets globally.' It is not a standalone standalone utterance.

itemVerdicts.item: Quote: 'Like most bubbles, the longer it goes on, the worse the crash will be'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the Yahoo/GuruFocus reproduction and independently in CNBC 2019-09-04 and in the Bloomberg excerpt reproduced elsewhere. Exact wording confirmed including the comma placement.

itemVerdicts.item: Burry gave no date, trigger, or magnitude
itemVerdicts.note: Directly supported: Burry ends the derivatives paragraph with 'However, I just don't know what the timeline will be.' No numeric magnitude anywhere in the interview. Caveat for precision: he does supply a MECHANISM even though he supplies no trigger event -- 'the impossibility of unwinding the derivatives and naked buy/sell strategies used to help so many of these funds pseudo-match flows and prices each and every day' -- and Bloomberg reported he said flows 'will reverse at some point' and 'it will be ugly'. So 'no date or magnitude' is airtight; 'no trigger' is fair only if it means no trigger EVENT, not no mechanism.
FRED series SP500 (price index, dividends excluded): 2019-09-03 = 2906.27; 2019-09-04 = 2937.78; 2019-09-05 = 2976.00. Exact match to the draft.

itemVerdicts.item: Current level 7,798.99 on 2026-08-13 and price-only gain of ~+165%
itemVerdicts.note: FRED series SP500: 2026-08-13 = 7798.99 (latest observation as of 2026-08-14). Recomputed: 7798.99 / 2937.78 = 2.65472, i.e. +165.47% price-only. Draft's '~+165%' is correct; +165.5% is the tighter figure. Flag on baseline choice: 2019-09-04 is the Bloomberg PUBLICATION date; the email interview was Tuesday 2019-09-03 (close 2906.27), which would give +168.4%. Either is defensible if labeled.

itemVerdicts.item: Scion Asset Management deregistered, SEC registration terminated ~2025-11-10
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as caliber): the approximate '~2025-11-10'. RIGHT: the date is exact. SEC IAPD primary record for SCION ASSET MANAGEMENT, LLC (firmId 167772, SEC# 801-113529) returns: 'registrationStatus': [{'secJurisdiction': 'SEC', 'status': 'Terminated', 'effectiveDate': '11/10/2025'}], with iaScope 'INACTIVE'. CNBC (published Nov 13 2025 6:24am ET, updated Nov 14) states: 'The Securities and Exchange Commission's database showed Scion's registration status as "terminated" as of November 10.' Drop the tilde.

itemVerdicts.item: Burry launched a paid Substack 'Cassandra Unchained' (~Nov 2025)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified at the publication itself: michaeljburry.substack.com, titled 'Cassandra Unchained', About page in Burry's own voice: 'After 25 years managing various Scion funds professionally, I've left the hedge fund business...' Archive API shows the earliest post is 2025-11-23 ('The Cardinal Sign of a Bubble: Supply-Side Gluttony'), confirming a ~Nov 2025 launch; consistent with Burry's X post 'On to much better things Nov 25th' quoted by CNBC. 'Paid' is confirmed primarily: nearly every archive entry carries audience 'only_paid'.

itemVerdicts.item: The Substack is 'focused on an AI-bubble thesis, not index funds'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'focused on an AI-bubble thesis' as a description of the publication's scope. RIGHT: the AI/hyperscaler bubble is its most publicized theme (Nvidia and Palantir pieces, hyperscaler depreciation-schedule accounting), but the archive is materially broader -- GameStop, Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac, Molina Healthcare, payments companies, Hong Kong equities, stock-based compensation, offshore insurers/private credit, and market-structure essays. Burry's own About page states the focus is 'stocks, market and economic trends, special situations, and investment manias.' The 'not index funds' half is separately unverified -- see next item.

itemVerdicts.item: Whether the Substack avoids the index-fund/passive topic
itemVerdicts.note: Could not verify the negative. Essentially all substantive posts are paywalled ('only_paid'). Two market-structure essays are live candidates for containing passive/indexing material -- 'Foundations: U.S. Market Structure & Value' (2026-03-03) and 'Foundations: Market Structure, Volatility Targeting, Pod Shops & Other Gremlins' (2026-07-31, plus an abridged 2026-08-03 version). The free preview of the July 31 post contains no occurrence of 'passive' or 'index', but it is truncated at the paywall, so absence there proves nothing. Do not assert that he has dropped the index-fund subject; assert only that he has not publicly revived the 2019 index-fund-as-CDO argument in the free/reported record.

itemVerdicts.item: Warning: acquirersmultiple.com reproduction retroactively edited with affiliate spam inside the quote
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed and worse than a generic warning. The page (acquirersmultiple.com/2019/09/michael-burry-explains-why-index-funds-are-like-subprime-cdos/) now reads: '"Like most bubbles, the longer it goes on, the worse the crash will be," said Burry, who oversees about $340 million at Scion Asset Management in Cupertino, California, and who has pointed to the proliferation of speculative retail products - from leveraged ETFs to the wave of crypto casino USA platforms absorbing disposable income that might otherwise sit in savings - as symptoms of the same late-cycle euphoria he has seen before.' The phrase 'crypto casino USA' is an anchor hyperlinked to binemon.io -- the only injected outbound link in the article body. Precision point: the insertion sits in the ATTRIBUTION clause immediately after the closing quotation mark, not literally between the quote marks, but it fabricates a claim about Burry that Bloomberg never published (the original continues 'in Cupertino, California. One reason he likes small-cap value stocks: they tend to be under-represented in passive funds.'). The Yahoo/GuruFocus reproduction was checked link-by-link and is clean.

corrections: Add a trailing ellipsis to the CDO quotation, or quote it in full. As drafted it ends at 'before the Great Financial Crisis', which is a mid-sentence cut presented as a sentence end. Burry's full sentence: 'This is very much like the bubble in synthetic asset-backed CDOs before the Great Financial Crisis in that price-setting in that market was not done by fundamental security-level analysis, but by massive capital flows based on Nobel-approved models of risk that proved to be untrue.'

Change '~2025-11-10' to the exact date. SEC IAPD's primary record for SCION ASSET MANAGEMENT, LLC (firmId 167772, SEC# 801-113529) gives registrationStatus status 'Terminated', effectiveDate '11/10/2025', iaScope 'INACTIVE'. No approximation is needed.

Replace 'a paid Substack "Cassandra Unchained" (~Nov 2025) focused on an AI-bubble thesis, not index funds' with a scope-accurate version, e.g. 'a paid Substack, Cassandra Unchained, launched in late November 2025 (first post 2025-11-23), whose most publicized theme has been the AI/hyperscaler bubble -- Nvidia and Palantir, and hyperscaler depreciation schedules -- rather than a revival of his 2019 index-fund argument.' Do not assert the publication is exclusively about AI: the archive also covers GameStop, Fannie/Freddie, Molina Healthcare, payments, Hong Kong equities, stock-based compensation, and market structure, and Burry's own About page describes the focus as 'stocks, market and economic trends, special situations, and investment manias.'

Do not state flatly that the Substack does not discuss index funds. Almost all posts are paywalled and two market-structure essays ('Foundations: U.S. Market Structure & Value', 2026-03-03; 'Foundations: Market Structure, Volatility Targeting, Pod Shops & Other Gremlins', 2026-07-31) could not be read. Claim only that he has not publicly revived the index-fund-as-CDO thesis in the free or reported record.

Label the S&P baseline as the Bloomberg PUBLICATION date, not the interview date. The email interview was conducted Tuesday 2019-09-03 (S&P close 2,906.27); Bloomberg published Wednesday 2019-09-04 (close 2,937.78). Using the 09-04 close gives +165.5%; using 09-03 would give +168.4%. State which one is used.
