itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' framing verbatim
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim at gs1980.txt line 40: 'We propose here a model in which there is an equilibrium degree of disequilibrium: prices reflect the information of informed individuals (arbitrageurs) but only partially, so that those who expend resources to obtain information do receive compensation.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Conjecture 2 + two-channel mechanism; 'more passive → higher active returns' is an unwritten contrapositive
itemVerdicts.note: Conjecture 2 verbatim (line 162-164): 'The more individuals who are informed, the lower the ratio of expected utility of the informed to the uninformed.' Two-channel mechanism spelled out at lines 126-156: (a) price system becomes more informative as more traders observe θ, shrinking the informed's informational edge; (b) even absent that, the changed ratio of informed-to-uninformed reduces the informed's per-capita relative gains from trade. Grepped the full text: zero occurrences of 'passive,' 'index fund,' or 'indexing' anywhere in the paper — the claim group's framing that 'more passive → higher active returns' is an inferred contrapositive the paper itself never states is accurate; GS1980 speaks only in terms of informed/uninformed fractions, not passive/active fund flows.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Conjecture 3: equilibrium informed fraction pinned down by cost of information; λ is an output, not a lever for exogenous fashion-driven indexing shocks
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (line 175-177): 'Conjecture 3: The higher the cost of information, the smaller will be the equilibrium percentage of individuals who are informed.' The model's exogenous parameters are cost of information, noise magnitude, and signal quality; the fraction informed (rendered as 'X' in this OCR extraction, almost certainly λ in original typesetting — no λ glyph survived the PDF-to-text conversion) is solved for endogenously via equal expected utility across informed/uninformed (lines 120-125). Nothing in the model treats an exogenous shift in investor preference toward indexing as a primitive shock; claim group's characterization is accurate.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Conjecture 6 / Section IV nonexistence result driven by noise→0, not by 'everyone indexes'
itemVerdicts.note: Conjecture 6 (line 198-204) and Section IV (lines 1218-1268) both confirm the nonexistence result is triggered when the noise terms vanish: 'when σ_a²=0 or Var(x*)=0, [the price signal], and thus price, does reflect all the information... Hence having any positive fraction informed is not an equilibrium. Having no one informed is also not an equilibrium.' This is exclusively about the noise/endowment-uncertainty parameters going to zero (prices becoming TOO informative), not about a scenario where 100% of investors choose to index while some remain willing to pay for information. Using this result to predict a breakdown from '100% passive adoption' is a misuse/mismatch of the model's actual comparative statics, exactly as the claim group states.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Conjecture 7: high-λ or low-λ corners predict thin markets, a volume claim not a mispricing claim
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (line 209-216): 'Conjecture 7: That, other things being equal, markets will be thinner under those conditions in which the percentage of individuals who are informed (X) is either near zero or near unity.' Section III (lines 1001-1042) develops this purely in terms of trading volume/magnitude of trade, driven by convergence of beliefs at the extremes — no claim about price-level distortion or mispricing appears in this section.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Authors' disclaimer: 'we have not been able to obtain a general proof of any of these propositions'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim at lines 219-221: 'Unfortunately, we have not been able to obtain a general proof of any of these propositions. What we have been able to do is to analyze in detail an interesting example...'

reasoning: Verified all six sub-claims against the local plaintext extraction of Grossman & Stiglitz (AER 1980), 'On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets,' pp. 393-408 (file gs1980.txt, 1797 lines). Read the full introduction (lines 1-245), the thinness-of-markets section (lines 1001-1042), and the perfect-markets/nonexistence section (lines 1218-1310) directly rather than relying on any summary or prior knowledge. Confirmed the 'equilibrium degree of disequilibrium' phrase verbatim; confirmed Conjectures 2, 3, 6, and 7 verbatim in the paper's own numbering and wording; confirmed the two-channel mechanism underlying Conjecture 2 is exactly as described (price-informativeness channel + per-capita relative-gains channel). Grepped the entire document for 'passive', 'index fund', 'indexing' — zero hits — confirming the claim group's point that any 'more passive → higher active returns' reading is an inference/contrapositive the authors never state; the paper is entirely about an informed/uninformed dichotomy, not fund flows or passive investing (which did not exist as a mainstream category in 1980). Confirmed the Section IV nonexistence result is driven strictly by the noise parameters (σ_a², Var(x*)) going to zero — i.e., prices becoming too informative — not by a scenario of universal indexing, so applying it to a '100%-passive market breaks down' claim would indeed be a model misuse as flagged by the claim group. Confirmed Conjecture 7 is stated purely as a trading-volume/thinness result, not a mispricing result. Confirmed the authors' explicit disclaimer that they lack a general proof of any conjecture, verbatim. No numerical, qualifier, or attribution slippage found anywhere in this claim group — every parenthetical caveat and nuance in the claim group (contrapositive framing, λ-as-output, noise-driven vs. participation-driven nonexistence, volume-not-mispricing) is not just uncontradicted but explicitly and precisely mirrored in the primary text's own language. Did not need external web fetches since every sub-claim is a direct textual claim about this one 1980 paper, fully checkable and fully confirmed against the primary source text itself; no later correction, retraction, or replication is at issue for a document-fidelity claim group of this kind.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) "equilibrium degree of disequilibrium" framing verbatim
itemVerdicts.note: Local gs1980.txt line 40: "there is an equilibrium degree of disequilibrium: prices reflect the information of informed individuals (arbitrageurs) but only partially, so that those who expend resources to obtain information do receive compensation." Exact match.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Conjecture 2 + two-channel mechanism; contrapositive note
itemVerdicts.note: Line 162-164: "Conjecture2: The more individuals who are informed, the lower the ratio of expected utility of the informed to the uninformed." Lines 125-155 give the two channels verbatim: (a) price system becomes more informative as more traders observe the signal, narrowing the informed's information edge; (b) as the ratio of informed to uninformed rises, informed traders' per-capita gains from trading with the uninformed shrink. Confirmed: the paper states only the 'more informed → lower relative utility' direction. Grepped the file for 'fewer'/'less informed'/'decrease...informed' language describing the reverse direction (fewer informed → higher active returns) — zero hits. The paper never writes out that inference; it is a converse/contrapositive inference readers draw from the monotonic Conjecture 2, not a sentence in the text. Note matches claim exactly.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Conjecture 3: informed fraction pinned by cost of information; λ as endogenous output
itemVerdicts.note: Line 175-177: "Conjecture 3: The higher the cost of information, the smaller will be the equilibrium percentage of individuals who are informed." The paper explicitly calls the informed fraction 'itself an endogenous variable in the model' (line 45-47). The model's symbol is X, not λ (the paper never uses λ; λ is the article's own notation choice, a cosmetic substitution, not a misrepresentation of the mechanism). The interpretive point — that an exogenous fashion-driven migration to indexing is not a shock-type the model contains, since the informed share is solved-for from primitives (cost, noise, signal quality) rather than imposed — is a fair reading; the model has no mechanism for an exogenous preference shock to X.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Conjecture 6 / Section II part I / Section IV nonexistence result driven by noise→0, not by universal indexing
itemVerdicts.note: Line 198-204 (Conjecture 6): "In the limit, when there is no noise, prices convey all information, and there is no incentive to purchase information. Hence, the only possible equilibrium is one with no information. But if everyone is uninformed, it clearly pays some individual to become informed... Thus, there does not exist a competitive equilibrium." Formal derivation at lines 859-928 shows nonexistence occurs 'as noise σ² goes to zero' (aε²=0 or Var x*=0), i.e. prices become TOO informative, not because participation collapses to universal passivity. Section IV (line 1218, "On the Possibility of Perfect Markets") restates this at lines 1255-1268: "when aε²=0 or Varx*=0, w*, and thus price, does reflect all the information... Hence having any positive fraction informed is not an equilibrium. Having no one informed is also not an equilibrium." Confirms the claim: nonexistence is a noise→0 result, and using it to argue a 100%-passive-indexing breakdown misreads the mechanism (the model's driver is signal/noise going to zero, not an exogenous mass migration to passive vehicles).

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Conjecture 7: high-λ or low-λ corners predict thin markets, a volume claim not a mispricing claim
itemVerdicts.note: Line 209-216: "Conjecture 7: That, other things being equal, markets will be thinner under those conditions in which the percentage of individuals who are informed (X) is either near zero or near unity... markets will be thin when there is very little noise in the system (so X is near zero), or when costs of information are very low (so X is near unity)." This is explicitly about market thinness (a volume/liquidity claim tied to belief homogeneity), confirmed also by Section III title 'On the Thinness of Speculative Markets' (line 1001) — not a mispricing claim.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) "we have not been able to obtain a general proof of any of these propositions"
itemVerdicts.note: Lines 217-222, verbatim: "In the last few paragraphs, we have provided a number of conjectures describing the nature of the equilibrium when prices convey information. Unfortunately, we have not been able to obtain a general proof of any of these propositions." Exact match.

reasoning: Verified all six sub-claims directly against the local extraction of Grossman & Stiglitz (AER 1980), "On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets" (gs1980.txt), which is a clean OCR of the JSTOR-hosted published version (pp. 393-408) matching the PIMS-hosted PDF cited. Read the full conjecture list (lines 140-239), the formal nonexistence derivation (lines 830-930), Section III's thin-markets discussion, and Section IV's restatement of the nonexistence result (lines 1218-1320) to confirm mechanism, not just label. Every quoted phrase in the claim group ("equilibrium degree of disequilibrium," each Conjecture's wording, and "we have not been able to obtain a general proof of any of these propositions") appears verbatim in the primary text at the cited locations. Confirmed via targeted grep (zero hits for 'fewer/less informed' phrasing) that the paper never writes out the passive-side converse of Conjecture 2 that the debate literature infers — this is genuinely the reader's contrapositive/converse inference, not a sentence in the paper. Confirmed the nonexistence result (Conjecture 6, formalized in Section II and restated in Section IV) is driven by the noise term (σ² of noisy supply or of the informed signal) going to zero — i.e., prices becoming too informative — and NOT by a scenario where everyone becomes passive/indexed; applying it to a "100% passive → market breakdown" argument is indeed a mechanism mismatch, as the claim group states. Confirmed Conjecture 7 is a market-thinness (volume/liquidity) claim, not a mispricing claim, cross-checked against Section III's title "On the Thinness of Speculative Markets." Ran one supplementary web search for errata/corrections/critiques of the 1980 AER paper; found none — this is the canonical, unmodified published version with no known corrigenda, and no later paper is known to have altered these specific propositions (only note is the notational point that the model uses X, not λ, for the informed fraction — a cosmetic labeling choice by the citing article, not a factual error, so it does not downgrade the verdict). All six sub-claims (a)-(f) check out with no caliber slippage between numerator/denominator, no version confusion, and no misattribution.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Green claims a breaking point at ~83% passive, derived with co-author Hari Krishnan, replicating an Andrew Lo-style 75-80% result; assumptions = all non-passive money fully active at elasticity 0.75-0.8, zero net flows; he calls 83% an 'outer limit' and says realistic assumptions move it lower
itemVerdicts.note: Every quoted element is verbatim in the transcript. Exact: 'that number of about 83% is actually a static number. That if you get to that level of passive effectively, the market becomes so impossibly volatile that it becomes an inevitable event that it will eventually cause its closure.' Assumptions: 'we are assuming that anyone who is not passive. Is fully active, effectively having a historical elasticity of about 0.75 to 0.8. Secondly, we are presuming no flows... It doesn't include any redemptions. It doesn't include any contributions'; 'And so we basically treat that 83% as an outer limit'; 'If we make some assumptions about declines in elasticity for active managers... That number moves significantly lower. If we start incorporating components of flow into that, that number also begins to fall dramatically.' WRONG as a present-tense characterization of the research: describing this as unpublished preliminary work with one co-author (Hari Krishnan) is stale as of 2026-08. RIGHT: the model is now a public SSRN preprint, Michael Green, Hari Krishnan and Stephan Sturm, 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market,' DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6438678, posted March 2026 (Crossref record: type posted-content, created 2026-03-27, three authors) — a THIRD co-author, Stephan Sturm. And the abstract's thresholds are NOT 83%: verbatim from Crossref-registered abstract, 'Once the passive share reaches around 65%, index volatility may increase sharply. At 90% share, an increase in volatility at cubic speed is nearly inevitable, leading to exaggerated boom and bust cycles.' Green's own 2026-07-12 Substack post repeats '~65%', not 83%: 'my model with Krishnan and Sturm showing that past calculable passive-share thresholds (as low as ~65%), violent boom-bust volatility becomes endogenous.' Also note the transcript is an auto-generated transcript with badly garbled proper names ('Xavier Bay'/'Xavier Gibe'/'Gbe' = Gabaix; 'Ralph Coy'/'Cogen' = Koijen; 'Andrew Lowe' = Andrew Lo; 'La Saint Peterson' = Lasse Pedersen; 'JP Booth' = almost certainly Jean-Philippe Bouchaud) — do not reproduce these spellings as quotations.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-sub) The Andrew Lo 75-80% result Green says he is replicating
itemVerdicts.note: I could not reach any Andrew Lo primary document (paper, book chapter, or transcript) stating a 75-80% passive threshold at which the market ceases to function. Multiple targeted searches over alo.mit.edu and the general web returned nothing containing that result. What IS verified is only that Green asserts it: 'is effectively a replication of work that was done by Andrew Lowe on a similar topic where he came to a very similar conclusion between 75 and 80% passive. The market would effectively cease functioning.' The article must attribute the 75-80% figure strictly to Green's characterization, never as an established Lo finding, and must not cite a Lo paper for it.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 'we're about 54% passive by market share and we picked up about 4% last year,' so 'five years out the world comes to an end'; the 54% denominator is undefined
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'my estimate is actually we're about 54% passive by market share and we picked up about 4% last year. So if that pace continues itself, we would be looking at somewhere in the neighborhood of five years out the world comes to an end.' The 'denominator undefined' charge is correct — the phrase 'by market share' is never defined anywhere in the transcript, and none of the three standard published denominators matches it: ICI 2026 Fact Book, 'At year-end 2025, index mutual funds and index ETFs together accounted for 52% of assets in long-term funds'; Morningstar Direct Dec-2025 monthly summary, 'As of year-end 2025, passively managed funds made up over 55% of net assets, increasing from 53% the year prior' (US funds universe); and ICI Fact Book Figure 2.6, index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs 'holding 19% of the value of US stocks at year-end 2025' (active domestic equity funds 11%, other investors 69%). So 54% is roughly the fund-assets measure and is nearly 3x the registered-fund share of US stock market capitalization.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Apple/CarMax arithmetic: Vanguard ~$350bn/yr inflows → Apple inflated ~23%/yr, 'that's actually more than Apple gained last year,' explained away via fundamentals
itemVerdicts.note: The quotes are verbatim: 'Vanguard's inflows last year were about $350 billion. The, that would suggest about a billion dollar order every day... Vanguard [sic — Apple] gets inflated by that order by 0.167%, right? CarMax gets inflated by 0.06%. If you scale that to an annual number, that works out to about a 6% increase in CarMax and about a 23% increase in Apple. By the way, that's actually more than Apple gained last year.' The ad hoc rescue is also verbatim: 'there are offsetting components to it among them, the fact that candidly, apple is not growing anymore. It doesn't have superior profitability or investment opportunities, it's failed in almost all of its new product introductions.' WRONG if the article presents $350bn as Vanguard's 2025 inflow: Morningstar Direct (Dec-2025 monthly summary) reports 'Vanguard's $240 billion inflow in 2025 was the second largest,' behind iShares at $366 billion, in the US long-term fund market. RIGHT: Green's $350bn is his own figure carried over from an earlier Substack piece ('Pay Attention to Your Privates') and does not match the 2025 US long-term-fund figure of ~$240bn.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(i) Gabaix-Koijen estimate the AGGREGATE market (stocks-vs-bonds) elasticity, point estimates 5.3/5.9/7.1/7.7/10.9 with SEs ~1.9-2.3
itemVerdicts.note: Aggregate stocks-vs-bonds framing CONFIRMED verbatim: 'when an investor sells $1 worth of bonds and buys $1 worth of stocks, what happens to the valuation of the aggregate stock market?' and 'the market's aggregate value goes up by about $5 (our estimates are between $3 and $8, and we will use $5 for simplicity in the theory and discussion).' All five point estimates CONFIRMED: Table 3 M = 7.08 and 5.28; text 'we estimate a multiplier of M = 7.1... The corresponding standard error is 1.9' and 'This lowers the multiplier estimate to M = 5.3'; derived 'M = 7.1 and M = 5.9'; Table 2 10.93 and 7.69, text 'the multiplier estimate equals M = 10.9' and 'the multiplier drops to M = 7.7 with a standard error of 2.3'. WRONG: 'SEs ~1.9-2.3'. RIGHT: the standard errors on those estimates span 1.10 to 2.64 — Table 3 gives 7.08 (1.86) and 5.28 (1.10); Table 2 gives 10.93 (2.64) and 7.69 (2.32); the 5.9 is a derived quantity (M = 1/(zeta+zeta_C)) with no directly reported SE. Also, if the article says Green 'cites the $1→$5 multiplier' in THIS transcript, that is a misquote: he says 'They estimated it was between five and eight' — GK's own stated range is '$3 and $8'.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(ii) GK contains essentially no analysis of passive indexing (one paraphrase of De Long 1990)
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED by exhaustive grep of the full May 12, 2022 Cowles/SSRN text: the word 'passive' appears exactly 3 times in the entire paper. One is a bibliography entry title (Haddad-Huebner-Loualiche, '...Implications for the Rise of Passive Investing'), one is an incidental modeling remark in an appendix ('we cannot model a plausible agent who would let his equity share drift passively'), and the only substantive use is the De Long paraphrase in the literature review: 'We build on the insights of De Long et al. (1990)... They discuss a rich set of qualitative ideas, some of which we can formally analyze and quantify, such as the failure of the Modigliani-Miller theorem and the notion that if most market participants passively hold the market portfolio, prices react sharply to flows. De Long et al. (1990) dealt with these issues qualitatively.' There is no index-fund share variable, no passive-ownership regression, and no indexing counterfactual anywhere in the paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (d)(iii) GK 'In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations' remains unpublished as of 2026-08 (NBER 28967 has no 'published as'); the companion GIV methods paper DID publish in JPE 2024
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED with a live fetch today (2026-08-14): nber.org/papers/w28967 contains no 'Published Versions' or 'Other Versions' block at all; its citation block reads 'NBER Working Paper 28967 (2021)'. Control test on the companion paper: nber.org/papers/w28204 DOES carry the block — 'Published Versions Xavier Gabaix & Ralph S. J. Koijen, 2024. "Granular Instrumental Variables," Journal of Political Economy, vol 132(7), pages 2274-2303' — so the field is populated when applicable. Crossref metadata for DOI 10.1086/728743 independently returns: title 'Granular Instrumental Variables', container 'Journal of Political Economy', volume 132, issue 7, pages 2274-2303, published 2024-07-01, authors Gabaix and Koijen.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Green left Simplify in 2026 to launch Tier1 Alpha, an ETF/SMA firm whose strategy trades passive-flow pressure
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED from Green's own first-person announcement (yesigiveafig.com, 'It's Time to Complicate', dated Aug 09, 2026), which I read directly rather than via a summarizer: 'After five extraordinary years, I am leaving Simplify Asset Management to found Tier1 Alpha Asset Management, where I will serve as CEO and CIO.' ETF/SMA structure confirmed verbatim: 'ETFs for RIAs and retail; SMAs and hedge funds for institutions. All built on the same underlying research.' Strategy confirmed verbatim: 'We seek to measure the smaller, continuous mechanical flow' and 'Our flagship implementation holds essentially the same securities as the leading U.S. large-cap benchmark, then tilts modestly and systematically toward the securities where our measurement suggests passive demand is strongest relative to available liquidity.' WRONG: 'launch Tier1 Alpha' — the Tier1 Alpha brand pre-dated the departure. RIGHT: he founded a new entity, Tier1 Alpha Asset Management, built on the pre-existing research arm: 'Tier1 Alpha Research, built alongside Simplify to fund my work on market structure, forms the core.' Green's own 2023 About page already said 'working with Tier1Alpha helped to reignite the writing itch.' Also note the timing: in the Jan-2026 podcast he is still 'Chief Investment strategist and portfolio manager at Simplify Asset Management' and refers to 'the team at Tier one Alpha' as collaborators — the departure is seven months after the interview.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Green called Vanguard's Aug-2025 paper 'intentionally misleading' with a composition objection (REIT/sector index funds diluting the mid-cap ownership stat)
itemVerdicts.note: CONFIRMED on both halves. The paper is Vanguard research, August 2025, 'Setting the record straight: The truths about index fund investing' (Rowley, Lawrence, Ryder-Green). Green uses 'intentionally misleading' twice — on the trading-volume chart ('They are being intentionally misleading in this chart') and on the mid-cap point ('I think that there's a couple of things, and again, I think they're being intentionally misleading'). The composition objection is verbatim: 'they're including index funds. That would be like the REIT index or nuclear power index... many of those are actually being forced into mid-caps by virtue of concentration limits... nobody in their 401k has the REIT ETF as their default investment vehicle.' Worth noting for balance: Vanguard's Figure 5 note says it covers 'index mutual funds for stocks in the Russell 3000 Index as of December 31, 2024,' and Vanguard itself concedes the aggregation point — 'Given the diversity of equity index fund offerings and investors using passive for active, it should not be a surprise that index funds' ownership of stocks is not market-cap proportional.'

itemVerdicts.item: Source metadata: Excess Returns transcript dated 2026-01-21
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 2026-01-21. RIGHT: the post's own machine-readable timestamp is datetime="2026-01-20T21:49:53.854Z" and the visible byline reads 'Jan 20, 2026'. That is Jan 20 in every US time zone.

corrections: Do not describe the 83% figure as the current state of the Green-Krishnan research. It is now a public SSRN preprint with a third co-author: Michael Green, Hari Krishnan and Stephan Sturm, 'A Model for Passive That Breaks the Market,' DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6438678, posted March 2026, still unpublished in any journal. Its abstract's thresholds are 65% and 90%, not 83%: 'Once the passive share reaches around 65%, index volatility may increase sharply. At 90% share, an increase in volatility at cubic speed is nearly inevitable, leading to exaggerated boom and bust cycles.' Green himself now writes '~65%' (yesigiveafig.com, 2026-07-12). If the article keeps the 83% number, label it explicitly as the preliminary figure Green gave on the January 2026 podcast, and add that the formalized paper reports a lower threshold.

Change the Gabaix-Koijen standard errors from '~1.9-2.3' to a range of 1.10 to 2.64. Exact pairings from the May 2022 Cowles/SSRN version: Table 3 M = 7.08 (SE 1.86) and M = 5.28 (SE 1.10); Table 2 M = 10.93 (SE 2.64) and M = 7.69 (SE 2.32). The 5.9 figure is derived as M = 1/(zeta + zeta_C) and has no directly reported standard error. Only the two SEs quoted in GK's running text (1.9 on the 7.1 estimate, 2.3 on the 7.7 estimate) fall in the '1.9-2.3' band.

Do not write that Green 'cites Gabaix-Koijen's $1→$5 multiplier' if the citation is to this transcript. In this transcript he says GK 'estimated it was between five and eight.' Gabaix-Koijen's own text says the aggregate value 'goes up by about $5 (our estimates are between $3 and $8, and we will use $5 for simplicity).' Either quote Green's 'five and eight' and note it misstates GK's $3-$8 range, or cite the $5 figure to GK directly rather than to Green.

Change 'launched Tier1 Alpha' to 'founded Tier1 Alpha Asset Management.' Green's own announcement (yesigiveafig.com, 'It's Time to Complicate,' Aug 09, 2026) reads: 'After five extraordinary years, I am leaving Simplify Asset Management to found Tier1 Alpha Asset Management, where I will serve as CEO and CIO.' The Tier1 Alpha research arm already existed — 'Tier1 Alpha Research, built alongside Simplify to fund my work on market structure, forms the core' — and Green was publicly working with Tier1Alpha as far back as 2023. Also state that at the time of the January 2026 interview he was still Simplify's chief investment strategist and portfolio manager; the departure came seven months later.
Change the transcript date from 2026-01-21 to 2026-01-20. The Substack post carries datetime="2026-01-20T21:49:53.854Z" and the byline 'Jan 20, 2026'.

If the article states Vanguard's inflows as ~$350bn for 2025, attribute it to Green rather than asserting it. Morningstar Direct's December 2025 monthly summary reports 'Vanguard's $240 billion inflow in 2025 was the second largest,' behind iShares' $366 billion, in the US long-term fund market. Green's $350bn figure is carried over from his earlier Substack piece 'Pay Attention to Your Privates' and is not the 2025 number.

When making the 'denominator is undefined' point about 54%, anchor it with the three published measures so readers can see the spread: ICI 2026 Fact Book — index mutual funds plus index ETFs were '52% of assets in long-term funds' at year-end 2025; Morningstar Direct — 'passively managed funds made up over 55% of net assets, increasing from 53% the year prior' (US funds universe); ICI Fact Book Figure 2.6 — index domestic equity mutual funds and ETFs hold '19% of the value of US stocks at year-end 2025' (active domestic equity funds 11%, all other investors 69%). Note that on the Morningstar denominator the 2025 gain was about 2 percentage points, not the 4 Green cites.

Attribute the 75-80% threshold strictly to Green's own characterization ('a replication of work that was done by Andrew Lowe [Lo]'). I could not locate any Andrew Lo primary source stating that result. Do not cite a Lo paper, book, or interview as support for it.

If the article quotes the transcript, silently correct or bracket the auto-transcription's garbled names rather than reproducing them: 'Xavier Bay'/'Xavier Gibe'/'Gbe' = Xavier Gabaix; 'Ralph Coy'/'Cogen' = Ralph Koijen; 'Andrew Lowe' = Andrew Lo; 'La Saint Peterson'/'Last St. Peterson' = Lasse Pedersen; 'Bill Sharp' = Bill Sharpe; 'JP Booth' (cited for the square-root market-impact law) = Jean-Philippe Bouchaud. Also note the transcript says 'Vanguard gets inflated by that order by 0.167%' where the context requires Apple.
newContradictions: Green's own five-year timeline does not reach his own threshold. He states 54% passive today, +4 points a year, and 'somewhere in the neighborhood of five years out the world comes to an end.' 54 + 4x5 = 74%, which is below the 83% 'outer limit' he had just described; reaching 83% at 4 points a year takes about 7.25 years. The five-year figure only works against a threshold in the 74-75% region, i.e. against the lower Lo-style number, not against his own model's headline. The article should not present '54% + 4%/yr → 83% → five years' as an internally consistent chain.

The Apple/CarMax daily and annual figures do not reconcile under any straightforward annualization. 0.167% per day over ~252 trading days is roughly 42% simple or 52% compounded, not the stated 23%; 0.06% per day is roughly 15%, not the stated 6%. The ratios also disagree (23/6 = 3.8 versus 0.167/0.06 = 2.8). Quote the annual figures as his stated outputs and do not present the daily numbers as the derivation, or the article inherits an arithmetic error that is not its own.

The paper that materialized in March 2026 makes a weaker and differently-shaped claim than the podcast. The SSRN abstract says volatility 'may increase sharply' at ~65% and cubic-speed volatility growth is 'nearly inevitable' at 90% — hedged language about volatility dynamics and 'exaggerated boom and bust cycles.' The podcast framing was a hard closure event ('the market becomes so impossibly volatile that it becomes an inevitable event that it will eventually cause its closure', 'once it becomes a mathematical certainty'). Any article treating the podcast's certainty language as the research's claim overstates what the written paper asserts.

Vanguard's August 2025 paper partly pre-concedes Green's composition objection rather than being contradicted by it: 'Given the diversity of equity index fund offerings and investors using passive for active, it should not be a surprise that index funds' ownership of stocks is not market-cap proportional.' Presenting the exchange as Green catching Vanguard in a hidden trick overstates the gap; the real dispute is over which fund population belongs in the denominator, and neither side quantifies the sector/REIT contribution to the mid-cap peak.

Green's 'roughly 80% of market volume' passive-trading figure in this transcript is sourced to 'Hagstrom in 2013' and 'market structure edge' and is defined to include market-making, ETF creation/redemption hedging, and index options hedging. That is a fundamentally different construct from Vanguard's Figure 6 (index fund trading volume adjusted for cash flows). If the article reports the 80% number, it must carry that definitional caveat; it is not comparable to any share-of-trading statistic Vanguard or the exchanges publish. I did not verify the 80% figure against any primary source.
reasoning: Documents reached verbatim: (1) the Excess Returns transcript page itself (local capture plus its embedded datetime attribute), which I dedented and read in full for every quoted string rather than relying on any summary; (2) the Gabaix-Koijen May 12 2022 Cowles/SSRN full text, where I read the abstract, the introduction's $1/$5 passage, the literature review's De Long paragraph, and Tables 2 and 3 including the parenthesized standard errors, and ran an exhaustive grep for 'passive' (3 hits total); (3) nber.org/papers/w28967 fetched live today, confirming no Published Versions block, with nber.org/papers/w28204 fetched as a control showing the block IS present and names JPE 132(7) 2274-2303; (4) Crossref API for DOI 10.1086/728743 (GIV, JPE 2024) and for DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6438678, which returned the Green-Krishnan-Sturm authorship, the posted-content type, the 2026-03-27 creation timestamp, and the JATS abstract text with the 65%/90% thresholds — registry metadata, not a summarizer; (5) Green's own Substack posts 'It's Time to Complicate' (Aug 09 2026) and 'You Can Lead a Horse to Water' (Jul 12 2026), fetched by curl and stripped to text so I read his words rather than a model's paraphrase; (6) Vanguard's August 2025 'Setting the record straight' full text, including the Figure 5 note and the mid-cap passage; (7) ICI 2026 Fact Book chapter 2 (Figure 2.6, 19% of US stock market cap) and ICI Perspective 32 (52% of long-term fund assets); (8) Morningstar Direct December 2025 monthly summary (55% passive share, up from 53%; Vanguard $240bn vs iShares $366bn). SSRN's own abstract page is Cloudflare-blocked to both curl and WebFetch, so the GKS paper's full text — and specifically whether 83% appears anywhere inside it — is unverified; I relied on Crossref's registered abstract and Green's own description of the paper, which agree on ~65%. The Andrew Lo 75-80% result is the one item I could not reach at all: no Lo paper, book passage, or interview surfaced containing it, so the article must carry it as Green's assertion only. I deliberately discarded two search-summary claims that could not be traced to document text (a 'March 18, 2026' posting date and various narrative gloss on the GKS model) and used only the Crossref timestamp instead. Remaining uncertain: the exact universe behind Green's 54% and 4%/yr, which he never defines and which matches no published series; whether his $350bn Vanguard figure refers to 2023, 2024, or global rather than US flows; and the provenance of his 80%-of-volume figure.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) EXPANSIÓN interview dated December 2025
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "Dec 2025 EXPANSIÓN interview." RIGHT: the interview was published Monday 3 November 2025, by Roberto Casado in Expansión. Verified two ways: Fundsmith's own reproduction is datelined "Monday, 3 November 2025 / By Roberto Casado, Expansión" (https://www.fundsmith.eu/news/2025/6539-expansion-interview-terry-smith-there-could-be-a-stock-market-bubble-more-extreme-than-the-one-in-2000/), and the Expansión original at https://www.expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/6904bb30e5fdea145f8b459b.html carries <meta name="date" content="2025-11-03T00:59:29Z"/> and <meta name="DC.date.issued" content="2025-11-03T00:59:29Z"/>. The "December 2025" almost certainly comes from The Acquirer's Multiple's re-post URL (acquirersmultiple.com/2025/12/...), which is a republication date, not the interview date.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quote: "More than 50% of assets are now invested through index funds, which are not actually passive; they are a momentum strategy"
itemVerdicts.note: Exact, including the semicolon, in Fundsmith's published English text: "The effects are profound. More than 50% of assets are now invested through index funds, which are not actually passive; they are a momentum strategy [investing in assets with the best recent performance]." Spanish original in Expansión: "Los efectos son profundos. Más del 50% de los activos están ahora invertidos a través de fondos indexados, que en realidad no son pasivos, son una estrategia de momentum..." Two caveats: (i) the bracketed gloss is the journalist's, not Smith's — do not include it inside the quotation; (ii) the page is headed "TRANSLATION FROM SPANISH", so the English is Fundsmith's rendering of Expansión's Spanish, not Smith's own recorded English words.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quote: "in 2000 less than 10% of funds were index funds, and now it's more than 50%"
itemVerdicts.note: Exact. Full sentence: "The effects are more extreme than in the dot-com bubble because in 2000 less than 10% of funds were index funds, and now it's more than 50%." Spanish: "Los efectos son más extremos que en la burbuja puntocom, porque en 2000 menos del 10% de los fondos eran indexados y ahora son más del 50%." The claim's own flag is correct: the denominator does switch from "activos"/assets in the first answer to "fondos"/funds here, and neither geography nor asset class is specified anywhere in the interview.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Letter quote: market "dominated by so-called passive or index funds (of which the majority are ETFs)" + AI
itemVerdicts.note: Exact, p.1 of the July 2026 semi-annual letter: "The backdrop to this continues to be a market which is dominated by so-called passive or index funds (of which the majority are ETFs) and the boom surrounding AI which have combined to produce a market dominated by momentum rather than any fundamental factors like profitability, returns on capital and growth — in other words the factors we focus on."

itemVerdicts.item: (b) momentum's relative performance "at a 30 year high and more extreme than in late 1999"
itemVerdicts.note: The words are exact — p.3: "It is at a 30 year high and more extreme than in late 1999 just before the Dotcom bubble burst." But the referent needs care. WRONG framing: presenting it as a measured statistic about "momentum's relative performance." RIGHT framing: Smith writes "the performance of momentum based investment is clear as this Bloomberg chart illustrates:" followed by an unlabelled chart sourced only to "Bloomberg"; "It" refers to that chart. The letter never names the momentum index/factor, the universe, the geography, or whether it is absolute or relative. Attribute as Smith's characterisation of an unspecified Bloomberg momentum series, not as a verified figure.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) "I profess no insight into how or when this passive-led momentum market will end, other than to say badly."
itemVerdicts.note: Exact, verbatim, p.6 of the letter.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Fundsmith Equity H1 2026 -2.9% vs MSCI World +11.2%, ~14.1pp shortfall, T-class GBP
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in the primary letter's performance table: Fundsmith Equity Fund -2.9, Equities +11.2 for "1st Jan to 30th June 2026" (% Total Return). Footnote 1: "T Class Accumulation shares, net of fees priced at midday UK time, Inception, 1.11.2010, source: Bloomberg." Footnote 2: "MSCI World Index, £ Net, priced at close of business US time, source: www.msci.com." So yes, T Class Accumulation, GBP. Body text states the gap itself: "Our Fund was down by 2.9% in the first six months of the year, 14.1 percentage points less than what is perhaps the most obvious comparator — the MSCI World Index (£ net)." Note for precision: the two series are struck at different times (fund at midday UK, index at US close), and the table carries the disclaimer "The Fund is not managed with reference to any benchmark; the above comparators are provided for information purposes only."

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~52% portfolio turnover in six months
itemVerdicts.note: Substantively right, but the letter gives two figures and the article should cite the precise one. WRONG (imprecise): "~52%." RIGHT: 51.8% — Appendix 1, verbatim: "Our portfolio turnover in the first half was 51.8%." The main body separately rounds it: "our portfolio turnover hit a high of 51% in the first half of this year as we made significant changes in the portfolio. However, you should not expect that level of turnover to become the norm." The letter also defines the measure in its endnotes: "total share purchases and sales less total creations and liquidations divided by the average net asset value of the fund" — i.e. it nets out flow-driven dealing. Same appendix: voluntary dealing cost £11,404,962 (0.084%); OCF for T Class Acc 1.05%; Total Cost of Investment 1.12%.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) explicit process change to incorporate momentum
itemVerdicts.note: Exact, p.6: "We will take more account of momentum — both fundamental and share price — in our investment decisions. In particular, we will be much less willing to deploy the time-honoured technique of buying quality companies when they hit a glitch." Also "You should therefore expect that we will be more active in future" and the framing that the third leg of the mantra ("Do nothing") "probably needs the most change." He also explicitly disclaims index-hugging: "We have no desire to hug the index."

itemVerdicts.item: Primary letter reachable at fundsmith.co.uk
itemVerdicts.note: Reached and downloaded directly: https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/lfhpxi1x/fundsmith-equity-fund-semi-annual-letter-to-shareholders-2026.pdf — HTTP 200, application/pdf, 1,887,462 bytes, MD5 c1705ca2348b0df90f3ea989b0fd13e6, 17 pages, PDF CreationDate Fri 24 Jul 2026. Saved to /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/v3_fs.pdf and extracted with pdftotext -layout to v3_fs.txt. The site's HTML pages are behind a Cloudflare challenge (403 to curl and WebFetch), but the /media/ PDF path serves directly. Sourcing no longer needs to rest on secondary reproductions.

corrections: Redate the EXPANSIÓN interview: it was published 3 November 2025 (Roberto Casado, Expansión, https://www.expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/6904bb30e5fdea145f8b459b.html), not December 2025. The December 2025 date is The Acquirer's Multiple's republication date.

Change '~52% portfolio turnover' to '51.8%' and cite Appendix 1 of the July 2026 letter ('Our portfolio turnover in the first half was 51.8%'). If quoting the body text instead, the figure there is 51% ('our portfolio turnover hit a high of 51% in the first half of this year'). Do not present 52%.

Cite the primary letter directly — https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/lfhpxi1x/fundsmith-equity-fund-semi-annual-letter-to-shareholders-2026.pdf (July 2026, 17pp) — and drop reliance on acquirersmultiple.com / valueandopportunity.com as the source of the quotes.

When quoting the interview in English, note that Fundsmith's own page is headed 'TRANSLATION FROM SPANISH': the interview was published in Spanish, and the English wording is a translation, not a transcript of Smith speaking. Do not include the journalist's bracketed gloss '[investing in assets with the best recent performance]' inside the quotation marks.

Qualify the '30 year high' figure. The letter attributes it to an unlabelled Bloomberg chart introduced as 'the performance of momentum based investment' and never specifies the momentum measure, universe, geography, or whether it is absolute or relative. Attribute it as Smith's characterisation of a Bloomberg chart, not as an independently verifiable statistic.

Specify the return basis precisely: -2.9% is Fundsmith Equity Fund T Class Accumulation shares, net of fees, priced midday UK time (source Bloomberg); +11.2% is MSCI World Index, £ Net, priced at US close. The two are struck at different times, and Fundsmith states the fund 'is not managed with reference to any benchmark; the above comparators are provided for information purposes only.'
newContradictions: Smith's own index-share numbers move within eight months without explanation: '>50% of assets' (Expansión, 3 Nov 2025) becomes 'AUM in index funds is now >60%' (July 2026 letter, p.3). If the article quotes both, it should not present them as a consistent series. Morningstar's year-end 2025 US fund flows report puts passive at a 55% market share of US fund assets — so the '>50%' is defensible for US open-end funds + ETFs, but the '>60%' is above Morningstar's US measure and far above any global-fund or share-of-market-cap measure. Neither Smith statement specifies a denominator.

The July 2026 letter contains a further unverified attribution the article may be tempted to pick up: 'According to Cboe Global Markets, having been 80% of trades in the 1990s, active funds share of trades is now down to just 10%.' No Cboe publication is cited, and this is a share-of-TRADING claim, not share of assets — a different denominator again. Treat as unverified if used.

The letter's UK example is borrowed second-hand from a Substack ('Wealth Yourself' by Simon Evan-Cook) rather than computed by Fundsmith: 'Vanguard's UK All Share tracker has made 66% over the past five years, trouncing the average UK equity fund's return of just 32%.' Same for '12 of the top 20 performers over five years are trackers' and 'Half of Vanguard's FTSE 100 tracker is held in just 10 stocks.' Any of these repeated in the article need their own verification chain.

Selection/attribution tension worth noting: Smith cites the H1 2026 shortfall as evidence that passive flows distort prices, but the letter simultaneously reports that the fund's five largest detractors were LVMH, Zoetis, IDEXX, Microsoft and Coloplast — stock-specific quality/valuation calls — and Appendix 2 attributes the sales to 'a complex mix of factors including lack of fundamental momentum, mismanagement and simple valuation.' The letter is therefore weaker support for a market-structure thesis than the headline quotes imply; it is an interested party's account of its own underperformance.
reasoning:
I reached the primary letter myself rather than relying on the pre-extracted scratchpad copy. fundsmith.co.uk HTML is behind a Cloudflare challenge (403 to both curl and WebFetch), but a web search surfaced the direct /media/ PDF path, which serves without challenge: https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/media/lfhpxi1x/fundsmith-equity-fund-semi-annual-letter-to-shareholders-2026.pdf returned HTTP 200, application/pdf, 1,887,462 bytes, MD5 c1705ca2348b0df90f3ea989b0fd13e6, 17 pages, PDF CreationDate 24 Jul 2026 (macOS Quartz). It is byte-identical (same MD5) to the earlier scratchpad copy v9_fs.pdf, which independently authenticates that copy. I ran pdftotext -layout myself and read the performance table, pp.1-9, and Appendix 1 verbatim. Every quote in sub-claims (b) and (c) matched exactly, character for character, including the semicolon-free em-dash phrasing. The only caliber slip in (c) is turnover: the article's '~52%' should be 51.8% (Appendix 1) or 51% (body text) — both figures appear in the letter, neither is 52.

For (a) I did not settle for the secondary reproductions. Fundsmith hosts the interview on fundsmith.eu, which is NOT Cloudflare-challenged (200, 76-85KB), in both Spanish and an English version explicitly headed 'TRANSLATION FROM SPANISH'; I stripped tags myself and read the full body of each. Both are datelined 'Monday, 3 November 2025'. I then reached the Expansión original at https://www.expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/6904bb30e5fdea145f8b459b.html (the exact URL is printed at the foot of the Fundsmith page; my first guessed URL 404'd), HTTP 200, and confirmed both <meta name="date"> and <meta name="DC.date.issued"> = 2025-11-03T00:59:29Z, and that the two Spanish sentences appear verbatim in the article body. So the interview is 3 November 2025, not December 2025 — the December date is The Acquirer's Multiple's republication slug. Both English quotations in the claim match Fundsmith's published translation word for word.

I searched for later corrections, replications or retractions up to August 2026 and found none — coverage in Trustnet, ii.co.uk, Forbes and valueandopportunity all reproduces 51.8%, -2.9% and +11.2% consistently with the primary letter. No Fundsmith erratum exists that I could find.

Remaining uncertainty: I did not independently recompute MSCI World £ Net H1 2026 (+11.2%) or the T Class Acc return (-2.9%) from MSCI/Bloomberg data — these are Fundsmith's own reported figures, sourced in the letter to msci.com and Bloomberg, and I verified only that the letter says what the article says it says. The '30 year high' momentum chart is an image in the PDF with no axis labels recoverable from text extraction and no underlying series named, so it is not independently checkable and should be attributed rather than asserted. Whether Smith's '>50% of assets' and '>60% AUM' index-share figures are themselves true is outside this claim group but flagged as a contradiction, since Morningstar's YE2025 figure of 55% for US fund assets sits between them.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Gârleanu & Pedersen, "Active and Passive Investing: Understanding Samuelson's Dictum" — result (5): cost of passive investing decreases → inefficiency increases, especially macro-inefficiency
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in gp.txt intro (p.2/lines 48-50): 'when the cost of passive investing decreases, market inefficiency increases, especially macro-inefficiency, the number of active mangers decreases, and active fees drop by less than passive fees.' Also restated in Conclusion (line ~1640): 'falling fees of passive investing will increase market inefficiency, lower active fees by less than the passive fees...'

itemVerdicts.item: (a) result (4): information costs decline → inefficiency decreases, especially macro (counter to Samuelson)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (line 49): 'when information costs decline, the number of active managers increases, active fees decrease, market inefficiency decreases, especially macro-inefficiency (counter to part of Samuelson's dictum)'. Also line ~160-162.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) both forces (falling info costs, falling passive costs) coexisted ~25 years, net prediction ambiguous
itemVerdicts.note: Not a verbatim claim in the paper — no line states a 25-year window or an explicit 'net effect ambiguous' synthesis of results (4)+(5). The paper DOES separately date the trends: declining information costs 'consistent with the development in the 1980s and 1990s' (line 165) and declining passive-management costs 'consistent with the development in the 2000s' (line 168-169) — a ~20-30 year span roughly matching '25 years,' and since (4) and (5) do point in opposite directions on inefficiency, ambiguity of the net effect is a fair logical inference. But this specific '25 years / net ambiguous' framing is the article's own synthesis, not a sentence the paper itself asserts — cite it as inference, not direct quote.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Pedersen is a principal at AQR (disclosed in paper)
itemVerdicts.note: Footnote on p.1 of gp.txt: 'Pedersen is at AQR Capital Management, Copenhagen Business School, and CEPR' plus a conflict-style disclosure sentence: 'AQR Capital Management is a global investment management firm, which may or may not apply similar investment techniques...The views expressed here are those of the authors and not necessarily those of AQR.' The paper discloses the AQR affiliation but does not itself use the word 'principal' — that title is accurate per Pedersen's public bio but is not the paper's own wording.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Publication venue/year: Review of Asset Pricing Studies, 2022
itemVerdicts.note: gp.txt's own citation line says '...The Review of Asset Pricing Studies, 2021' (likely acceptance/online-first year), but WebSearch confirms the actual published version is Vol. 12, Issue 2, June 2022, pp.389-446 (academic.oup.com/raps/article/12/2/389/6350496). Claim's '2022' is the correct published year.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Bond & Garcia, "The Equilibrium Consequences of Indexing" — participation decisions are strategic complements, footnote contrasting with G-S substitutability
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim footnote 3 (bondgarcia.txt lines 66-71): 'Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) analyze traders' decisions to become informed...and show that information acquisition decisions are strategic substitutes...In contrast, we consider a setting without exogenous noise traders, and analyze traders' participation decisions.' Main text (line 62): 'participation decisions are strategic complements.' Self-reinforcing dynamic confirmed explicitly at line ~1277: 'because of the strategic complementarities established in Proposition 3, participation is self-reinforcing.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) indexing raises welfare even of uninformed traders
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim (bondgarcia.txt line 56-57): 'investor welfare increases, even for the least informed investors, as we discuss below.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) falling indexing costs reduce index price efficiency, raise relative price efficiency of individual stocks
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim abstract: 'A decline in indexing costs directly increases the prevalence of indexing, thereby reducing the price efficiency of the index and augmenting relative price efficiency.' Restated (line ~68-69): 'As indexing costs fall, and indexing increases, price efficiency of the index as a whole falls, while the relative price efficiency of individual stocks increases.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Publication venue/year: Review of Financial Studies, 2022
itemVerdicts.note: Local file header shows working-paper drafts (Sept 2016 / April 2019), but WebSearch confirms published version: Review of Financial Studies, Vol. 35, Issue 7, July 2022, pp.3175-3230 (academic.oup.com/rfs/article-abstract/35/7/3175/6371883).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Chabakauri & Rytchkov — indexing decreases market volatility in their model
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim abstract (cr.txt): 'Overall, indexing decreases market volatility but has an ambiguous effect on the correlations.' This directly contradicts the fabrication scenario described in the prompt (a summarizer claiming indexing RAISES volatility) — the real paper says the opposite, DECREASES.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Chabakauri & Rytchkov — makes no informativeness claim
itemVerdicts.note: Searched cr.txt (7738 lines, full accepted-manuscript text) for the string 'informativ' — zero matches anywhere in the document. Confirms the paper makes no price-informativeness claim at all; the fabrication warning in the prompt (that a summarizer invented an informativeness claim) is correct to flag as fabricated.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Publication venue/year: Journal of Financial Economics, 2021
itemVerdicts.note: cr.txt header: 'Journal of Financial Economics, 141(1), 195-216' with DOI 10.1016/j.jfineco.2020.06.023 — this is the LSE Research Online 'Accepted Version' of the JFE 2021 publication, consistent with claim.

corrections: (a) The '25 years' / explicit 'net prediction is ambiguous' framing combining results (4) and (5) is not a sentence stated verbatim anywhere in Gârleanu & Pedersen (RAPS 2022) — it is a reasonable synthesis by the article's author, not a direct paper quote. The paper separately dates the two trends: declining information costs 'consistent with the development in the 1980s and 1990s' and declining passive-management costs 'consistent with the development in the 2000s' (gp.txt lines 165-169). If the article presents the '25 years, net ambiguous' line as if it were the paper's own statement, reword to attribute it as an inference from combining the paper's two separately-dated trends and its two directionally-opposite results, not as a quoted finding.

(a) The paper's own citation line (gp.txt, p.1) lists the published version as 'The Review of Asset Pricing Studies, 2021' — this is likely an online-first/acceptance date on the authors' working-paper PDF. The actual print publication is Vol. 12, Issue 2, June 2022 (confirmed via Oxford Academic). The article's claim of 'RAPS 2022' is correct; flag only if the article cites '2021' anywhere, which would need updating to 2022.
reasoning:
Checked all three local extraction files verbatim in the scratchpad. gp.txt (3616 lines, Gârleanu & Pedersen working paper with published-version citation banner) contains the numbered findings list on p.2 verbatim: result (4) 'when information costs decline...market inefficiency decreases, especially macro-inefficiency (counter to part of Samuelson's dictum)' and result (5) 'when the cost of passive investing decreases, market inefficiency increases, especially macro-inefficiency...'. Confirmed via WebSearch that the actual published venue is Rev. Asset Pricing Studies Vol 12(2), June 2022 (the paper's own citation banner says 2021, likely acceptance year). Pedersen's AQR affiliation is disclosed in the footnote. No sentence in gp.txt explicitly frames the '25 years / net ambiguous' synthesis — this appears to be the claim-group's own reasonable inference from the paper's two separately-dated trend discussions (1980s-90s info costs; 2000s passive costs) plus the opposite-signed results 4 and 5; flagged as a caveat rather than a fabrication since it's logically consistent with the paper.

bondgarcia.txt (3892 lines, Bond & Garcia working-paper draft, April 2019) confirms verbatim: abstract states falling indexing costs 'reduc[e] the price efficiency of the index and augment[] relative price efficiency,' and 'raise the welfare of uninformed traders.' Footnote 3 explicitly contrasts their strategic-complements finding with Grossman-Stiglitz (1980) strategic-substitutes result, exactly as the claim describes. Text explicitly states welfare increases 'even for the least informed investors' and that 'participation is self-reinforcing' due to strategic complementarity. WebSearch confirms actual publication: Review of Financial Studies Vol 35(7), July 2022.

cr.txt (7738 lines, Chabakauri & Rytchkov LSE-hosted accepted manuscript) abstract states verbatim: 'Overall, indexing decreases market volatility but has an ambiguous effect on the correlations' — confirming the DECREASE direction and directly refuting the fabrication scenario described in the prompt. A full-text grep for 'informativ' across all 7738 lines returned zero matches, confirming the paper makes no informativeness claim whatsoever — the fabrication-warning scenario is correctly identified as fabricated. Header confirms JFE 141(1), 195-216, 2021, matching claim.

All three sub-claims (a), (b), (c) check out on the specific numerical/directional assertions and publication venues/years. The only soft spot is the '25 years / net prediction ambiguous' composite framing in (a), which is an interpretive synthesis rather than a verbatim paper statement — logically consistent with the paper's content but should be presented as inference, not quotation.

itemVerdicts.item: Garleanu & Pedersen (2022) Result (5): passive-investing cost decline → inefficiency increases, especially macro
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in gp.txt Proposition 7 (p.39): 'As the cost of passive investing kp = fp decreases, the overall asset price inefficiency (η) increases and the macro-inefficiency η_βv increases by more than the total micro-inefficiency ... as long as n is not too small.' Matches abstract item (5) exactly.

itemVerdicts.item: Garleanu & Pedersen (2022) Result (4): information-cost decline → inefficiency decreases, especially macro
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in gp.txt Proposition 6 (p.38): 'When the cost of information k decreases, overall asset price inefficiency η decreases and the macro-inefficiency η_βv decreases by more than the total micro-inefficiency ... as long as n is not too small.' Matches abstract item (4) exactly, including the 'counter to part of Samuelson's dictum' framing.

itemVerdicts.item: GP 'two forces coexisted over the last 25 years → ambiguous net prediction'
itemVerdicts.note: This synthesis is NOT a direct quote from the paper. The paper attributes the information-cost decline to the 1980s/1990s ('consistent with the development in the 1980s and 1990s') and the passive-cost decline to the 2000s ('consistent with the development in the 2000s') — i.e., it frames them as sequential trends, not as two forces both operating over a single generic 25-year window. The logical inference (opposite signs on macro-inefficiency ⇒ ambiguous net effect if both operate) is sound and follows directly from Propositions 6 and 7, but the paper itself never states a combined 'net prediction is ambiguous' sentence — that is the article's own synthesis, not a GP quote. RIGHT version: attribute the 'net ambiguous' framing to the deep-research article's own reasoning from combining Props 6+7, not to an explicit GP statement; and note GP's own timing language is '1980s-1990s' + '2000s', not a uniform 'last 25 years.'

itemVerdicts.item: GP publication venue/year: Review of Asset Pricing Studies, 2022
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed via Oxford Academic: Gârleanu & Pedersen, 'Active and Passive Investing: Understanding Samuelson's Dictum,' The Review of Asset Pricing Studies, Vol. 12, Issue 2, June 2022, pp. 389-446 (Editor's Choice, Open Access). Note the local file gp.txt's own cover page says 'The Review of Asset Pricing Studies, 2021' — that appears to be an early-view/forthcoming date; the citable published issue is 2022 as the claim states.

itemVerdicts.item: Pedersen disclosed as principal at AQR
itemVerdicts.note: gp.txt footnote (p.1) discloses 'Pedersen is at AQR Capital Management, Copenhagen Business School, and CEPR' plus a conflict disclaimer ('AQR ... may or may not apply similar investment techniques ... views expressed here are those of the authors and not necessarily those of AQR'). The paper itself does not use the word 'principal,' but AQR's own site/LinkedIn confirm Pedersen holds the title Principal at AQR since 2009 — so the claim's characterization is accurate, sourced externally rather than verbatim from the paper's footnote.

itemVerdicts.item: Bond & Garcia (2022): participation decisions are strategic complements, contrasted with G-S substitutability, in a footnote
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in bondgarcia.txt: 'Put differently, participation decisions are strategic complements.[3]' with footnote 3: 'Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) analyze traders' decisions to become informed ... and show that information acquisition decisions are strategic substitutes: the incremental trading profits from private information decline as more traders become informed. In contrast, we consider a setting without exogenous noise traders, and analyze traders' participation decisions.' Exact match to claim.

itemVerdicts.item: Bond & Garcia: drift to indexing self-reinforcing, no restoring force
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'We find that the direct consequences are self-reinforcing' answering their own question 'do equilibrium forces dampen the direct consequences, or are the direct consequences instead self-reinforcing?' Also 'participation is self-reinforcing' (line 1278) and 'strategic complementarities ... established' throughout Section on Proposition 3.

itemVerdicts.item: Bond & Garcia: indexing raises welfare even of uninformed/least-informed traders
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'investor welfare increases, even for the least informed investors' and abstract: '...raise the welfare of uninformed traders.'

itemVerdicts.item: Bond & Garcia: falling indexing costs reduce index price efficiency, raise relative price efficiency of individual stocks
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim abstract: 'A decline in indexing costs directly increases the prevalence of indexing, thereby reducing the price efficiency of the index and augmenting relative price efficiency.' And in intro: 'As indexing costs fall, and indexing increases, price efficiency of the index as a whole falls, while the relative price efficiency of individual stocks increases.' Exact match.

itemVerdicts.item: Bond & Garcia publication venue/year: RFS 2022
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed via Oxford Academic/IDEAS: Bond & García, 'The Equilibrium Consequences of Indexing,' The Review of Financial Studies, Vol. 35, Issue 7, 2022, pp. 3175-3230. Local file bondgarcia.txt is a 2019 working-paper draft (first draft Sept 2016, this draft April 2019) — content matches published abstract, so no substantive drift between versions on the claims checked.

itemVerdicts.item: Chabakauri & Rytchkov (2021): indexing decreases market volatility, no informativeness claim
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim abstract in cr.txt: 'We identify two effects of indexing: lockstep trading of stocks increases market volatility and stock return correlations but reduction in risk sharing decreases them. Overall, indexing decreases market volatility but has an ambiguous effect on the correlations.' A full-text grep for 'informativ' across the entire cr.txt (7738 lines) returns ZERO hits — the paper makes no informativeness claim whatsoever. This directly confirms the claim group's statement and directly refutes the fabrication-warning example (the fabricated version claimed indexing raises volatility and reduces informativeness — both false; the real paper says volatility DECREASES and says nothing about informativeness).

itemVerdicts.item: Chabakauri & Rytchkov publication venue/year: JFE 2021
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed: Chabakauri, G. & Rytchkov, O. (2021), 'Asset pricing with index investing,' Journal of Financial Economics, 141(1), 195-216, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2020.06.023. (Note: correct title is 'Asset pricing with index investing,' not 'indexing' — a minor title-word nuance the claim group's paraphrase should preserve.)

corrections: No numeric/attribution errors found in the core theoretical claims for any of the three papers — all propositions, footnotes, and abstract statements check out verbatim against the local extracted files.

Minor: the framing 'the two forces [G-P results 4 and 5] coexisted over the last 25 years so the net prediction is ambiguous' is the deep-research article's own synthesis, not a sentence GP actually wrote. GP frames the two trends as sequential/distinct historical periods — information costs falling in the 1980s-1990s, passive costs falling in the 2000s — not as a single generic 'last 25 years' window in which both forces operated simultaneously. The logical ambiguity itself (opposite signs on macro-inefficiency in Props 6 vs 7) is correctly derived, but attribute the 'net ambiguous' framing to editorial synthesis, not to a GP quote.

Minor: Chabakauri & Rytchkov's paper title is 'Asset pricing with index investing' (singular focus on index investing effects), not 'indexing' — trivial wording, but if the article quotes a title, use the exact wording.
reasoning:

corrections: Redate the Expansión interview: it was published 3 November 2025, not December 2025. The Expansión article's own metadata reads datePublished 2025-11-03T00:59:29Z (https://www.expansion.com/mercados/2025/11/03/6904bb30e5fdea145f8b459b.html). December 2025 is only the date of The Acquirer's Multiple's republication.

Label the Expansión quotes as translated from Spanish, and say by whom. The interview exists in Spanish only; Fundsmith's own site hosts the Spanish text and its English-language equivalent URL 404s. The English wording currently used ('More than 50% of assets are now invested through index funds, which are not actually passive; they are a momentum strategy' / 'The effects are more extreme than in the dot-com bubble because in 2000 less than 10% of funds were index funds, and now it's more than 50%') is The Acquirer's Multiple's unofficial translation of 'Más del 50% de los activos están ahora invertidos a través de fondos indexados, que en realidad no son pasivos, son una estrategia de momentum' and 'en 2000 menos del 10% de los fondos eran indexados y ahora son más del 50%'.

Change the turnover figure from '~52%' to 51.8%. The letter prints 51% in the main text and 51.8% in Appendix 1; 52% appears nowhere. If the cost of that turnover is mentioned, the letter's figures are voluntary dealing cost £11,404,962 (0.084%) for the half year, OCF 1.05% on T Class Accumulation, Total Cost of Investment 1.12%.

When citing the '30 year high' claim, specify the underlying chart rather than saying 'momentum's relative performance' unqualified. The chart is a Bloomberg chart Smith reproduces titled 'Momentum Is Showing Record Outperformance', plotting 'MSCI US Momentum QoQ vs MSCI US QoQ' in percentage points from 1995 to 2026 — i.e. a US-only, quarter-over-quarter relative-return spread whose '30 year high' spans the full length of the series shown, not a longer history.

Attribute the '-2.9% vs +11.2%' pair precisely: Fundsmith Equity Fund T Class Accumulation shares, net of fees, priced at midday UK time (source Bloomberg), against the MSCI World Index, £ Net, priced at close of business US time. Both legs are sterling. The 14.1pp shortfall is the letter's own stated figure.

Do not present Smith's supporting statistics as verified data. Within the same letter he asserts, without citation, that 'AUM in index funds is now >60%' and, citing Cboe Global Markets, that active funds' share of trades has fallen from 80% in the 1990s to 'just 10%', plus a US calculation that 'index funds outperformed active funds on average by 24%' over five years to end-May. Sourcing in the letter is only the blanket 'Sources: Fundsmith LLP, and Bloomberg unless otherwise stated.' Attribute these to Smith rather than stating them.

Add the counterweight from the letter itself if the piece frames this as capitulation: Smith writes 'We have no desire to hug the index. You can buy index funds which are much cheaper than us or any other active manager, so what would be the point?', restates that the mantra's first two legs are unchanged, and attributes the need to adapt partly to redemptions from his open-ended structure ('We run open-ended funds, and you can and increasingly have been taking money out'), not purely to a changed market view.

If the letter is cited by URL, cite the version live from 3 August 2026 onward. Fundsmith re-issued the PDF at the same URL between 10 July and 3 August 2026 with copy-edits ('Not overpay'→'Don't overpay', 'Poleman'→'Polman', 'Fernando Fernandes'→'Fernando Fernandez', etc.). No figures or quoted sentences changed, but the mantra as printed in the current version reads 'Buy good companies / Don't overpay / Do nothing'.
newContradictions: Smith's own passive-share denominator moved from 'more than 50% of assets' (Expansión, 3 Nov 2025) to 'AUM in index funds is now >60%' (semi-annual letter, July 2026) in eight months, with no source given for either and no geography or asset class specified in either. Using both in the same article without noting the drift would be self-undermining.

The Expansión interview itself contains the denominator switch flagged in the claim, and it is Smith's, not a translation artefact: 'más del 50% de los activos' (assets) in one answer, 'menos del 10% de los fondos ... ahora son más del 50%' (funds) in the next. The '<10% in 2000' figure is a fund-count claim, so it is not comparable to the assets claim it is set against.

The letter's Cboe-attributed claim that active funds' share of trades fell from 80% in the 1990s to 10% treats 'not an active fund' as equivalent to 'passive', which ignores HFT/market makers, hedge funds, retail and dealer flow. Smith uses it to argue 'the trading activity which drives prices is now driven not by active fund management decisions but by the momentum feedback loop' — a stronger inference than the statistic supports. Any use should be quoted and attributed, not asserted.

The letter's parenthetical 'of which the majority are ETFs' is unsourced and cuts against ICI/Morningstar-type breakdowns in which index mutual funds still hold a very large share of index assets, especially in US retirement channels. Worth checking against whichever fund-assets source the article uses elsewhere before repeating.

Smith's five-year US comparison ('index funds outperformed active funds on average by 24%') sets an index total return against a simple average of 3,107 open-ended US equity funds, i.e. equal-weighted and survivorship-exposed, which is a different construction from SPIVA/Morningstar asset-weighted persistence measures the article likely cites elsewhere. Do not mix the two as if they measure the same thing.

Secondary reproductions add words Smith did not write. The Acquirer's Multiple's July 2026 piece paraphrases 'Smith notes that its relative performance has reached a 30-year high' — the letter's own antecedent is a chart, not a sentence, so any wording beyond the two quoted sentences should be dropped.
reasoning: I reached both primary documents verbatim rather than relying on the secondary reproductions. (1) The Fundsmith Equity Fund semi-annual letter to shareholders 2026: fundsmith.co.uk returns 403 to curl and WebFetch, so I enumerated the domain via the Wayback CDX API, located the letter PDF at /media/lfhpxi1x/, downloaded two captures (10 July and 3 August 2026), ran pdftotext -layout on both, and read the full 17-page text. I also rendered page 3 as an image to read the momentum chart's title and axis labels, which pdftotext could not extract. (2) The Expansión interview: Fundsmith's EU site serves the Spanish text un-403'd, and it links the original at expansion.com, which I fetched directly and grepped for both quoted passages and the JSON-LD datePublished. All five quoted strings in the claim group appear verbatim in the primaries. Three things are off. The interview is dated 3 November 2025, not December 2025 — the December date belongs to the Acquirer's Multiple republication. The turnover figure is 51.8% (Appendix 1) or 51% (main text), never 52%. And the '30 year high' sentence needs its referent stated: the chart is 'Momentum Is Showing Record Outperformance', MSCI US Momentum QoQ minus MSCI US QoQ in percentage points, series starting 1995, so it is US-only, quarter-over-quarter, and the 'high' spans exactly the data plotted. The English wording of the Expansión quotes is an unofficial translation and should be labelled as such. I also verified that Fundsmith silently re-issued the letter PDF at the same URL between 10 July and 3 August; a word-level diff shows only seven copy-edits (including 'Not overpay'→'Don't overpay' and two misspelled names), with every number and every quoted sentence unchanged. What I did not independently verify, because it sits outside this claim group: whether Smith's supporting statistics (>60% index AUM, Cboe's 80%→10% trading share, the 24% five-year US index-vs-active gap) are correct — I confirmed only that he asserts them in the letter without citation beyond a blanket 'Fundsmith LLP, and Bloomberg' note. I found no later correction, retraction, or contradicting statement from Fundsmith up to 2026-08.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Garleanu & Pedersen 2022 RAPS — 'result (5)': falling passive costs raise inefficiency, especially macro
itemVerdicts.note: Substance holds but the label is wrong. The paper (gp.txt, published version, RAPS 12(2):389–446, June 2022, DOI 10.1093/rapstu/raab020 — confirmed via Oxford Academic listing) never uses 'Result N' numbering at all (grepped, zero hits); its numbered claims are 'Proposition N.' The passive-cost claim is actually Proposition 7 (line 1503): 'As the cost of passive investing kp = fp decreases, the overall asset price inefficiency (η) increases and the macro-inefficiency η_βv increases by more than the total micro-inefficiency ... as long as n is not too small.' WRONG: 'result (5)'. RIGHT: Proposition 7.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Garleanu & Pedersen 2022 RAPS — 'result (4)': falling information costs lower inefficiency, especially macro
itemVerdicts.note: Substance holds but mislabeled the same way. This is Proposition 6 (line 1483): 'When the cost of information k decreases, overall asset price inefficiency η decreases and the macro-inefficiency η_βv decreases by more than the total micro-inefficiency ... as long as n is not too small.' WRONG: 'result (4)'. RIGHT: Proposition 6. Note also: Propositions 4 and 5 in the actual paper are unrelated results (macro-vs-micro-efficiency existence, and an APT limiting result for n→∞), so '(4)' and '(5)' don't even map to adjacent mislabeled propositions — they map to 6 and 7.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 'the two forces coexisted over the last 25 years so the net prediction is ambiguous'
itemVerdicts.note: Not a verbatim or even paraphrased claim in the paper — this exact synthesis/ambiguity statement doesn't appear. The paper does frame info-cost decline as consistent with '1980s and 1990s' trends (line 162) and passive-cost decline as a 'trend over the past decades'/'2000s' (lines 163-173) — i.e., it does discuss both trends as historically overlapping — but it never states the combined net prediction is 'ambiguous.' This should be flagged in the article as the deep-research author's own synthesis of Props 6+7, not a quoted or directly sourced claim from GP.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Pedersen is a principal at AQR (disclosed)
itemVerdicts.note: gp.txt affiliation line: 'Pedersen is at AQR Capital Management, Copenhagen Business School, and CEPR,' with an explicit conflict disclosure: 'AQR Capital Management is a global investment management firm ... The views expressed here are those of the authors and not necessarily those of AQR.' Web search (AQR's own site, LinkedIn/AQR posts) confirms his title is specifically 'Principal' at AQR, held since 2009.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Bond & Garcia RFS 2022 — participation decisions are strategic complements, footnote contrasting G-S substitutability
itemVerdicts.note: bondgarcia.txt line 62: 'Put differently, participation decisions are strategic complements.3' Footnote 3 (line 69-72, verbatim): 'Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) analyze traders' decisions to become informed, taking the set of trading agents as given, and show that information acquisition decisions are strategic substitutes: the incremental trading profits from private information decline as more traders become informed. In contrast, we consider a setting without exogenous noise traders, and analyze traders' participation decisions.' Published version confirmed: RFS Vol. 35, Issue 7 (July 2022), pp. 3175-3230 (Oxford Academic / IDEAS RePEc).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) drift to indexing is self-reinforcing, no restoring force
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, lines 51-54: 'do equilibrium forces dampen the direct consequences, or are the direct consequences instead self-reinforcing? We find that the direct consequences are self-reinforcing.' This directly answers and refutes the 'dampening/restoring force' alternative the authors themselves posed.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) indexing raises welfare even of uninformed traders
itemVerdicts.note: Abstract (line 15): '...raise the welfare of uninformed traders.' Body (lines 55-56): 'investor welfare increases, even for the least informed investors, as we discuss below.'
