IVD cannot: Sammon states 'The sample for IV D is shorter than for the other three measures ... because OptionMetrics coverage begins in 1996,' and Table 1 discussion says the IVD sample is smallest 'owing both to having fewer years of data, and having a limited number of equities with sufficiently rich option coverage.' So the IVD 0.02→0.05 series is effectively ~1996-2019 (Sammon's own prose is loose here). Two further caliber notes: (i) PJ's sample is 'less than half the overall sample, because of the non-event filter'; (ii) the Figure 1 series the text describes are VALUE-WEIGHTED averages, not equal-weighted. Also the body says PJ went 'from 0.2 to over 0.5' (intro rounds to 0.5).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 90th-vs-10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27% vs 3% of shares) → 152bp higher |Ret| (~1/3 of the 476bp mean)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Section 3: 'The point estimate implies that a firm in the 90th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (27%) has a 152 basis point higher |Ret| than a firm in the 10th percentile of passive ownership in 2019 (3%). For reference, 152 basis points is roughly 1/3rd of |Ret|'s whole sample mean of 476 basis points and 1/4th of its whole sample standard deviation of 621 basis points.' Internal arithmetic checks out (27-3 = 24pp spread; the intro separately says 'the difference in passive ownership share between these two percentiles is 24%'; 152bp/24pp × 15pp = 95bp, which matches Sammon's 15%-increase figure of '95 basis point higher |Ret|'). Caliber note the article should carry: this is NOT a 2019 cross-section. Table 2 is a pooled 1990-2019 panel with firm AND year-quarter fixed effects; the pooled coefficient is applied to the 2019 percentile spread. Sammon also reports (col 5) that 'Using value weights shrinks the estimated coefficient,' though it stays significant at 1%.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) IV estimates (same Russell design as CHR + S&P 500 additions; first-stage F>200) are 2.5-4x the OLS; published headline (15% passive → −1/4 of mean) is the conservative OLS average; reduced form 'not always significant'
itemVerdicts.note: All three parts verified. (i) 'In fact, across all four measures, the IV estimates are 2.5-4 times as large as the OLS estimates.' (ii) Design: 'I use data on index membership from FTSE Russell and follow the method in Coles et al. (2022). Using their May market capitalization proxy...' plus S&P 500 additions (Qin and Singal 2015; Bennett et al. 2020b). First-stage F-statistics in Table 3 are 251.6 (Russell) and 201.1 (S&P); text: 'the first stage is very strong (F > 200 for both experiments).' (iii) Headline is explicitly OLS-derived — Conclusion: 'taking the average of the point estimates from the OLS regressions implies that a 15% increase in passive ownership decreases pre-earnings announcement price informativeness by 1/4th of its whole sample mean and 1/6th of its whole sample standard deviation.' Section 3: 'An equal weighted average of these effects relative to variables' means is 0.23 (roughly 1/4th), while an equal weighted average of these effects relative to variables' standard deviations is 0.16 (roughly 1/6th).' Since IV > OLS and reverse causality would bias OLS UP, OLS is indeed the conservative number. (iv) 'not always significant' is verbatim main text: 'the coefficient on Passive Gap × Treated × Post is not always significant.' CAUTION: the appendix is blunter — 'the reduced form coefficient on the interaction term ... is almost always insignificant' (D.4) and 'the reduced form regressions show a consistently insignificant coefficient on one of the two instruments' (D.5). The article quotes the mildest of his three phrasings. One more caveat: the ABSTRACT attributes the 1/4 figure to 'Estimates across several research designs,' so 'the published headline is the OLS average' is true of the body/conclusion, not of the abstract's own wording.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Sammon's own reconciliation with CHR: different TIMING — CHR show information fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift; Sammon shows less was in prices BEFORE; presenting them as contradiction misstates both
itemVerdicts.note: Two independent failures. FIRST, the CHR characterization is WRONG. Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg ('On index investing,' JFE 2022, 145(3):665-683) do NOT find 'no exploitable drift.' The '2 days' sentence is their DEFINITION of the null benchmark: 'A value of BetaPEAD = 0 corresponds to no post-earnings-announcement drift i.e. the stock incorporates all the information contained in the earnings announcement, on average, within 2 trading days after the announcement.' Their actual empirical result is the opposite: 'The mean BetaPEAD in our sample is 4.3%; in other words, a 1% standard deviation positive surprise in the stock's earnings announcement is followed by a predictable post-announcement return drift of 4.3%. The sample mean has a standard error of 0.6% and so the mean is strongly different from zero; that is, in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' CHR's null result is that Russell index ASSIGNMENT does not CHANGE PEAD ('passive investing is not associated with any change in the speed of incorporation of new information into stock prices'), not that drift is absent. RIGHT version: CHR find economically significant PEAD on average and a precisely-estimated ZERO TREATMENT EFFECT of index inclusion on it. SECOND, the reconciliation is mis-sourced. The October 2023 PDF at the cited URL (marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf — MD5-verified as the file the article cites) contains ZERO occurrences of 'PEAD', 'post-earnings' or 'drift'; it cites Coles et al. (2022) only as one of the 'papers which document no relationship between passive ownership and price informativeness.' The timing reconciliation appears in the EARLIER March 2023 HBS draft: 'Another possible reason for a small PEAD, however, is that the earnings information was incorporated into prices before the announcement itself. Therefore, the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small is consistent with the idea that prices were uninformative before earnings announcements but information is rapidly incorporated after earnings announcements. In other words, passive ownership may be reducing price informativeness without meaningfully changing PEADs.' Note that even Sammon's own gloss ('the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small') misreads CHR, who report significant PEAD. THIRD, 'presenting them as contradiction misstates both' is too strong: CHR's stated conclusion is that 'price informativeness remains unchanged' and 'index investing does not alter price efficiency or market function' — a genuine tension with Sammon's causal conclusion using the same Russell design. The timing story is Sammon's PROPOSED reconciliation, not a demonstrated fact.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) His passive denominator: <1% → ~15% of US market cap 1990-2019 — nowhere near 50%
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim: 'From 1990 to 2019, the share of U.S. equities held by passive investors rose from less than 1% to almost 15%'; Figure 1 discussion: 'From 1990 to 2019, average passive ownership went from nearly zero to owning almost 15% of the US stock market. These numbers closely mirror those in the ICI factbook'; Conclusion: 'passive ownership is still small, owning only about 15% of the US stock market.' Definition (precise): 'the fraction of a stock's shares outstanding which are held by passive funds ... Following Appel et al. (2016), I identify passive funds using the CRSP mutual fund database, selecting all index funds, all ETFs and all funds with names that identify them as index funds' (holdings via MFLINKS → Thomson S12). So it is a share of SHARES OUTSTANDING held by index MUTUAL FUNDS AND ETFs — not a share of trading, and not the full 'passive' universe. Sammon's own footnote 16 concedes the measure 'misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally.'

itemVerdicts.item: Publication status: Management Science, 2025 (MS 2023.00836), PDF at marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (or at least incomplete): treating the linked PDF as the Management Science 2025 article. RIGHT: Crossref for 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836 gives Management Science 71(6):4582-4598, print June 2025; Sammon's own research page lists it as 'Management Science, 9/2024' (article-in-advance). The PDF at the cited URL is the OCTOBER 2023 working paper (I byte-verified it, MD5 cf9b544c38b7d01ba0c11d7482e49620), not the published version. The published abstract, retrieved verbatim from Crossref, matches in substance: 'the amount of information incorporated into prices ahead of earnings announcements to decline by approximately one-fourth of its whole-sample mean and one-sixth of its whole-sample standard deviation. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance.' Beware: an earlier March 2023 HBS draft had a DIFFERENT headline ('decline by roughly 16%') and different measures (e.g. QVS falling 92.1%→72.4%), so version discipline matters here.

itemVerdicts.item: Full text of the published Management Science version (to confirm the Oct 2023 numbers survived into print)
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the published article text. pubsonline.informs.org returns a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' interstitial to curl and to r.jina.ai; SSRN abstract page and delivery PDF return 403; the HBS item page 403s and its faculty error page returns no citation. What I could verify of the published version is the Crossref-registered abstract (identical in substance to the Oct 2023 draft) and the volume/issue/pages. All numeric sub-claims above are therefore verified against the October 2023 working paper at the URL the article itself cites, not against the June 2025 print text.

corrections: Fix the time window for the IV-difference measure. WRONG: 'all four measures deteriorated 1990-2019, including IV-difference 0.02→0.05.' RIGHT: |Ret|, |Ret|/SD and the price-jump measure span 1990-2019; the implied-volatility-difference series effectively begins in 1996 because, in Sammon's words, 'OptionMetrics coverage begins in 1996.' Either say 'three measures over 1990-2019 and IVD from the mid-1990s' or drop the explicit window from the IVD figure.

Replace the CHR characterization. WRONG: 'CHR show information is fully impounded within ~2 days after announcements with no exploitable drift.' RIGHT: Coles, Heath and Ringgenberg (JFE 2022) report a mean post-earnings-announcement-drift coefficient of 4.3% with a standard error of 0.6%, and state that 'in our sample of mid-cap stocks, there is significant PEAD on average.' Their zero result is a zero TREATMENT EFFECT — Russell 2000 assignment does not change the speed at which earnings information is impounded. The '2 trading days' phrase is their definition of the BetaPEAD = 0 benchmark, not a finding.

Fix the attribution of the timing reconciliation. WRONG: attributing a Sammon-vs-CHR timing reconciliation to the paper at marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf. RIGHT: that October 2023 draft never mentions PEAD or drift at all and cites Coles et al. (2022) only as a paper finding 'no relationship between passive ownership and price informativeness.' The reconciliation appears in Sammon's earlier March 2023 HBS draft, whose exact wording is: 'the Coles et al. (2022) result that PEADs are small is consistent with the idea that prices were uninformative before earnings announcements but information is rapidly incorporated after earnings announcements. In other words, passive ownership may be reducing price informativeness without meaningfully changing PEADs.' Cite that draft, and flag that Sammon's own gloss ('PEADs are small') itself understates what CHR report.

Soften 'presenting them as contradiction misstates both.' RIGHT: CHR's headline conclusion — 'price informativeness remains unchanged' and 'index investing does not alter price efficiency or market function' — is in genuine tension with Sammon's causal conclusion drawn from the same Russell design. The timing story is Sammon's PROPOSED reconciliation of the two, not an established fact; say so rather than asserting the contradiction is illusory.

Note the reduced-form soft spot at Sammon's own strongest calibration, not his mildest. The main text says the triple-interaction coefficient 'is not always significant'; Appendix D.4 says it 'is almost always insignificant' and D.5 says the reduced form 'show[s] a consistently insignificant coefficient on one of the two instruments.' Quote the appendix language if the article is presenting this as the paper's weak point.

Label claim (b) correctly as a panel, not a 2019 cross-section. Sammon's Table 2 is a pooled 1990-2019 regression with firm and year-quarter fixed effects; the 152bp figure applies that pooled coefficient to the 2019 90th-vs-10th percentile passive-ownership spread (27% vs 3%). Also note that value-weighting shrinks the coefficient (col 5), though it remains significant at 1%.

Fix the citation line. RIGHT: Marco Sammon, 'Passive Ownership and Price Informativeness,' Management Science 71(6):4582-4598 (print June 2025; published online September 2024), DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836. State explicitly that the freely available PDF at marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf is the October 2023 working paper, since an earlier March 2023 draft carried a different headline ('decline by roughly 16%') and different measures.

Add the caveat that '~15%' is index funds and ETFs only. Sammon's Passive is the fraction of shares outstanding held by CRSP-flagged index funds, ETFs and name-identified index funds (Appel et al. 2016 method). His own footnote 16 concedes it 'misses e.g., shadow index funds (Mauboussin, 2019), as well as institutions that do index replication internally.' Do not let '15%, nowhere near 50%' read as a claim about the true passive share — see the contradiction below.
newContradictions: Sammon contradicts his own denominator elsewhere. Chinco and Sammon, 'The Passive Ownership Share Is Double What You Think It Is' (JFE, 7/2024), abstract: 'While index funds held 16% of the US stock market in 2021, we put the overall passive ownership share at 33.5%. Our headline number is twice as large because it reflects index funds as well as other kinds of passive investors, such as institutional investors with internally managed index portfolios and active managers who are closet indexing.' If the article uses Sammon's ~15% to argue the passive share is far below the headline numbers skeptics cite, it is using one Sammon paper against another. 33.5% is still not 50%, so the 'nowhere near 50%' framing survives — but the ~15% figure does not.

Sammon's paper itself invokes the understated-denominator argument to explain why his IV estimates exceed OLS: footnote 16 says 'My measure, Passive, only captures funds that are explicitly passive, and misses e.g., shadow index funds ..., as well as institutions that do index replication internally. If firms added to the S&P 500 experience an increase in these types of non-explicit passive ownership as well, we might expect their price informativeness to decline more than would be explained by index fund holdings alone.' So the 15% denominator and the 2.5-4x IV/OLS gap are not independent facts — the paper offers measurement error in the former as one explanation for the latter.

Sammon's time-series finding runs against Bai-Philippon-Savov (2016) and Davila-Parlatore, and he concedes this rather than resolving it: 'The findings in Figure 1 seem striking, as previous literature (e.g., Bai et al. (2016), Davila and Parlatore (2018)) have shown a time series trend toward increased price informativeness. My analysis focuses on a different question, namely when information is incorporated into prices.' Any article using Sammon as evidence that prices have become less informative should carry this qualifier — his measures are about TIMING relative to earnings dates, not about the price-fundamental link that the informativeness-is-rising literature measures.

Kacperczyk, Nosal and Sundaresan use the SAME price-jump measure (Weller 2018) as Sammon and reach the opposite sign. Sammon's footnote 8 concedes this and rebuts on the ground that their shocks are contaminated: 'the MSCI shock translates to a 0.013 increase in active ownership and a 0.006 increase in passive ownership, while the JGTRRA shock is associated with an 0.010 increase in active ownership and 0.0004 increase in passive ownership.' Worth surfacing if the article treats the PJ evidence as one-directional.
reasoning: I verified against primary documents rather than summaries. (1) I byte-confirmed that the article's cited URL, https://marcosammon.com/images/sammon_passive.pdf, is the OCTOBER 2023 working paper by downloading it fresh and matching MD5 cf9b544c38b7d01ba0c11d7482e49620 against the local scratchpad copy (sammon.pdf), then read the extracted text directly. Every number in sub-claims (a), (b), (c) and (e) appears verbatim in that document, and I quoted only strings I read myself: the four-measure trends in the Introduction and Section 2.3; the '152 basis point / 27% / 3% / 476 basis points' passage in Section 3; 'across all four measures, the IV estimates are 2.5-4 times as large as the OLS estimates'; Table 3 first-stage F-statistics of 251.6 (Russell) and 201.1 (S&P) with the text 'F > 200 for both experiments'; the conclusion's explicit OLS attribution of the 1/4-of-mean headline; and 'the share of U.S. equities held by passive investors rose from less than 1% to almost 15%.' I also ran an internal arithmetic consistency check (152bp over a 24pp spread scaled to 15pp gives 95bp, matching Sammon's own 15%-increase figure) to confirm the extraction was not garbled. (2) Sub-claim (d) fails twice. I grepped the entire October 2023 text for 'PEAD', 'post-earnings' and 'drift' and got zero hits — the reconciliation the article attributes to that paper is not in it; Coles et al. (2022) appears there only in a list of papers finding 'no relationship.' I then downloaded the March 2023 HBS draft (hbs.edu/ris/Publication Files/sammon_passive march 23_...pdf), extracted it, and found the reconciliation paragraph there verbatim. Separately, I read the actual Coles-Heath-Ringgenberg text in two independent drafts (October 2017 and January 2022) and found that the '2 trading days' sentence is the definition of the BetaPEAD = 0 benchmark, while their empirical finding is a mean drift of 4.3% with a 0.6% standard error that is 'strongly different from zero' — 'there is significant PEAD on average.' Their zero is a zero treatment effect of index assignment, not an absence of drift. This is a clean, document-level refutation. (3) Publication metadata came from the Crossref API for DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2023.00836 (Management Science 71(6):4582-4598, June 2025) plus Sammon's own research page HTML, which lists 'Management Science, 9/2024'. (4) The Chinco-Sammon 33.5% figure is quoted from the local extraction of that paper's abstract. WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAIN: I could not reach the full text of the published June 2025 Management Science article — INFORMS serves a Cloudflare challenge to both curl and r.jina.ai, and SSRN returns 403 on both the abstract page and the delivery PDF. So I cannot rule out that the published version restored a Coles reconciliation paragraph or adjusted a figure between October 2023 and print. The Crossref-registered published abstract is substantively identical to the October 2023 abstract (and clearly distinct from the March 2023 abstract, which said 'decline by roughly 16%'), which is good evidence the October 2023 lineage is the accepted one, but it is not proof about interior paragraphs. I found no post-publication critique, comment or replication of Sammon (2025) through August 2026.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) One-SD increase in PassiveFlow_SP500 (mean 0.05%, SD 0.09% quarterly, 1996-2020, 99 quarters) raises quarterly excess returns: top-10 +0.687% (t=2.46), top-50 +0.528% (t=3.66), top-100 +0.303%, top-150 +0.208%, top-200 +0.145% (t=1.64, insignificant)
itemVerdicts.note: All coefficients and t-stats confirmed verbatim in Table 6.2 Panel B (all with controls, value-weighted): 0.00687 (2.46), 0.00528 (3.66), 0.00303 (3.02), 0.00208 (2.28), 0.00145 (1.64). Table 6.1 confirms PassiveFlow_SP500 mean 0.05, Std Dev 0.09, N=99. TWO caliber fixes. (1) Sample window: WRONG as 'quarterly 1996-2020' if read as full years; RIGHT is 'second quarter of 1996 ... fourth quarter of 2020' (1996Q2-2020Q4 = 99 quarters). The S&P600 placebo sample is a different, shorter window (2001Q4-2020Q4, N=77). (2) The label 'insignificant' for t=1.64 is the article's own gloss, not the paper's: JVZ report only t-statistics with NO significance stars and never characterize the top-200 estimate as insignificant. t=1.64 falls 0.005 short of the 10% two-tailed critical value (1.645) and would be significant at 5% one-tailed against their directional prediction. WRONG: '(t=1.64, insignificant)'. RIGHT: '(t=1.64, only marginally distinguishable from zero; the paper reports no significance stars).' Also note these are returns in excess of the S&P500 INDEX return, not excess of the risk-free rate.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The '29%' is the authors' own linear extrapolation (0.528% x (0.05/0.09) x 99 = 29.04%); the calibrated model predicts only 0-4%; authors say the estimate 'is larger than in our calibration' and can partly mean-revert
itemVerdicts.note: Substantively confirmed verbatim. Paper: 'the cumulative effect of PassiveFlow_SP500 on the excess return on the value-weighted top-50 firm portfolio is 0.528% x (0.05%/0.09%) x 99 = 29.04%. According to this estimate, the rise in passive investing over the past 25 years caused a firm that was in the top 50 of the S&P500 index during the entire period to rise by 29% more than the index.' Next paragraph: 'The estimated 29% effect of passive flows in Table 6.2 is larger than in our calibration. For example, the difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4 and 5 in Tables 5.2-5.5 ranges from zero (Table 5.2, switch from active to passive, all firms in index) to 4% (Table 5.5, switch from active to passive, size groups 3-5 in index).' And: 'Second, the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' TWO caliber fixes. (1) 'for the same object' is too strong: the empirical object is top-50 vs the whole index; the calibration object is model size group 5 vs the average of size groups 3-5. WRONG: 'the calibrated model predicts only 0-4% for the same object.' RIGHT: 'the authors' own model counterpart of this quantity ranges from 0% to 4% across their calibration tables.' (2) The paper itself is internally inconsistent, writing '29%' twice then 'the 30% estimate' in the mean-reversion sentence; quote 29% and do not treat 30% as a separate finding. Note the 29% extrapolation is NEW to the RFS version -- it appears nowhere in the Sept 2022 NBER w28253 revision I downloaded and searched.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Mechanism is explicitly NOT informational ('information in our model is symmetric'); using JVZ as 'passive breaks price discovery' evidence misreads it; it is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim
itemVerdicts.note: First two parts confirmed verbatim. Intro: 'These effects are generated by a different mechanism than in the REE and index-addition literatures because information in our model is symmetric and the effects arise even when indices include all firms.' The paper makes no price-informativeness finding of its own. Third part is a caliber slip in the OTHER direction. WRONG: 'it is [only] a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim.' RIGHT: the EMPIRICAL result (Table 6.2, the 29%) is relative -- excess return over the index -- but the paper's headline THEORETICAL claim is a level claim: the abstract says 'the aggregate market can rise even when flows are entirely due to investors switching from active to passive funds.' Also, JVZ do not deny that passive growth worsens mispricing: 'A switch from active to passive exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in our model as well. Our main results, however, concern how the effects of passive flows depend on stock size, and hold even in the absence of noise traders.' So the correct framing is: JVZ's size-dependent result does not run through information asymmetry and is not evidence about price informativeness; but JVZ is not confined to relative prices either.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Placebo: no significant effect for large stocks in the S&P 600
itemVerdicts.note: Table 6.4 confirmed: PassiveFlow_SP600 coefficients on top-60 S&P600 excess returns are -0.00541 (-1.26), -0.00540 (-1.04), -0.00397 (-0.94), -0.00392 (-0.75); N=77 (76 with controls). Text: 'Consistent with our model, the relationship between passive flows and excess returns on large stocks in the S&P600 is statistically insignificant.' Precision note for the article: the portfolio is the top 60 S&P600 firms (the top size decile, counterpart of the top 50 in the S&P500), the coefficients are NEGATIVE not merely zero, and the S&P600 sample is 2001Q4-2020Q4, a shorter window than the main test.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Idiosyncratic volatility: top-50 differential significant (t=2.53) but non-top-50 main effect NOT (t=1.21)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 6.3 column 1 confirmed: L.PassiveFlow_SP500 x Top50 = 19.32 (2.53); L.PassiveFlow_SP500 = 20.63 (1.21); N=45,737. Text: 'the incremental effect for large firms is statistically significant while the effect for other firms is not,' with magnitudes 1.86% (=20.63 x 0.09%) outside the top 50 and 3.60% (=(19.32+20.63) x 0.09%) inside. Precision note: these regressions use ONE-QUARTER LAGGED flows (L.), unlike the contemporaneous return regressions; the dependent variable is log idiosyncratic volatility (FF3 residual daily returns); column 2 with time fixed effects gives interaction 18.46 (2.45) and drops the main effect entirely.

itemVerdicts.item: Citation metadata: RFS 38(12) 2025, 3461-3496; source URL personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos/Papers/PIRMF_RFSf.pdf
itemVerdicts.note: Crossref record for DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhaf085 returns: title 'Passive Investing and the Rise of Mega-Firms', authors Jiang/Vayanos/Zheng, container 'The Review of Financial Studies', volume 38, issue 12, pages 3461-3496, published online 2025-10-10, print 2025-12-01. I re-downloaded the cited LSE URL and it is byte-identical (MD5 23b7e1e108cad33ce876f38403cf1582) to the local scratchpad copy I verified against; it is the authors' RFS-final manuscript dated June 19, 2025.

corrections: Fix the sample window: write '1996Q2 through 2020Q4 (99 quarters)', not '1996-2020'. The S&P600 placebo runs on a different, shorter window, 2001Q4-2020Q4 (N=77).

Drop the flat word 'insignificant' for the top-200 estimate. JVZ report t-statistics with no significance stars and never label it insignificant; t=1.64 is 0.005 below the 10% two-tailed critical value (1.645) and clears 5% one-tailed against their directional prediction. Write '+0.145% (t=1.64), only marginally distinguishable from zero' or 'the monotone decline runs from +0.687% at the top 10 to +0.145% at the top 200, where statistical support thins out.'

Do not say the calibrated model predicts 0-4% 'for the same object.' The empirical object is the top-50 portfolio versus the whole S&P500 index; the calibration object is model size group 5 versus the average of size groups 3-5 across Tables 5.2-5.5. Write: 'the authors' own model counterpart of this quantity ranges from 0% to 4%, and they concede the reduced-form estimate is larger than in their calibration and partly mean-reverting.'
Quote the 29% figure, not 30%. The paper writes '29%' twice and then slips to 'the 30% estimate' in the mean-reversion sentence; these are the same number, not two findings.

Do not characterize JVZ as purely a relative-price claim. The empirical 29% is relative (excess over the index), but the paper's headline theoretical result is a level claim: the abstract states that 'the aggregate market can rise even when flows are entirely due to investors switching from active to passive funds.' Correct framing: JVZ's size-dependent result does not run through information asymmetry and is not evidence about price informativeness, but the paper is not confined to relative prices.

When saying JVZ is not a price-discovery paper, add that they do not deny mispricing amplification either: 'A switch from active to passive exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in our model as well. Our main results, however, concern how the effects of passive flows depend on stock size, and hold even in the absence of noise traders.'

State that the idiosyncratic-volatility test uses ONE-QUARTER LAGGED passive flows on log FF3-residual volatility, while the return tests are contemporaneous. Do not present the two as the same timing.
Describe the S&P600 placebo precisely: the portfolio is the top 60 S&P600 firms (its top size decile), and the coefficients are negative (-0.39% to -0.54%, t from -0.75 to -1.26), not merely zero.

Cite only the RFS version (38(12), 2025, 3461-3496, DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhaf085). Numbers changed across versions: the Sept 2022 NBER w28253 revision reports 0.525 (t=3.64) for the value-weighted large-stock portfolio with controls, has no top-10/100/150/200 breakdown, and contains no 29% cumulative extrapolation at all. Do not mix figures from the working paper into the RFS citation.
Note the returns are excess of the S&P500 INDEX return, not excess of the risk-free rate, so the 29% means 'rose 29% more than the index,' which is JVZ's own wording.
newContradictions: The paper is internally inconsistent on its own headline figure: it computes and states '29%' twice, then refers to 'the 30% estimate' one sentence later when discussing mean reversion. No erratum found.

Version drift is real and material here. The Sept 2022 NBER revision (w28253.rev1) tests a single 'large stocks' portfolio (0.549/0.550 univariate, 0.523/0.525 with controls; t 3.60-4.14), reports total as well as idiosyncratic volatility, and contains NO 99-quarter cumulative extrapolation. The 29% number, the top-10/50/100/150/200 size ladder, and the explicit calibration-vs-reduced-form reconciliation are all additions in the RFS version. Any secondary source quoting a '0.55%' coefficient or omitting the 29% caveat is reading the working paper.

JVZ's calibration is not neutral about the relative-price mechanism's size: their own model's counterpart to the 29% is 0-4%, i.e. roughly one order of magnitude smaller. The article should present 29% as an upper-bound reduced-form extrapolation that the authors themselves cannot reproduce structurally, not as a settled estimate of how much passive investing inflated mega-caps.

JVZ cite Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (2018, Table IV) and Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche (2025, Figure 3) as corroborating that large firms have lower demand elasticities. If the article cites HHL elsewhere as a contrary or deflationary source on passive effects, that tension should be resolved rather than left implicit.
reasoning:
I treated every sub-claim as false until read in the primary document. The primary document I read is the authors' RFS-final PDF dated June 19, 2025; I re-downloaded the exact cited URL (personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos/Papers/PIRMF_RFSf.pdf) and confirmed it is byte-identical (MD5 23b7e1e108cad33ce876f38403cf1582) to the local scratchpad copy, so nothing rests on a stale or garbled extraction. I read Table 6.1, Table 6.2 Panels A and B, Table 6.3 and Table 6.4 directly out of the PDF with pdftotext -layout to defeat column-scrambling, and I re-read the surrounding prose rather than relying on any fetch summary. Every quoted string in my verdict is one I saw in the extracted text.

Numerator/denominator/window checks: PassiveFlow_SP500 is defined as the CHANGE in the ratio of S&P500 index fund net assets to S&P500 index market capitalization, i.e. a flow scaled by index cap, not a share of fund assets and not a share of trading. Table 6.1 gives mean 0.05, SD 0.09, N=99. The window is 1996Q2-2020Q4 (99 quarters), not calendar 1996-2020; the S&P600 placebo is 2001Q4-2020Q4, N=77. Dependent variables are returns in excess of the INDEX return, value-weighted (Panel B), with controls (S&P500 return, lagged S&P500 return, VIX) and Newey-West three-lag t-stats. Panel B coefficients and t-stats matched the claim exactly: 0.00687 (2.46), 0.00528 (3.66), 0.00303 (3.02), 0.00208 (2.28), 0.00145 (1.64). Panel A's top-50 value-weighted with controls is the same 0.00528 (3.66), so the claim does not double-count across panels. The 29.04% arithmetic reproduces exactly (0.528 x 0.05/0.09 x 99). The volatility table is on LAGGED flows, and column 1 gives interaction 19.32 (2.53) and main effect 20.63 (1.21) with N=45,737, as claimed. The S&P600 placebo coefficients are negative and insignificant.

Version-status check, which the literature warning demanded: I downloaded the Sept 2022 NBER revision w28253.rev1 and searched it. Its return regression is a single 'large stocks' portfolio with coefficients 0.549/0.550/0.523/0.525 and t-stats 3.60-4.14, there is no size ladder, and the 29% cumulative extrapolation is absent entirely. So the claimed numbers are correct for the RFS version and only that version. Publication metadata is confirmed independently via the Crossref API for DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhaf085: RFS vol 38, issue 12, pages 3461-3496, online 2025-10-10, print December 2025.

What I could not reach: the OUP typeset PDF itself (403 on the article-pdf route, expired Silverchair token, and the OUP article page returns only navigation chrome to the fetcher). I therefore verified against the authors' RFS-final accepted manuscript rather than the copyedited typeset file. This is a real residual, though copyediting does not normally alter table values, and no erratum or correction notice surfaced in searching up to 2026-08.

Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS on three caliber points, none of which touches a number: (1) 'insignificant' for t=1.64 is the article's own gloss and is marginal by 0.005 against the 10% two-tailed threshold, in a paper that reports no significance stars at all; (2) 'for the same object' overstates the empirical/calibration correspondence, which is top-50-vs-index versus model size group 5 versus the average of groups 3-5; (3) 'it is a relative-price distortion claim' understates the paper in the opposite direction from the usual misreading, since JVZ's headline theoretical result is that the AGGREGATE market can rise on a pure active-to-passive switch, and they explicitly grant that such a switch exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in their model. The article's core corrective use of JVZ -- that the 29% is the authors' own linear extrapolation, that their calibration delivers only 0-4%, that the authors flag it as larger than their calibration and partly mean-reverting, and that the mechanism is symmetric-information and therefore not price-discovery evidence -- all holds verbatim.

itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Table 6.2 Panel B of the exact cited PDF (my local jvz.pdf is byte-identical to https://personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos/Papers/PIRMF_RFSf.pdf, MD5 23b7e1e108cad33ce876f38403cf1582). N=99 in every column. Text: 'A one-standard-deviation increase in PassiveFlow_SP500 is associated with an increase in the quarterly excess return on the value-weighted portfolio of the top 200 firms by 0.145%, the top 150 firms by 0.208%, the top 100 firms by 0.303%, the top 50 firms by 0.528% and the top 10 firms by 0.687%.' CALIBER GUARD (not an error, but must be preserved): 'excess return' here means in excess of the S&P500 INDEX return, not the risk-free rate — Table 6.1 describes 'quarterly returns on portfolios of large stocks in the S&P500 index in excess of the index return.' The 0.528/t=3.66 pair is specifically the value-weighted-with-controls column; the paper's own summary range for top-50 across the four Panel A columns is 0.528%–0.557% with t from 3.65 to 4.19. itemVerdicts.item: (b) The '29%' is the authors' own linear extrapolation (0.528% × (0.05/0.09) × 99 = 29.04%); the calibrated model predicts only 0-4%; authors say the reduced-form estimate 'is larger than in our calibration' and can partly mean-revert
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, p.35-36: 'Converting our quarterly estimates to cumulative estimates over the length of our sample yields large effects. Recall from Table 6.1 that the mean and standard deviation of PassiveFlow_SP500 are 0.05% and 0.09%, respectively. Since our sample comprises 99 quarters, the cumulative effect of PassiveFlow_SP500 on the excess return on the value-weighted top-50 firm portfolio is 0.528% × 0.05%/0.09% × 99 = 29.04%. According to this estimate, the rise in passive investing over the past 25 years caused a firm that was in the top 50 of the S&P500 index during the entire period to rise by 29% more than the index.' And: 'The estimated 29% effect of passive flows in Table 6.2 is larger than in our calibration. For example, the difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4 and 5 in Tables 5.2-5.5 ranges from zero (Table 5.2, switch from active to passive, all firms in index) to 4% (Table 5.5, switch from active to passive, size groups 3-5 in index). ... First, the fraction of truly active investors might be smaller than in our calibration. Second, the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' I independently recomputed the 0-4% endpoints from the model tables: Table 5.2 switch-from-active columns are all exactly 0 for every size group (0% endpoint); Table 5.5 switch-from-active, constant-b_n: group 5 avg (2.05,10.03)=6.04 vs avg of groups 3-5 = 2.41, difference 3.63%; varying-b_n gives 3.37% — i.e. 'to 4%'. Two precision notes: (i) the model object is the authors' ANALOGUE (size-group-5 return minus the average of size groups 3-5), not literally 'top-50 vs the whole index' — but the authors themselves set up the comparison, so calling it 'the same object' is their framing, not the article's invention; (ii) the 0% endpoint comes from the baseline where a pure active-to-passive switch has zero price effect on ALL stocks (no noise traders, index includes all firms), i.e. the mechanism switched off — the live-mechanism calibration is ~3.4-3.6%. Also note the paper is internally inconsistent, writing '29%' then '30%' for the same figure, so a '30%' quotation is also literally in the paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Mechanism is explicitly NOT informational ('information in our model is symmetric'); using JVZ as 'passive breaks price discovery' evidence misreads it; it is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from the introduction (p.2 of the cited PDF, line 79 of the layout extraction): 'These effects are generated by a different mechanism than in the REE and index-addition literatures because information in our model is symmetric and the effects arise even when indices include all firms.' I grepped the whole 100+ page PDF: 'informativ' / 'informational efficiency' / 'price discovery' appear ONLY in the literature review describing OTHER papers (Grossman-Stiglitz, Garleanu-Pedersen, Bond-Garcia, Glosten-Nallareddy-Zou, Israeli-Lee-Sridharan, Brogaard-Ringgenberg-Sovich) — never as a JVZ result. The stated mechanism is instead idiosyncratic risk: 'passive flows increase the idiosyncratic risk of large firms in high demand, which discourages investors from correcting the flows' effects on prices.' The relative-price reading is confirmed by the dependent variables being returns in excess of the S&P500 index return, and by the 29% being described as rising '29% more than the index.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Placebo: no significant effect for large stocks in the S&P 600
itemVerdicts.note: Table 6.4 verified verbatim: PassiveFlow_S&P600 coefficients -0.00541 (-1.26), -0.00540 (-1.04), -0.00397 (-0.94), -0.00392 (-0.75); N=77/77/76/76; S&P600 sample runs 2001Q4-2020Q4. Text: 'Consistent with our model, the relationship between passive flows and excess returns on large stocks in the S&P600 is statistically insignificant.' Two caliber guards: the S&P600 portfolio is the TOP 60 firms (the top size decile, 'the counterpart of the top 50 firms in the S&P500'), not top 50; and the authors frame this as a test of their model's SECOND PREDICTION ('passive flows into an index can disproportionately raise the stock prices of the index's largest firms only when these firms are also the largest in the economy'), not as a 'placebo' in their own language. Also note it is a low-power null: all four point estimates are NEGATIVE and non-trivially sized (-0.39% to -0.54% per SD) with only 76-77 observations, so it is an imprecise zero rather than a tightly estimated one — do not overstate it as a sharp falsification test.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Idiosyncratic volatility: top-50 differential significant (t=2.53), non-top-50 main effect NOT significant (t=1.21)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 6.3 verified verbatim: L.PassiveFlow_SP500 × Top50 = 19.32 (2.53) in column 1 (firm FE + controls) and 18.46 (2.45) in column 2 (time FE); L.PassiveFlow_SP500 main effect = 20.63 (1.21), present only in column 1. Observations 45,737; standard errors double-clustered by firm and time. Paper's own text: 'An one-standard-deviation increase in PassiveFlow_SP500 is associated with an increase in idiosyncratic volatility by 1.86% (=20.63 × 0.09%) for firms outside the top 50, and this effect approximately doubles to 3.60% (=(19.32 + 20.63) × 0.09%) for firms in the top 50. Moreover, the incremental effect for large firms is statistically significant while the effect for other firms is not.' Note the regressor is ONE-QUARTER LAGGED passive flow, and the dependent variable is log(VolIdio) where VolIdio is the quarterly SD of daily Fama-French three-factor residual returns.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) One-SD PassiveFlow_SP500 (mean 0.05%, SD 0.09% quarterly, 1996-2020, 99 quarters) raises quarterly excess returns: top-10 +0.687% (t=2.46), top-50 +0.528% (t=3.66), top-100 +0.303%, top-150 +0.208%, top-200 +0.145% (t=1.64, insignificant)
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Table 6.2 Panel B of the cited PDF (which is byte-identical, md5 23b7e1e108cad33ce876f38403cf1582, to https://personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos/Papers/PIRMF_RFSf.pdf): coefficients 0.00687 (2.46), 0.00528 (3.66), 0.00303 (3.02), 0.00208 (2.28), 0.00145 (1.64), all N=99, value-weighted, with controls (S&P500 return, lagged S&P500 return, VIX), Newey-West 3 lags. Table 6.1 Panel A gives PassiveFlow_SP500 mean 0.05, SD 0.09, N=99. Sample stated as 'begins in the second quarter of 1996 and ends in the fourth quarter of 2020'. Two things the article must not blur: (i) 'excess return' here means IN EXCESS OF THE S&P500 INDEX RETURN, not excess of the risk-free rate — the paper: 'quarterly returns on portfolios of large stocks in the S&P500 index in excess of the index return'; (ii) the paper's own headline range for top-50 is 0.528%-0.557% with t from 3.65 to 4.19 across the four Panel A specs; 0.528%/t=3.66 is specifically the value-weighted, with-controls spec. Also note PassiveFlow is defined as the CHANGE in the ratio of S&P500 index-fund net assets to S&P500 index market cap (an ownership-share change, contemporaneous with returns), not a dollar-flow-over-cap measure.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) The '29%' is the authors' own linear extrapolation (0.528% x (0.05/0.09) x 99 = 29.04%); the calibrated model predicts only 0-4% for the same object; authors say the reduced-form estimate 'is larger than in our calibration' and can partly mean-revert
itemVerdicts.note: Arithmetic and quotes confirmed verbatim: 'the cumulative effect of PassiveFlow_SP500 on the excess return on the value-weighted top-50 firm portfolio is 0.528% x 0.05%/0.09% x 99 = 29.04%'; 'The estimated 29% effect of passive flows in Table 6.2 is larger than in our calibration'; '...ranges from zero (Table 5.2, switch from active to passive, all firms in index) to 4% (Table 5.5, switch from active to passive, size groups 3-5 in index)'; 'the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert' (the paper itself slips between '29%' and '30%' in adjacent sentences). CORRECTION to the qualifier: WRONG — 'their calibrated model predicts only 0-4% for the SAME OBJECT'. RIGHT — the 0-4% is the model ANALOGUE, not the same object: it is 'the difference between the return on size group 5 and the average return on size groups 3, 4 and 5' in the five-size-group calibration, and it is generated by a counterfactual far larger than the data (passive measure mu2 raised 0.1 -> 0.6 with active mu1 lowered 0.9 -> 0.4), whereas the empirical 4.95% cumulative rise in S&P500 index-fund ownership share is what the 29% is scaled off. Stating it as the model analogue makes the gap starker, not weaker.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The mechanism is explicitly NOT informational ('information in our model is symmetric'); using JVZ as 'passive breaks price discovery' evidence misreads it; it is a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim
itemVerdicts.note: The core is confirmed verbatim: 'These effects are generated by a different mechanism than in the REE and index-addition literatures because information in our model is symmetric and the effects arise even when indices include all firms.' Every occurrence of 'informational efficiency' / 'less informative' in the paper describes OTHER papers (Grossman-Stiglitz, Garleanu-Pedersen, Subrahmanyam, Glosten et al.), never JVZ's own mechanism; the paper makes no price-informativeness estimate. So citing JVZ for 'passive breaks price discovery' is indeed a misreading. CORRECTION to the second qualifier: WRONG — 'it is [only] a relative-price (top-50 vs index) distortion claim'. RIGHT — the EMPIRICS are relative (dependent variables are returns in excess of the index return), but the THEORY also makes an absolute, aggregate-level claim: 'the aggregate market can rise even when flows are entirely due to investors switching from active to passive funds' (abstract), with the Table 5.5 calibration putting that aggregate rise at 1.47% (constant-b) / 1.68% (varying-b). The paper also states 'A switch from active to passive exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in our model as well' — i.e., JVZ do have a mispricing channel, just not an information-asymmetry one.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Placebo: no significant effect for large stocks in the S&P600
itemVerdicts.note: Table 6.4 confirmed: PassiveFlow_S&P600 coefficients on the top-60 S&P600 portfolio are -0.00541 (t=-1.26), -0.00540 (t=-1.04), -0.00397 (t=-0.94), -0.00392 (t=-0.75); N=77 (76 with controls); sample Q4 2001-Q4 2020. Text: 'the relationship between passive flows and excess returns on large stocks in the S&P600 is statistically insignificant.' Two precisions worth carrying: the placebo portfolio is the TOP 60 firms of the S&P600 (chosen as the top size decile, the counterpart of the top 50 of the S&P500), and the point estimates are NEGATIVE, not near zero; the shorter 77-quarter sample also means lower power, so this is a failure to reject, not a demonstrated zero.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Idiosyncratic volatility: top-50 differential significant (t=2.53), non-top-50 main effect NOT (t=1.21)
itemVerdicts.note: Table 6.3 confirmed: L.PassiveFlow_SP500 x Top50 = 19.32 (t=2.53) in the firm-FE spec and 18.46 (t=2.45) with time FE added; L.PassiveFlow_SP500 = 20.63 (t=1.21); L.Top50 = -0.0477 (t=-2.86) / -0.0671 (t=-4.83); N=45,737; standard errors double-clustered by firm and time. Text: 'the incremental effect for large firms is statistically significant while the effect for other firms is not.' Precisions: the dependent variable is log(VolIdio) (quarterly SD of daily Fama-French three-factor residuals) and the regressor is ONE-QUARTER LAGGED flow; the paper still reports the economic magnitudes as +1.86% (=20.63 x 0.09%) for non-top-50 and +3.60% (=(19.32+20.63) x 0.09%) for top-50, so the article should not quote 1.86% as an established effect.

corrections: Say 'excess of the S&P500 index return', not bare 'excess returns'. JVZ's dependent variables are portfolio returns minus the index return; nothing in Table 6.2 is an excess-over-risk-free or an abnormal-return-vs-factor-model number. A reader who takes '+0.687% quarterly excess return' as an absolute alpha has been misled.

Do not write that JVZ's calibrated model predicts 0-4% 'for the same object'. Write: the reduced-form 29% is far above the model ANALOGUE, which is the gap between the price change of size group 5 and the average of size groups 3-5 in the calibration, and which ranges from 0% (Table 5.2, all firms in index) to 4% (Table 5.5, partial index) — and the calibration gets even that from a much larger passive shift (passive measure 0.1 -> 0.6, active 0.9 -> 0.4) than the 4.95% of index market cap actually cumulated in the data.

Attribute the 29% to the authors and label it as their linear extrapolation, quoting their own hedges: 'The estimated 29% effect of passive flows in Table 6.2 is larger than in our calibration' and 'the 30% estimate concerns a contemporaneous effect of passive flows, which can partly mean-revert.' Do not present 29% as a measured cumulative distortion. Note also that the paper writes '29%' and '30%' for the same quantity in adjacent sentences, so quote 29.04% / 29% and not 30%.

Never cite JVZ as evidence that passive investing degrades price discovery or price informativeness. The paper states 'information in our model is symmetric' and makes no informativeness estimate; it explicitly distinguishes its mechanism from the Grossman-Stiglitz REE channel.

Do not describe JVZ as a purely relative-price result either. Their theory predicts the aggregate market rises even under a pure active-to-passive switch (calibrated at 1.47%-1.68% in Table 5.5), and the paper says a switch to passive 'exacerbates noise-trader mispricing in our model as well.' The correct framing: the EMPIRICAL 29% is relative (top-50 vs index); the MODEL additionally has an aggregate-level and a noise-trader-mispricing implication, neither of which is an information channel.

If the top-50 coefficient is quoted as a single number, add that the paper's stated range is 0.528%-0.557% with t-statistics from 3.65 to 4.19 across value-/equal-weighted and with/without controls; 0.528% (t=3.66) is the value-weighted, with-controls specification.

State the placebo precisely: the S&P600 test uses the top 60 firms (top size decile) of the S&P600, coefficients are negative (-0.00541 to -0.00392) and insignificant (t from -1.26 to -0.75), on a shorter Q4-2001-to-Q4-2020 sample of 77 quarters. It is a failure to reject on lower power, not a demonstrated zero.

For the volatility result, specify that the regressor is one-quarter LAGGED passive flow and the dependent variable is log idiosyncratic volatility (quarterly SD of daily Fama-French three-factor residuals), with double-clustered errors; the significant term is the top-50 interaction (19.32, t=2.53), while the effect for non-top-50 firms (20.63, t=1.21) is not statistically distinguishable from zero — so do not report the paper's +1.86% non-top-50 magnitude as an established effect.

Cite the publication correctly: The Review of Financial Studies 38(12), December 2025, 3461-3496, doi:10.1093/rfs/hhaf085. Confirmed via the OUP article page and the OUP PDF path /rfs/article-pdf/38/12/3461/64613750/hhaf085.pdf. Do not cite the NBER working paper (w28253) numbers alongside these — the working-paper version does not contain 0.687/0.528/0.303/0.208/0.145 or the 29.04% calculation.
newContradictions: JVZ's PassiveFlow_SP500 regressor is contemporaneous with the dependent variable and is itself constructed from prices — it is the change in (S&P500 index-fund net assets / S&P500 index market cap), i.e. an ownership-SHARE change, not dollar flows scaled by cap. The 29% is therefore a contemporaneous association, which the authors concede 'can partly mean-revert.' Their only quasi-exogenous check is a beginning-of-month dummy (401(k) paycheck flows), reported in Appendix E.3 as a sign/pattern result, not as an IV estimate of the 29%. Any article language implying a causal cumulative 29% price distortion goes beyond what the paper's identification supports.

The empirical passive measure is narrow: S&P500-tracking index mutual funds plus three plain-vanilla S&P500 ETFs (SPDR, iShares Core, Vanguard), cumulating to 4.95% of index market cap over 1996-2020 — not total passive ownership (~16% of the US market by 2021 on the paper's own intro figure). The 29% is scaled off that narrow measure, so it cannot be rescaled to 'all passive' without a further assumption the paper does not make.

JVZ's cited corroborations are consistent-with, not independent replications: Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (2018) Table IV and Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche (2025) Figure 3 are invoked for the size-gradient pattern only. If the article stacks these as separate confirming studies of the 29% magnitude, that is stacking that the paper does not do.

No erratum, correction, published comment, or replication of RFS 38(12) 3461-3496 / doi 10.1093/rfs/hhaf085 was found in searches through 2026-08. Absence of a found critique is not proof none exists, but nothing surfaced.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) The paper's own text says a one-SD increase in ETF ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with 'a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the NBER WP (both April 2014 rev0 and June 2014 revisions), Section 4.3: 'In Column (1), a one standard deviation increase in stock ownership for S&P 500 stocks (1.44%) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable.' Footnote 15 gives the arithmetic: (0.146 * 1.440) / 1.290 = 0.1630. Table 2 Panel B confirms the inputs: S&P 500 monthly sample, ETF ownership mean 2.110%, SD 1.440; daily stock volatility mean 2.080%, SD 1.290. IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT: this sentence is verified in the 2014 NBER working paper, NOT in the published JF 2018 text, which I could not reach (see 'unreachable' item). Useful extra calibration: 20 bps on a 2.08% mean daily volatility is only about a 10% relative increase.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Extended to smaller stocks (Russell 3000) the effect is ~5% of a standard deviation
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the NBER WP: 'Extending the universe to smaller stocks (Column (4)), the effect is diluted, amounting to about 5% of a standard deviation.' Footnote 16: (0.044 * 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511. CAVEAT: version-specific. In the March 2015 revision (SEC comment file s71115-1.pdf) the same pair of numbers had already moved to '15% of a standard deviation' (S&P 500, no lagged dependent variable), '9.3% of a standard deviation' (with lagged DV), and 'about 3.7% of a standard deviation' (Russell 3000).

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Quoting the result as '16% higher volatility' is a caliber error
itemVerdicts.note: Substantively right but the attribution of the error is wrong. WRONG framing: that '16% higher volatility' is a citers' distortion. RIGHT: that phrasing is the AUTHORS' OWN, in the NBER WP abstract — 'We estimate that an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility' — which is still the abstract shown on nber.org/papers/w20071 today. Anyone quoting '16% higher volatility' and citing the NBER WP is quoting the abstract accurately; the body text is what discloses that 16% is 16% of a cross-sectional standard deviation of daily volatility, not a 16% proportional rise.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CRITICAL: does the PUBLISHED JF abstract contain the '16%' phrasing?
itemVerdicts.note: SETTLED — NO. The published JF 73(6) 2018 abstract contains no '16%' and no 'one standard deviation' at all. Verbatim, from two independent publisher-fed sources (Crossref publisher-deposited JATS abstract for DOI 10.1111/jofi.12727, and the American Finance Association's own issue page afajof.org/issue/volume-73-issue-6/, pages 2471-2535): 'Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly.' The RePEc/IDEAS reproduction is therefore correct. CONTAMINATION PATH IDENTIFIED: Semantic Scholar's record for DOI 10.1111/JOFI.12727 serves the 2014 NBER working-paper abstract (with the '16%') as if it were the published abstract — a plausible source of the misattribution.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ETF ownership raises negative autocorrelation
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published JF abstract: 'ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days (so ~55% permanent)
itemVerdicts.note: Version-specific, and OVERTURNED for the published paper. WRONG (if attributed to JF 2018): '~45% reverts in 20 days, so ~55% is permanent.' RIGHT: 45% is the 2014 NBER WP number — 'after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted... which suggests that on average flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares.' The March 2015 revision had already moved to 8.3/17.5 = 0.47 ('almost half'). The PUBLISHED version's own Internet Appendix (authors' copy, people.lu.usi.ch/franzonf/ETF internet appendix.pdf) says the flow-impact table was 'updated through 2015 and reported in Table VII' and states verbatim: 'the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days', and elsewhere 'consistent with our evidence in Table VII that the price impact of flows is fully reversed.' So the published paper reports FULL reversal with a ~10-day half-life, not ~55% permanent.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The efficiency deterioration is at 15-SECOND horizons (microstructure), not allocative informativeness
itemVerdicts.note: Half right. RIGHT: the paper never tests allocative/fundamental price informativeness — its efficiency measure is deviation of a variance ratio from a random walk, plus return reversals. WRONG: that the deterioration is only at 15-second horizons. That is true of the 2014 WP alone (variance of 15-second log returns over 3x variance of 5-second log returns). By the March 2015 revision the paper reports TWO variance ratios — VR15 (15-second, monthly sample) and VR5 (five-day return variance over five times one-day return variance, quarterly sample) — and states 'The effect is twice as large at the intraday frequency as it is at the five-day frequency (10% of a standard deviation of VR 15 for a one-standard-deviation change in ETF ownership, for S&P 500 stocks). It is, however, statistically and economically significant for the 5-day frequency as well.' The published Internet Appendix's variable-definition table (I.A. Table AI) defines 'Variance ratio 5 days', confirming the daily/weekly-horizon measure survived into JF 2018. The 2015 abstract likewise says departures from a random walk occur 'at the intraday and daily frequencies.'

itemVerdicts.item: Published JF 2018 main-text body (does '16% of a standard deviation' survive in the printed article?)
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach. Wiley (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs and /doi/ for 10.1111/jofi.12727) returns HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl; SSRN 2430066 and 1967599 are behind Cloudflare (403 'Just a moment...'); Unpaywall/OpenAlex/CORE list no OA copy of the final version (the only 'OA' link is the 2014 NBER WP); no author-hosted final PDF exists on fisher.osu.edu, u.osu.edu/ben-david.1 (which links only to SSRN), or people.lu.usi.ch/franzonf (which hosts the Internet Appendix but not the article). What I CAN say from the published Internet Appendix: the published version reframes economic magnitude entirely — I.A. Table AIX ('Magnitude Estimation') reports that for S&P 500 without lags of the dependent variable (col. (2) of published Table IV) 'the standard deviation in ETF ownership is about 1.8%, which leads the daily volatility of the median stock to increase by about 20 bps to 2.3%. This new level corresponds to the 64th percentile of the volatility distribution', falling to the 58th percentile with three lags, and 57th/55th for Russell 3000 — followed by the authors' own gloss: 'Although the economic magnitudes appear significant, they do not seem excessively large.' Note 1.8% (within-percentile SD at the 50th/51st percentiles) is a different construct from the WP's 1.44% unconditional SD.

corrections: Do not cite the '16%' to Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi, Journal of Finance 73(6) 2018. The published JF abstract does not contain it. The '16%' belongs to NBER Working Paper 20071 (April 2014, rev. June 2014). If the article keeps the figure, cite the working paper explicitly, e.g. 'Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (NBER WP 20071, 2014); the figure does not appear in the published Journal of Finance version.'

State the '16%' with its actual denominator: in the 2014 working paper, a one-standard-deviation increase in ETF ownership of an S&P 500 stock (1.44 percentage points of the stock's market cap) is associated with a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, 'which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable' (footnote: 0.146 x 1.440 / 1.290 = 0.1630). It is 16% of a cross-sectional standard deviation of daily volatility, not a 16% proportional rise. Against the S&P 500 sample mean daily volatility of 2.08%, 20 bps is roughly a 10% relative increase.

Add the population qualifier: the 16% figure is S&P 500 stocks only. Extending to Russell 3000 stocks, the working paper reports the effect 'diluted, amounting to about 5% of a standard deviation' (0.044 x 1.730 / 1.490 = 0.0511).

Do not attribute the loose '16% higher volatility' phrasing to sloppy citers. The authors' own NBER working-paper abstract says 'an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility' — and nber.org/papers/w20071 still displays that abstract. The clarification that it is 16% of a standard deviation appears only in the body text.

Quote the published Journal of Finance abstract if the article characterizes what the published paper claims: 'Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly.' (Journal of Finance 73(6), 2471-2535, December 2018; confirmed via Crossref publisher deposit and the AFA's own issue listing.)

Drop or re-source the claim that '~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days, so ~55% is permanent.' The 45%/20-day figure is the 2014 working paper (Table 6), where the authors read it as flows conveying 'fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares.' The published version's own Internet Appendix says the flow-impact evidence was updated through 2015 and reported in Table VII, and states that 'the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days' and that 'the price impact of flows is fully reversed.' If the article cites JF 2018, the correct characterization is full reversal with roughly a 10-day half-life, which strengthens rather than weakens the noise interpretation.

Correct the horizon claim about price efficiency. The 15-second-only characterization is true of the 2014 working paper alone. From the March 2015 revision onward the paper reports two variance ratios — VR15 (15-second vs 5-second returns) and VR5 (five-day return variance over five times one-day return variance, estimated within a quarter) — finding the effect 'twice as large at the intraday frequency as it is at the five-day frequency (10% of a standard deviation of VR 15 for a one-standard-deviation change in ETF ownership, for S&P 500 stocks)' but 'statistically and economically significant for the 5-day frequency as well.' The published Internet Appendix's variable list defines 'Variance ratio 5 days', confirming the lower-frequency measure is in the published paper. The claim that survives is narrower and safer: the paper measures departures from a random walk, never fundamental/allocative price informativeness.

If the article wants the published paper's own statement of economic magnitude, use the published Internet Appendix (I.A. Table AIX, 'Magnitude Estimation'): for S&P 500 stocks without lags of the dependent variable, a one-standard-deviation change in ETF ownership (about 1.8%) raises the median stock's daily volatility 'by about 20 bps to 2.3%', moving it from the 50th to the 64th percentile of the volatility distribution (58th with three lags of the dependent variable; 57th and 55th respectively for Russell 3000) — and the authors' own verdict: 'Although the economic magnitudes appear significant, they do not seem excessively large.'

Beware Semantic Scholar as a source for this paper: its record for DOI 10.1111/JOFI.12727 serves the 2014 NBER working-paper abstract (containing the '16%') in place of the real published abstract. Verify against Crossref or afajof.org instead.

Footnote 16: "(0.044 * 1.730) / 1.490 = 0.0511." One precision point: Column (4) is the RUSSELL 3000 universe, which contains the S&P 500 stocks too, not a smaller-stocks-only sample; "extending the universe to smaller stocks" is the paper's own shorthand.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-cont) Quoting it as "16% higher volatility" is a caliber error
itemVerdicts.note: Correct, and doubly wrong in the popular rendering. The 16% is a fraction of the STANDARD DEVIATION of the dependent variable (SD of daily stock volatility = 1.290 percentage points), not a percentage increase in volatility. Measured against the sample MEAN daily volatility of 2.080%, the same 20 bps is about 10%, not 16%. Note the origin of the slippage: the NBER WP's own ABSTRACT says verbatim "an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility" - the authors themselves compressed it loosely there, which is why the misquote propagated.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CRITICAL: does the PUBLISHED JF abstract contain the "16%" phrasing?
itemVerdicts.note: RESOLVED - the published JF abstract does NOT contain "16%" anywhere, and the RePEc text is the real published abstract, not a reproduction artifact. Published abstract VERBATIM: "Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly." Identical across four independent renderings: (1) Crossref API JATS abstract for 10.1111/jofi.12727, which IS Wiley's own metadata deposit; (2) OpenAlex inverted index for the same DOI; (3) afajof.org's own Volume 73 Issue 6 issue-listing page, the AFA being the journal owner, pages 2471-2535; (4) ideas.repec.org. Wiley's page itself returns HTTP 403/Cloudflare to automated fetch and the Chrome extension was not connected, so it was not read directly. "56 basis points MONTHLY" is correct wording, not a mis-transcription of "annually". CAUTION: Semantic Scholar's API serves the NBER WP abstract (with "16%") under the JF DOI - a known contamination source that must not be cited as the published abstract.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ETF ownership raises negative autocorrelation
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published JF abstract: "ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices." This exact phrasing exists ONLY in the published version; the 2014 WP never uses "negative autocorrelation" for this result - it says ETFs "inflate the mean-reverting component of stock prices." So this sub-claim is correctly attributed to JF 2018.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) ~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert within 20 days, so ~55% permanent
itemVerdicts.note: True of the 2014 WP; FALSE - indeed inverted - for the published JF 2018 paper. WRONG version (WP, Section 4.4, verbatim): "In terms of magnitude, after twenty days, about 45% of the initial shock has reverted. Extending the horizon farther out to forty days does not increase the magnitude of reversals (not reported), which suggests that on average flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares." RIGHT version (published Internet Appendix, verbatim): "consistent with our evidence in Table VII that the price impact of flows is fully reversed" and "our evidence on the price impact of ETF flows, which we have updated through 2015 and reported in Table VII, suggests that, following ETF flows, the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days." So the published paper concludes the flow-driven price impact is ENTIRELY transitory/non-fundamental - the opposite of "~55% permanent." Caveat: this rests on the published Internet Appendix (people.lu.usi.ch/franzonf/ETF internet appendix.pdf; 64pp, sample through Dec 2015, Moussawi at Villanova, JF roman-numeral table numbering), not on the paywalled JF main text.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) The efficiency deterioration is at 15-SECOND horizons (microstructure), not allocative informativeness
itemVerdicts.note: Half right, and it understates the paper. RIGHT: the variance-ratio test is indeed 15-second - WP verbatim: "we measure single-period returns from transaction prices at five-second intervals and choose k = 3, so that multi-period returns are measured over fifteen-second intervals" and "price efficiency deteriorates for stocks with higher ETF ownership at the fifteen second frequency, which captures the investment horizon of ETF arbitrageurs." WRONG: saying the deterioration is ONLY at 15 seconds. The same WP introduction says verbatim "ETFs appear to inflate the mean-reverting component of stock prices which suggests a deterioration in price efficiency, both intraday and at the daily frequency." The published version adds a multi-day measure: Internet Appendix Table AI defines "Variance ratio 5 days: The ratio of 5-day return variance divided by 5 times the 1-day return variance minus 1... computed using daily and 5-day returns within a quarter." And the published abstract escalates to priced, undiversifiable risk (56 bps monthly). The "not allocative informativeness" half is fair: the paper makes no claim about fundamental/allocative price informativeness anywhere.

itemVerdicts.item: Later corrections, replications or contradictions through 2026-08
itemVerdicts.note: No corrigendum overturns the paper. The authors published a web-only note in the JF Replications and Corrigenda series - Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (Oct 2019), "An Improved Method to Predict Assignment of Stocks into Russell Indexes" (afajof.org/wp-content/uploads/20191016-Note-for-JF.pdf) - redoing the fuzzy RDD with a better Russell ranking predictor, concluding VERBATIM: "the fuzzy RDD confirms the results in our 2018 article in terms of both significance and magnitude." Critically, that note states the published paper's own headline magnitude VERBATIM: "the magnitude of the median estimate is about 31%, which is almost identical to the result presented in our 2018 paper of about 31% of a standard deviation." A genuine contradicting primary source exists: Glosten, Nallareddy & Zou (2021, Management Science 67(1), DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2019.3427), Crossref-deposited abstract verbatim: "We find that ETF activity increases short-run informational efficiency for stocks with weak information environments."

corrections: Do not attribute the sentence 'a 20 bps increase in daily volatility, which represents 16% of a standard deviation of the dependent variable' to the Journal of Finance 2018 article. It is verbatim from the NBER working paper version (Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi, NBER WP 20071, April 2014, revised June 2014, Section 4.3), whose sample runs 2000-2012. Cite it as the working-paper OLS panel estimate, or drop the 16% entirely.

The published JF abstract (73(6), Dec 2018, pp. 2471-2535) contains no '16%'. Its verbatim text is: 'Due to their low trading costs, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a potential catalyst for short-horizon liquidity traders. The liquidity shocks can propagate to the underlying securities through the arbitrage channel, and ETFs may increase the nonfundamental volatility of the securities in their baskets. We exploit exogenous changes in index membership and find that stocks with higher ETF ownership display significantly higher volatility. ETF ownership increases the negative autocorrelation in stock prices. The increase in volatility appears to introduce undiversifiable risk in prices because stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly.' If the article quotes a BFM abstract it must quote this one, not the NBER one. Semantic Scholar serves the NBER abstract under the JF DOI - do not use it as a source.

Never write '16% higher volatility'. The 16% is 16% of one standard deviation of the dependent variable (SD of daily stock volatility = 1.290 percentage points), produced by a one-standard-deviation (1.44 percentage point) increase in ETF ownership among S&P 500 stocks only. Against the sample mean daily volatility of 2.080%, the same 20 bps is roughly a 10% increase, not 16%.

If the article wants the magnitude the PUBLISHED paper actually headlines, use about 31% of a standard deviation, not 16%. The authors' own 2019 JF web-only note states: 'the magnitude of the median estimate is about 31%, which is almost identical to the result presented in our 2018 paper of about 31% of a standard deviation.' That estimate comes from the Russell 1000/2000 reconstitution fuzzy RDD/IV, which is the published version's main identification strategy - a different design from the 16% OLS panel.

Delete any claim that only ~45% of flow-driven price shocks revert, implying ~55% permanent or 'flows are roughly half fundamental'. That is the 2014 working paper. The published JF version, with data extended through December 2015, reports the opposite: its Internet Appendix states 'the price impact of flows is fully reversed' and that 'the half-life to convergence of prices to the initial level is about 10 days' (Table VII). When citing the published paper, say: fully reversed, half-life about 10 days.

Do not describe the price-efficiency result as confined to 15-second (microstructure) horizons. The 15-second variance ratio is real (5-second returns, k=3), but the paper's own introduction says the deterioration is 'both intraday and at the daily frequency', the published version also uses a 5-day-versus-1-day variance ratio computed within a quarter, and the published abstract escalates to priced, undiversifiable risk of 'up to 56 basis points monthly'. Safe formulation: the efficiency evidence concerns departures from a random walk (intraday and multi-day) and non-fundamental volatility - it is not evidence about allocative or fundamental price informativeness.

If quoting numbers, keep the versions straight: WP sample 2000-2012 with S&P 500 ETF-ownership SD of 1.44%; published version sample January 2000 to December 2015, with the published Internet Appendix using an S&P 500 ETF-ownership SD of 1.8% (2.3% for Russell 3000) and framing the effect as moving the median stock's daily volatility from 2.1% to 2.3%, i.e. from the 50th to the 64th percentile of the volatility distribution.
newContradictions: Glosten, Nallareddy & Zou (2021), 'ETF Activity and Informational Efficiency of Underlying Securities', Management Science 67(1), DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2019.3427 - verbatim from the publisher-deposited abstract: 'We find that ETF activity increases short-run informational efficiency for stocks with weak information environments. The increase in informational efficiency results from the timely incorporation of systematic earnings information.' This cuts against using BFM as evidence that ETFs degrade price efficiency generally.

The BFM published abstract's strongest claim - 'stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly' - is a large number (roughly 7% annualized) that the article should either state accurately (monthly, 'up to') or avoid. It is not verified here beyond the abstract; the underlying portfolio-sort table was not reachable.

The authors' 2019 JF Replications and Corrigenda note exists specifically because the Russell 1000/2000 ranking variable is proprietary and prior approximations misclassify stocks; it engages Appel, Gormley & Keim (2019b) and Wei & Young (2017) as competing methodologies. Any article leaning on BFM's RDD identification should acknowledge this methodological dispute rather than presenting the design as clean.

Sec. 4.3 is written specifically to rebut the 'washed out over longer horizons' objection, and the published abstract's negative-autocorrelation and risk-premium claims are at daily/monthly frequency.

The NBER working paper's own abstract says, verbatim, 'We estimate that an increase of one standard deviation in ETF ownership is associated with an increase of 16% in daily stock volatility.' The caliber error originates in the authors' own working-paper abstract and was dropped from the published abstract — which is itself the more interesting fact to report.

Fix the 15-second framing. It is correct that the variance-ratio price-efficiency test is at the 15-second frequency and that the paper uses no measure of allocative/fundamental informativeness. It is NOT correct that the efficiency deterioration is confined to microstructure horizons. The paper states, verbatim: 'At the daily frequency, ETF flows trigger price reversals suggesting a persistence of liquidity shocks at lower frequencies as well.
