In sum, ETFs appear to inflate the mean-reverting component of stock prices which suggests a deterioration in price efficiency, both intraday and at the daily frequency.' Section 4.3 exists precisely to rebut the 'washed out over longer horizons' objection.

Qualify the 45% reversal: it is conditional on stock-level ETF FLOWS (weighted daily creations/redemptions as a fraction of prior-day AUM), not on ETF ownership, and the authors' own gloss is that 'flows convey fundamental and non-fundamental shocks in roughly equal shares' — the 40-day check that supports the '~55% permanent' reading is explicitly 'not reported'.

If the article cites the paper's own abstract, note that ETF ownership in this paper is ETF ownership as a share of a stock's market capitalization (mean 2.11%, SD 1.44% in the S&P 500 monthly sample) — a share-of-market-cap measure, not a share of fund assets or of trading volume.

Do not source this paper's abstract from Semantic Scholar or similar aggregators: Semantic Scholar serves the 2014 working-paper abstract (containing '16%') under the published DOI 10.1111/jofi.12727.
newContradictions: The published JF abstract's headline economic magnitude is a RETURN result, not a volatility result: 'stocks with high ETF ownership earn a significant risk premium of up to 56 basis points monthly.' This is absent from the 2014 WP entirely (the WP contains no risk-premium section; grep for 'risk premium' returns only an unrelated theory sentence). Any article treating the JF paper as purely a volatility paper is using the working-paper version. The CFA Institute digest of the published article reports the associated numbers as a long-short top-minus-bottom-quintile premium 'of up to 0.50% monthly' and 'A one standard deviation increase in ETF ownership corresponds to a 0.14% increase in returns' — figures that appear nowhere in the working paper, further evidence the published magnitudes were re-estimated.

Working-paper-vs-published divergence extends to identification: the WP headlines panel OLS/2SLS on 'mechanical variation in ETF ownership'; the published paper headlines 'exogenous changes in index membership' (Russell 1000/2000 reconstitution). The authors themselves later flagged that the Russell reconstitution literature attracted a methodological critique (Wei and Young 2017; Appel, Gormley, and Keim 2019; Glossner 2019) about June market-cap rankings, and argued their use of MAY CRSP market cap exempts them — see NBER w26370, which re-runs the JF tests with an improved Russell-assignment prediction and reports 'volatility is about 20% of a standard deviation higher for stocks in the Russell 2000 than for stocks in the Russell 1000.' If the article leans on the RD result, that follow-up is the current version of it.

Contested in the recent literature, though not a formal replication failure: an AEA 2025 conference poster (Chen Lin, University of Mannheim, 'How Do ETFs Affect Stock Volatility?') frames the field as containing 'seemingly opposing evidence' and argues ETF ownership and ETF trading have opposite signs (arbitrage transmits shocks; secondary-market ETF trading absorbs them), estimating the 2011-2021 increase in average-stock daily volatility at only 5 (OLS) to 36 (IV) basis points. Unpublished poster — do not cite as settled, but it means 'ETFs increase volatility' should not be presented as uncontested as of 2026.

Scope caution for an index-bubble article: this is an ETF paper, not an index-fund paper, and the WP's own Table 4 columns (3)/(6) show index MUTUAL fund ownership has a positive but 'at least an order of magnitude smaller' coefficient than ETF ownership, which the authors attribute to ETFs' exchange-listed high-frequency arbitrage channel that index mutual funds lack. Using BFM to indict passive/index investing generally overstates what the paper identifies.
reasoning:
I read the NBER working paper text directly (local bdfm.txt and bdfm2.txt, cross-checked against a freshly downloaded w20071 rev0 PDF converted with pdftotext) and located the exact sentences, the summary-statistics table, and footnotes 15 and 16, which let me redo the authors' own arithmetic. That confirms sub-claim (a) verbatim, confirms the ~5%-of-a-SD Russell 3000 dilution, and lets me quantify the caliber error precisely: 20 bps against a 2.080% mean is ~10%, and the 16% is 16% of the 1.290 pp SD of the dependent variable. I also confirmed the 45%/20-day reversal sentence and the 15-second variance-ratio sentence verbatim, and found the sentence that undercuts the 'microstructure only' framing ('both intraday and at the daily frequency').

For the critical open item, I deliberately avoided summarizer output. Wiley and SSRN are Cloudflare-gated (403 to WebFetch, curl, and the browser pane; I did not attempt to defeat the bot check). Instead I obtained the published abstract as raw text from three independent publisher-side channels: the Crossref publisher deposit for 10.1111/jofi.12727 (JATS abstract, fetched via curl and parsed locally), the EconPapers/RePEc page (raw HTML, parsed locally), and the American Finance Association's own journal site afajof.org/issue/volume-73-issue-6/ (raw HTML, parsed locally). All three are byte-identical in substance and contain no '16%' — they contain the negative-autocorrelation sentence and the 56-basis-points-monthly risk-premium sentence. That settles item (b): the RePEc headline is the real published abstract. I separately noted that Semantic Scholar serves the working-paper abstract under the published DOI, which is likely the origin of the confusion.

What remains uncertain: the published JF BODY. No open-access accepted manuscript exists (Unpaywall and OpenAlex list only the NBER WP; CORE, BASE and scholar.archive.org returned 403/429/empty; the authors' own pages link only to the paywalled SSRN record). I therefore could not verify whether the '20 bps / 16% of a standard deviation' sentence survived into print. Circumstantial primary evidence that the published version was materially re-estimated: it grew to 65 pages, its abstract swapped identification strategy and headline magnitude, its Internet Appendix (downloaded from Franzoni's USI page) references main-text Tables IV, V, VII, VIII and X — a numbering that does not match the WP — and the authors' own NBER w26370 (downloaded and read) describes the JF paper's reconstitution analysis as 'Table V in the original article' over a June 2000-May 2007 sample. Hence my correction to cite w20071 for those numbers, or check the JF print directly.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) BSW JFE 2005: univariate daily S&P beta increase 0.067 (1976-87) vs 0.214 (1988-2000); 0.326/-0.319 is the bivariate spec
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the JFE 2005 text (local bsw.txt). Body text: 'stocks added to the S&P during 1976–1987 experience an average increase in daily S&P beta of 0.067 after inclusion, the average increase in the 1988–2000 period is 0.214.' Table (Panel A, daily returns) confirms: Additions 1976–1987 N=196, univariate Δβ=0.067*** (s.e. 0.023), bivariate ΔβSP500=0.286***, ΔβnonSP500=-0.301***; 1988–2000 N=259, univariate Δβ=0.214*** (s.e. 0.032), bivariate 0.357***/-0.332***. The 0.326/-0.319 pair is indeed bivariate but is the POOLED 1976–2000 daily row (N=455): 'S&P betas increase by 0.326 on average over the 1976–2000 period, while non-S&P betas fall by an average of 0.319.' The article must label the window or a reader will pair it against the 1988-2000 univariate figure. Estimation windows are [-12,-1] and [+1,+12] months for daily/weekly data.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CSW JFE 2016: bivariate spec uninformative; univariate diff-of-diff +0.020 (t=0.76) 1976-87, +0.199 (t=4.94) 1988-2000, -0.004 (t=-0.14) 2001-2012
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in CSW, JFE 121 (2016) 624-644, Table 1 Panel A (local csw.txt). Column 'Diff. of diff. Δβ2 − Δβ1': 1976–1987 nobs=197, 0.020, t=0.763; 1988–2000 nobs=269, 0.199, t=4.938; 2001–2012 nobs=214, -0.004, t=-0.137; 1976–2012 nobs=680, 0.083, t=4.080. Abstract confirms the bivariate critique verbatim: bivariate regressions 'provide little information about the economic magnitude of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors.' CALIBER NOTE: 'difference-of-differences' here is (change in S&P beta) minus (change in non-S&P beta) WITHIN the event sample from two separate univariate regressions — it is CSW's own column label, but it is not event-vs-control. The event-vs-matched-control results are Table 6 ('Sample minus match', Dimson-adjusted): 1976-87 -0.046, 1988-2000 +0.018 (t=0.601), 2001-12 -0.009 (t=-0.458), 1976-2012 -0.009 — i.e. after matching even the 1988-2000 effect goes insignificant, which strengthens the article's case if cited correctly.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Kasch-Sarkar NY Fed SR 484: no permanent value/comovement effect after pre-inclusion momentum; declines bivariate spec because regressors correlate >93%
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in Staff Report No. 484 (Feb 2011, revised Nov 2012), local nyfed484.txt. Abstract: '...after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance – index inclusion has no permanent effect on value and comovement.' Footnote 25 verbatim: 'We have measured the value-weighted return of non-S&P 500 stocks, following the procedure described in Table 1 of Barberis et al. (2005), and documented that the correlation between S&P 500 and non-S&P 500 stock returns exceeds 93%. The concern regarding a multiple regression with highly correlated regressors is that its parameter estimates are likely to be regression artifacts, rendering their interpretation difficult. Therefore, we do not consider specifications which include both of these highly correlated indices in one regression.' Note there is also a published version (CSW cite it as 'Kasch and Sarkar (2014)'), so cite the staff report explicitly if quoting the >93% footnote.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS March 2018: correlation 0.45→0.52 on inclusion, 462 stocks, 2000-2017, raw before/after with no matched control
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets', BIS Quarterly Review March 2018, Graph 3 (local bis2018.txt). Left panel 'Correlation with the S&P 500 index': 0.45 'Before joining (from t−200 to t−1)' vs 0.52 'After joining (from t+1 to t+200)'. Footnote 1: 'Sample based on 462 stocks joining the S&P 500 between January 2000 and September 2017. Stocks subject to mergers and acquisitions, stocks with poor data availability and those that have left the index during the first 30 days after the inclusion date are excluded.' Footnote 2: 'Correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 index.' The note describes only exclusions — no control group, no matching, no momentum adjustment — so the article's characterisation as a raw before/after is accurate. Fair to add that the BIS panel measures a RAW CORRELATION, not a beta, so it is not a like-for-like rebuttal target for CSW's beta diff-of-diff.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: +0.005 correlation per 1pp passive ownership, euro area, stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV, base correlation 0.50
itemVerdicts.note: The headline number is verbatim; the specification attribution is off. Verbatim (ecb_box2.txt, Dieckelmann/Siciliano/Sowiński, FSR November 2024): 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024, a 1 percentage point increase in the passive ownership share of a euro area stock was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index.' Base correlation confirmed in footnote 4: 'the average return correlation coefficient of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX index between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024 is 0.50.' WRONG: describing the estimate as coming from an 'index-inclusion IV' specification. RIGHT: the Chart B panel a notes say the estimate 'is based on a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects that regress correlation with the EURO STOXX index on the passive ownership share of constituent stocks, controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and 1 autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient' — the IV is a robustness check only: 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share.' Two further caliber points: the ECB never states the '10pp → +0.05' extrapolation (that is the article's own linear scaling), and because the regression includes an AR(1) lag of the dependent variable, 0.005 is an impact coefficient, so naive linear extrapolation is not the long-run effect.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Fed Anadu et al. Table 4: 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001'
itemVerdicts.note: The string is verbatim but the framing overstates it as an independent Fed finding. Verified in Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe & Osambela, FEDS 2018-060r1 (revised, local anadu.txt), Table 4, row 'Comovement of returns', column 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?': 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001'. WRONG: presenting this as the Fed's independent verdict corroborating CSW. RIGHT: the cell is a one-line summary OF CSW — the body text (Section 4) says 'the evidence is mixed on whether return comovement has increased more broadly with the growth of passive investing', cites Kamara-Lou-Sadka (2008, 2010) and Bolla-Kohler-Wittig (2017) finding betas trending UP, and then says 'In contrast, Chen, Singal, and Whitelaw (2016)... do not find evidence of an upward trend in recent years.' The paper's own abstract concludes 'evidence is mixed on the links between indexing and comovement of asset returns and liquidity.' Also one-sided: the adjacent Table 4 row 'Comovement of liquidity' reads 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years.' Cite as FEDS 2018-060r1 (orig. 2018, revised 2020).

corrections: Label the BSW bivariate pair with its window: 0.326 / -0.319 is the POOLED 1976–2000 daily bivariate result (N=455). The subperiod bivariate figures are 0.286 / -0.301 (1976-87, N=196) and 0.357 / -0.332 (1988-2000, N=259). Do not set the pooled bivariate pair beside the subperiod univariate 0.067/0.214 without saying the windows differ.

Clarify what CSW's 'difference-of-differences' is: it is (change in S&P beta) minus (change in non-S&P beta) estimated from two SEPARATE univariate regressions on the event stocks — CSW's own Table 1 Panel A column label — not an event-vs-control comparison. Table 1 has no control sample. If the article wants the event-vs-control result, cite CSW Table 6 'Sample minus match' (Dimson-adjusted): 1976-87 -0.046, 1988-2000 +0.018 (t=0.60), 2001-12 -0.009 (t=-0.46), 1976-2012 -0.009 — after momentum matching even the 1988-2000 effect is insignificant.

Fix the ECB specification description. The 0.005-per-1pp estimate does NOT come from an index-inclusion IV. The ECB's stated spec is 'a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects that regress correlation with the EURO STOXX index on the passive ownership share of constituent stocks, controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and 1 autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient.' The IV is a robustness check: 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share.'

Attribute the '10pp passive rise maps to +0.05' scaling to the article, not the ECB — the box states only the per-1pp association. Because the regression includes an AR(1) lag of the dependent variable, the 0.005 is an impact coefficient and linear extrapolation understates the implied long-run effect; either drop the extrapolation or flag it as the article's own arithmetic.

Do not present Anadu et al. Table 4's comovement-of-returns cell as independent Fed corroboration of CSW — it is a summary OF CSW. The same paper's abstract says 'evidence is mixed on the links between indexing and comovement of asset returns and liquidity', and its body cites Kamara-Lou-Sadka (2008, 2010) and Bolla-Kohler-Wittig (2017) finding betas trending up. Also note the adjacent Table 4 row: 'Systematic liquidity associated with index investing has increased in recent years' — the returns row and the liquidity row point in opposite directions.
Cite the Anadu paper as FEDS 2018-060r1 (Board of Governors, 2018, revised 2020), which is the version containing Table 4.

Acknowledge the published 2025 challenge to CSW: DeCoste, J., 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership', Global Finance Journal 65 (2025), doi 10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110. Abstract verbatim: 'Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity approach I show that membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term... I show that the previous lack of evidence for excess comovement shown in Chen, Singal, Whitelaw (2016) is due to heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members.' CSW cannot be presented as the settled last word on equity comovement.

Note that the BIS Graph 3 measures a raw return CORRELATION with the index, while BSW/CSW measure BETAS from event-window regressions — so 0.45→0.52 is not a like-for-like counterpart to CSW's diff-of-diff, in addition to lacking a control sample.
newContradictions: DeCoste, Joseph (2025), 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership', Global Finance Journal vol. 65(C), doi 10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110 — published, peer-reviewed, directly targets CSW. Abstract read verbatim via the RePEc/IDEAS record: fuzzy regression discontinuity finds 'membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term', attributes CSW's null to 'heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members', and finds 'no evidence that liquidity is driving excess comovement'. This is the single strongest live rebuttal to the article's comovement narrative and is currently unaddressed.

Liao, Y., Coakley, J. & Kellard, N. (2022), 'Index tracking and beta arbitrage effects in comovement', International Review of Financial Analysis vol. 83 — abstract read verbatim via IDEAS: the comovement effect has two offsetting components; pre-event LOW beta additions drive the average beta increase, while 'arbitrageur shorting of high beta additions diminishes or sometimes reverses the beta increases for these stocks driven by indexers'. Implication: an average diff-of-diff near zero (CSW's 2001-2012 -0.004) is consistent with two large offsetting effects, not with no effect. The article's 'statistically ZERO' phrasing should not be read as 'nothing is happening'.

Internal tension the article should resolve rather than paper over: Anadu et al.'s own body text calls the return-comovement evidence 'mixed' and cites Kamara, Lou & Sadka (2008, 2010) and Bolla, Kohler & Wittig (2017) finding rising betas over 2002-2014, and its Table 4 says systematic LIQUIDITY comovement 'has increased in recent years'. Using only the returns cell as the Fed's verdict is selective quotation from a table whose neighbouring row cuts the other way.
reasoning:
I reached every primary document except one (DeCoste's full text, paywalled at ScienceDirect; I verified its abstract verbatim from the RePEc/IDEAS record instead). All numeric sub-claims survive.

Documents read verbatim: (1) BSW, JFE 75 (2005) 283-317, local bsw.txt — introduction text and Table Panel A daily-returns rows; confirmed 0.067 (1976-87, N=196), 0.214 (1988-2000, N=259) univariate, and 0.326/-0.319 as the POOLED 1976-2000 bivariate row, with subperiod bivariates 0.286/-0.301 and 0.357/-0.332. (2) CSW, JFE 121 (2016) 624-644, local csw.txt — Table 1 Panel A confirms 0.020/t=0.763, 0.199/t=4.938, -0.004/t=-0.137 with nobs 197/269/214; abstract confirms the bivariate-uninformativeness claim verbatim; I additionally pulled Table 6 to check the matched-control version (Sample minus match: -0.046, +0.018 t=0.601, -0.009 t=-0.458). (3) Kasch & Sarkar, FRBNY Staff Report 484 (Feb 2011, rev. Nov 2012), local nyfed484.txt — abstract and footnote 25 confirm both the 'no permanent effect on value and comovement' conclusion and the verbatim >93%-correlation refusal to run the bivariate spec. (4) BIS QR March 2018 (Sushko & Turner), local bis2018.txt — Graph 3 confirms 0.45→0.52, 462 stocks, Jan 2000-Sep 2017, t-200..t-1 vs t+1..t+200, with no control sample described. (5) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box (Dieckelmann, Siciliano, Sowiński), local ecb_box2.txt — the 0.005-per-1pp sentence and the 0.50 base correlation (footnote 4) are verbatim, but the Chart B notes show the headline spec is a stock+time FE panel with an AR(1) lag of the dependent variable and market-cap/liquidity/valuation controls, with the index-inclusion IV only as a 'results also hold' robustness check. (6) Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe & Osambela, FEDS 2018-060r1, local anadu.txt — Table 4 comovement-of-returns cell is verbatim, but I also read the abstract and Section 4 body, which say the evidence is 'mixed' and ground the Table 4 cell entirely in CSW, and the adjacent liquidity-comovement row runs the other way.

Adversarial searching to 2026-08 surfaced one genuinely contradicting published source (DeCoste 2025, Global Finance Journal) and one heterogeneity result (Liao, Coakley & Kellard 2022, IRFA), neither of which the claim group accounts for. Greenwood & Sammon, 'The Disappearing Index Effect', Journal of Finance 80(2), April 2025, is directionally supportive but concerns the VALUATION effect, not comovement, and should not be conflated with it.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not read DeCoste's full text, so I cannot independently assess whether his fuzzy-RD design survives CSW's own critiques (momentum matching, Dimson adjustment). I also did not verify whether the peer-reviewed Kasch-Sarkar (2014) version retains the >93% footnote — the article should cite the staff report, which I did verify. Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: no number is wrong, but the ECB specification is misattributed to an IV design, the Anadu Table 4 cell is presented as independent corroboration when it is a restatement of CSW, the BSW bivariate pair lacks its window label, and a published 2025 rebuttal to the central CSW result is unacknowledged.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Barberis-Shleifer-Wurgler (JFE 2005): S&P daily beta increase on inclusion 0.067 (1976-87) vs 0.214 (1988-2000); the 0.326/-0.319 pair is the BIVARIATE spec
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the JFE 2005 text (local bsw.txt). Text p.286: 'While stocks added to the S&P during 1976–1987 experience an average increase in daily S&P beta of 0.067 after inclusion, the average increase in the 1988–2000 period is 0.214.' Table 1 Panel A (daily returns), univariate Δβ: 1976–1987 N=196, 0.067*** (s.e. 0.023); 1988–2000 N=259, 0.214*** (s.e. 0.032); full 1976–2000 N=455, 0.151***. Bivariate columns confirm the famous pair: 'S&P betas increase by 0.326 on average over the 1976–2000 period, while non-S&P betas fall by an average of 0.319' — Table 1: ΔβSP500 0.326*** (0.027), ΔβnonSP500 −0.319*** (0.033). One precision point for the article: 0.326/−0.319 is the FULL-sample 1976–2000 bivariate daily estimate, not a subperiod; the bivariate subperiod pairs are 0.286/−0.301 (1976–87) and 0.357/−0.332 (1988–2000). Pre/post windows are [−12,−1] and [+1,+12] months of daily returns, October 1987 excluded.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Chen-Singal-Whitelaw (JFE 2016): bivariate spec uninformative; univariate diff-of-diffs +0.020 (t=0.76) 1976-87, +0.199 (t=4.94) 1988-2000, -0.004 (t=-0.14) 2001-2012
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in JFE 121 (2016) 624–644, Table 1 Panel A, 'Diff. of diff.' column Δβ2−Δβ1: 1976–1987 nobs 197, 0.020 with t 0.763; 1988–2000 nobs 269, 0.199 with t 4.938; 2001–2012 nobs 214, −0.004 with t −0.137; full 1976–2012 nobs 680, 0.083 (t 4.080). Identical numbers in the NBER WP 21281 (June 2015) version, so no working-paper/published drift. Abstract supports the 'uninformative' gloss verbatim: 'the bivariate regressions in this literature provide little information about the economic magnitude of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors.' Body: 'the measure of total excess comovement, the difference between these changes (Δβ2–Δβ1), is small and statistically insignificant for these two subperiods' [1976–87 and 2001–12]. TWO caliber cautions the article must respect: (i) the ZERO is the DIFFERENTIAL, not the raw beta — in 2001–2012 the S&P-beta change is +0.071 with t=2.439 (significant), but the non-S&P-beta change is +0.075 with t=2.496, which is what nets it to −0.004; CSW's own words are that the S&P effect 'is less than a third as large (0.071 vs. 0.214) for the very last subperiod'. (ii) CSW's sample ENDS in 2012, so it cannot speak to 2013–2024, when the passive share grew most; 'the decade passive grew fastest' overstates reach. Supporting (not required) detail: with Dimson adjustment plus momentum-matched controls (Table 5), even 1988–2000 collapses to sample-minus-match DiD 0.018, t=0.601.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Kasch-Sarkar (NY Fed staff report 484): no permanent value or comovement effect after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum; declines the bivariate spec because regressors correlate >93%
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed, one qualifier off. WRONG: 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum.' RIGHT: the abstract says 'after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance' — which they define as 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum'; momentum is one of three components, not the whole control. Abstract verbatim: 'our results indicate that – after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance – index inclusion has no permanent effect on value and comovement.' The bivariate refusal is verbatim (footnote 25, verified against the live sr484.pdf): 'we have measured the value-weighted return of non-S&P 500 stocks, following the procedure described in Table 1 of Barberis et al. (2005), and documented that the correlation between S&P 500 and non-S&P 500 stock returns exceeds 93%. The concern regarding a multiple regression with highly correlated regressors is that its parameter estimates are likely to be regression artifacts, rendering their interpretation difficult. Therefore, we do not consider specifications which include both of these highly correlated indices in one regression.' Also worth stating: SR 484 is February 2011, revised November 2012, and was never journal-published — CSW's reference list carries it as 'Kasch, M., Sarkar, A., 2014. Is there an S&P500 index effect? Unpublished working paper.' Do not call it peer-reviewed.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS March 2018: correlation 0.45→0.52 on inclusion (462 stocks, 2000-2017), raw before/after with no matched control
itemVerdicts.note: Verified in local bis2018.txt = Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets', BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, p.119, Graph 3. Data labels 0.45 (before joining, t−200 to t−1) and 0.52 (after joining, t+1 to t+200). Footnote 1: 'Sample based on 462 stocks joining the S&P 500 between January 2000 and September 2017. Stocks subject to mergers and acquisitions, stocks with poor data availability and those that have left the index during the first 30 days after the inclusion date are excluded.' Footnote 2: 'Correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 index.' The design characterisation is accurate: nothing in the note describes a control or matched sample, so it is a raw pre/post mean comparison. TWO precision points: the metric is a raw return CORRELATION coefficient, not a beta, and the window is ±200 trading days; and 'exactly the design CSW demolish' is one notch too strong — CSW attacked univariate/bivariate beta regressions lacking momentum-matched controls and never examined a 2000–2017 correlation statistic. Safer phrasing: 'vulnerable to precisely the critique CSW raise — no matched control for the fact that added stocks are momentum winners.'

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: +0.005 correlation per 1pp passive ownership share (euro area, stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV, base correlation 0.50); a 10pp passive rise maps to +0.05
itemVerdicts.note: Number and base confirmed; the specification attribution is wrong. Verified against the live ECB page (Dieckelmann, Siciliano, Sowiński, FSR November 2024 box): 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024, a 1 percentage point increase in the passive ownership share of a euro area stock was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index.' Footnote 4: 'the average return correlation coefficient of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX index between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024 is 0.50.' WRONG: presenting 0.005 as coming from an index-inclusion IV specification. RIGHT: the Chart B panel a notes say the estimate 'is based on a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects that regress correlation with the EURO STOXX index on the passive ownership share of constituent stocks, controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and 1 autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient'; the IV appears only as an unquantified robustness check — 'The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share' — with no IV coefficient reported. Second issue: '10pp maps to +0.05' is the article's own linear extrapolation, not the ECB's; the ECB states no such scaling, uses associational language ('was associated with'), and because the spec includes an AR(1) lag of the dependent variable, 0.005 is a short-run partial effect whose long-run counterpart would differ, so straight-line multiplication is not implied by the source. Also state the sample window (Q1 2010–Q1 2024) whenever the 0.005 is used.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Fed's Anadu et al. Table 4 verdict: 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001.'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim against the live federalreserve.gov PDF of FEDS 2018-060r1 (this draft: May 15, 2020), Table 4 'Impact of active-to-passive shift on index-inclusion effects and financial stability', 'Comovement of returns' row, rightmost column 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?': 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001'. (The Valuation row of the same table reads 'since 2000', not 2001 — do not mix them.) TWO caliber cautions: (i) this is a summary-table judgement resting on CSW (2016), not an Anadu et al. empirical result — their body text reads 'the evidence is mixed on whether return comovement has increased more broadly with the growth of passive investing' and 'the evidence on trends and causality is mixed', and they cite Kamara-Lou-Sadka and Bolla-Kohler-Wittig on the other side, plus Da & Shive (2018) finding ETF ownership boosts comovement; (ii) 'Table 4' is the numbering in the FEDS working paper 2018-060r1 — the paper was also published as Financial Analysts Journal 76(4), 2020, where numbering may differ, so cite the FEDS version explicitly.

corrections: ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: do NOT attribute the +0.005-per-1pp estimate to an index-inclusion IV. The headline figure comes from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects controlling for market capitalisation, liquidity, valuation and one autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient; the index-inclusion instrumental variable appears only as an unquantified robustness check ('The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share'), with no IV coefficient published.

ECB box: state the sample window — 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024' — and use the ECB's associational language ('was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index'). Base correlation 0.50 is correct but comes from footnote 4, not the body.

Drop or explicitly flag as the author's own arithmetic the step 'a 10pp passive rise maps to +0.05'. The ECB never scales the coefficient, and because the specification includes an AR(1) lag of the dependent variable, 0.005 is a short-run partial effect; linear extrapolation is not implied by the source.

Kasch-Sarkar: the control is not 'pre-inclusion momentum' alone. The abstract's phrase is 'after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance', defined as 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum'. Also note that NY Fed Staff Report 484 (Feb 2011, revised Nov 2012) was never journal-published — Chen-Singal-Whitelaw cite it as an unpublished working paper.

CSW 2001–2012: make clear the ZERO is the difference-in-differences, not the raw beta. In 2001–2012 the S&P-beta change is +0.071 (t=2.439, significant); the non-S&P-beta change is +0.075 (t=2.496); the −0.004 (t=−0.137) is the difference. Writing that added stocks showed 'no beta increase' after 2001 would be false.

CSW's sample ends in 2012. Do not say the effect is zero 'in the decade passive grew fastest' as though it covers the post-2012 passive surge; say instead that the effect had already gone to zero by 2001–2012, and that no comparable index-inclusion beta test extends the series through 2024.

BSW: specify that 0.326 / −0.319 is the FULL-sample 1976–2000 daily BIVARIATE estimate. The bivariate subperiod pairs are 0.286/−0.301 (1976–87) and 0.357/−0.332 (1988–2000), and the full-sample univariate figure is 0.151.

BIS March 2018: the 0.45→0.52 figures are a raw return CORRELATION with the S&P 500 (not a beta), measured over t−200 to t−1 versus t+1 to t+200 trading days, from Graph 3 of Sushko & Turner, BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, p.119. Soften 'exactly the design CSW demolish' to 'vulnerable to precisely the critique CSW raise — no matched control for the fact that added stocks are momentum winners', since CSW attacked beta regressions, not this correlation statistic.

Anadu et al.: cite the FEDS working paper version explicitly (Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2018-060r1, draft 15 May 2020), Table 4, since table numbering may differ in the published Financial Analysts Journal 76(4) 2020 version. Present the line as the authors' summary judgement resting on Chen-Singal-Whitelaw, not as a Fed empirical finding: their body text says 'the evidence is mixed on whether return comovement has increased more broadly with the growth of passive investing' and cites Da & Shive (2018) and Kamara-Lou-Sadka on the other side. Note also that the adjacent Valuation row of the same table says 'since 2000', not 2001.

Add the post-2016 rebuttal: DeCoste, J. (2025), 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership', Global Finance Journal 65, doi:10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110, uses a fuzzy regression discontinuity design and reports that 'membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term', arguing the CSW null 'is due to heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members'. Presenting the comovement literature as settled against excess comovement without this is one-sided.
newContradictions: DeCoste, J. (2025), 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership', Global Finance Journal 65(C), doi:10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110 — published, peer-reviewed, post-dates every source in this claim group. Abstract (verified verbatim via RePEc/IDEAS record eee:glofin:v:65:y:2025:i:c:s1044028325000377; the ScienceDirect full text is paywalled and I could not read the tables): 'Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity approach I show that membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term... I show that the previous lack of evidence for excess comovement shown in Chen, Singal, Whitelaw (2016) is due to heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members.' This directly targets the load-bearing CSW null the claim group leans on. It does not refute CSW's Table 1 arithmetic, but it does refute the framing that index-inclusion excess comovement has been definitively demolished.

Internal tension the article should not paper over: the ECB Nov 2024 box (+0.005 per 1pp passive ownership, euro area, Q1 2010–Q1 2024) and Anadu et al. Table 4 ('comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001') are measuring different objects — a continuous passive-ownership-share panel versus discrete index-inclusion event studies. They are not directly contradictory, and presenting them as a single 'the effect has vanished' trail conflates two literatures.

Anadu et al.'s own body text contradicts the tidy reading of their Table 4 line: 'However, the evidence is mixed on whether return comovement has increased more broadly with the growth of passive investing', citing Kamara-Lou-Sadka (2008, 2010) and Bolla-Kohler-Wittig (2017) for rising betas, and Da & Shive (2018) for ETF ownership boosting return comovement.
reasoning: Primary documents reached and read verbatim, not summarised. (a) BSW, JFE 75 (2005) 283–317, full text (local bsw.txt): intro sentence on p.286 and Table 1 Panel A read directly; 0.067 / 0.214 / 0.326 / −0.319 all confirmed, with the caveat that 0.326/−0.319 is the full 1976–2000 bivariate daily row. (b) CSW, JFE 121 (2016) 624–644, full text: Table 1 Panel A 'Diff. of diff.' column read cell by cell — 0.020 (t 0.763), 0.199 (t 4.938), −0.004 (t −0.137); cross-checked against NBER WP 21281 (June 2015) which reproduces identical means and t-stats, ruling out version drift. Also read CSW's Table 5 (Dimson + momentum-matched control) showing 1988–2000 sample-minus-match DiD 0.018, t 0.601. (c) Kasch-Sarkar SR 484: local extraction confirmed against the live newyorkfed.org PDF; the '>93%' footnote 25 sentence matches at line 646 of the freshly downloaded, freshly converted PDF. The abstract's control is 'preinclusion performance' (earnings, market value, momentum), not momentum alone — that is the one qualifier off. (d) BIS QR March 2018 p.119 Graph 3 and its footnotes read directly; 0.45/0.52, 462 stocks, Jan 2000–Sep 2017, ±200 trading days, no control sample described. (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box re-fetched live with curl (not a summariser) and the 0.005 sentence, the footnote-4 base of 0.50, and the Chart B panel a methodology note extracted verbatim — this is where the claim slips: the 0.005 is a stock+time-FE panel estimate with controls including an AR(1) lag, and the index-inclusion IV is only an unquantified robustness check. The 10pp→0.05 scaling is the article's inference, not the ECB's. (f) Anadu et al. Table 4 confirmed verbatim in the local file and re-verified by downloading and converting the live federalreserve.gov FEDS 2018-060r1 PDF ('For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001'). Adversarial search up to 2026-08 surfaced one genuine post-dating rebuttal, DeCoste (2025, Global Finance Journal), whose abstract I read on the RePEc record; I could NOT reach its full text or tables (ScienceDirect paywall returned only the SPA shell), so I report its abstract claim without endorsing its magnitudes. Remaining uncertainty: (i) whether the published Financial Analysts Journal 76(4) version of Anadu et al. keeps the same table number and wording — I only verified the FEDS working paper; (ii) DeCoste's actual point estimates and sample, unverified behind the paywall; (iii) the ECB provides no standard error or coefficient table for the 0.005, only a 95% interval drawn in Chart B panel a, so its precision cannot be checked.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published JF abstract: additions 7.4% (1990s) → <1% (2010-2020); deletions large negative → +0.1% (2010-2020); JF 80(2), Apr 2025, 657-698
itemVerdicts.note: Confirmed verbatim from two independent primary routes. Crossref (10.1111/jofi.13410) and OpenAlex both return: 'The abnormal return associated with a stock being added to the S&P 500 has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1% over the past decade. This has occurred despite a significant increase in the share of stock market assets linked to the index. A similar pattern has occurred for index deletions, with large negative abnormal returns during the 1990s, but only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020.' The same abstract appears verbatim on the accepted manuscript (March 2024) deposited at Harvard DASH (bitstream 647cc3b7-4803-4748-b181-e5ec8b343de7, header: 'Published version https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13410'). Bibliographic data confirmed: Journal of Finance vol 80, issue 2, pp. 657-698, print April 2025, online 2024-12-20. No minus sign on the 0.1% in any of the three deposits. Note the exact wording is 'over the past decade' for additions (not '2010-2020'); '2010 and 2020' is used only in the deletions sentence. Crossref shows no erratum/update-to/updated-by.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-NOTE) Version drift: Dec-2022 NBER WP says 3.4%/7.6%/0.8% and deletions -0.6%; deletions 'FLIPPED SIGN between versions'
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG (as framed): that the deletion FINDING flipped sign between versions. RIGHT: only the ABSTRACT wording changed; the underlying table cell never flipped. Dec-2022 NBER WP w30748 abstract verbatim: 'fallen from an average of 3.4% in the 1980s and 7.6% in the 1990s to 0.8% over the past decade... but only -0.6% between 2010 and 2020' — confirmed. But the 2010s deletion total abnormal return is NEGATIVE in every version's table: -0.603% (Dec-2022 WP Table 2), -0.62% (June-2023 WP Table 2), and -0.62% in the PUBLISHED paper's Table 1. The published body text still reads: 'The deletion effect fell in magnitude to -12.4% in the 2000s and disappeared in the 2010s, with an average abnormal return of -0.6%.' The published abstract's '+0.1%' is contradicted by the paper's own table; the only ~+0.1 deletions figure anywhere is the 2010s EFFECTIVE-DATE CAR of +0.13% (Table 1). Do not build any argument on a sign flip. Also note a third abstract variant: HBS Faculty & Research and DASH metadata both render the additions figure as '0.3% over the past decade' instead of 'less than 1%' — yet the paper's Table 1 says 0.83%. The abstract numbers are unstable and not always consistent with the tables; cite the tables.

itemVerdicts.item: (a-SOURCE) Cited source marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf for the published abstract
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: that URL does not contain the published abstract. As fetched, marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf is the 'Revised, June 2023' working paper (byte-identical to the local gs2.txt/gs_final.txt/v19_gs_live.txt, 146,244 chars), whose abstract reads '3.4% in the 1980s and 7.6% in the 1990s to 0.8% over the past two decades... only -0.6% between 2010 and 2020'. RIGHT: the published-version text is the March 2024 accepted manuscript at Harvard DASH: https://dash.harvard.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/647cc3b7-4803-4748-b181-e5ec8b343de7/content (also SSRN 4294297); the published record of the abstract is Crossref/Wiley 10.1111/jofi.13410.

WRONG: attributing these to 'the WP' generically, and to 'Table 2' if citing the JF article. RIGHT on the numbers for ONE specific version. Verified June-2023 WP Table 2 exactly: additions 0.0342 / 0.0725 / 0.0514 / 0.00804 (SE 0.005, no stars = ns); deletions -0.0464 / -0.161 / -0.124 / -0.0062 (SE 0.011, ns); deletion N = 39/56/85/87. The Dec-2022 NBER WP Table 2 has DIFFERENT cells: additions 0.0342 / 0.0759 / 0.0521 / 0.00799; deletions -0.0464 / -0.166 / -0.123 / -0.00603; deletion N = 39/51/86/87. In the PUBLISHED paper the decade table is TABLE 1 (published Table 2 is the characteristics regression), and its cells are: additions 3.42% / 7.39% / 5.16% / 0.83% (2010s ns); deletions -4.64% / -16.11% / -12.39% / -0.62% (2010s ns); deletion N = 39/56/85/87. So '39-87 events' holds in all versions; the specific percentages must be version-tagged.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) S&P-500-tracking funds grew from ~0 to ~7% of market cap
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published version: 'funds tracking the S&P 500 in the form of mutual funds or ETFs have grown from essentially zero in the 1980s to approximately 7 percent of market capitalization in recent years.' Denominator is market capitalization, confirmed. (The Dec-2022 WP says 'approximately 7 percent' without naming the denominator in the same sentence.) The paper also notes other estimates (trading-volume-based, sell-side) are higher, and cites a UBS-derived industry figure of ~13% for 2022.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Trackers buy 7-8% of shares outstanding on addition, yet total institutional ownership barely moves
itemVerdicts.note: Published text: 'for the average addition in 2020, index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding. However, institutional ownership only increases by 0.65% of shares outstanding... The same pattern appears for deletions: in 2020, index trackers sell an average of 8.45% of shares outstanding upon deletion, but institutional ownership overall falls by only 1.42%.' Caliber caveat: Table 7 reports MEDIANS by year ('We compute the median of this quantity among additions and deletions each year'), so 7.53% is the 2020 median, not a mean; the whole-sample figure (mean of yearly medians) is 3.04% for trackers vs 0.85% for 13F institutions. Also version drift: the June-2023 WP said institutional ownership 'falls by 0.75%' for 2020 additions; the published version says it 'only increases by 0.65%'. Elsewhere the paper's Figure-1 summary is 'over 6%' for recent additions, so '7-8%' is specific to 2020.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) '...active investors provide the liquidity'
itemVerdicts.note: The paper says the opposite about active funds. Published text verbatim: 'The "Active" column shows that active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge funds, pension fund, endowments) are the primary liquidity providers around addition events.' The framing sentence is 'liquidity is provided, on average, by other institutions exiting their positions, rather than accommodation by other parties such as retail investors.' So: OTHER (largely non-13F-mutual-fund) institutions, explicitly NOT active mutual funds, and explicitly not retail.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Migrations rose from ~40% to >80% of additions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG for the published paper. RIGHT (published, March 2024/JF 2025): introduction — 'From the 1990s to the present day, migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%. The trend toward more migrations is even stronger among S&P 500 index deletions.' Body §2.2 — 'In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' So in the published version the migration share of ADDITIONS barely rises (~69% → >70%); the dramatic rise is in DELETIONS (<10% → >70%). The '40% → over 80%' figure exists only in the Dec-2022 NBER WP introduction, which contradicts its own body ('In the mid-1990s, migrations were about 40% of additions and 0% of drops. In recent years, they both make up over 60% of index changes'); the June-2023 WP says 50%→>70% (intro) and 60%→>70% (body). Definition confirmed: 'a migration [is] any stock which is added to (dropped from) the S&P 500 and dropped from (added to) the S&P MidCap within 5 calendar days.'

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s; that figure is Tesla-driven; ex-Tesla the 2020 average inclusion effect was -3bp
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 5.3% if citing the JF article. RIGHT: the published version says 5.4% — 'for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s. The large positive return in the last period is driven by Tesla, which... had a massive return of 53.35% between its announcement and effective dates.' (5.3% / Table 4 coefficient 5.337*** is the June-2023 WP; migrations by the 2010s = -1.8% in both.) The Tesla attribution is verbatim and confirmed. The -3bp figure is also verbatim — 'Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points' — but it is the 2020 average across ALL additions, NOT an ex-Tesla recomputation of the 5.4% direct-addition 2010s coefficient; splicing the two implies a number the paper never reports.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Authors frame the decay as arbitrage/anomaly decay (McLean-Pontiff), not as evidence passive is harmless
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published introduction: '...the decline of the index effect is much like the evidence for other anomalies: they decline once they are well recognized by the market (McLean and Pontiff, 2016).' Nowhere does the paper claim passive investing is harmless. Caliber note: the CONCLUSION's headline framing is Lo's adaptive markets hypothesis — 'when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact, in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis' — with the decline attributed primarily to (i) migrations and (ii) an overall increase in the market's ability to provide liquidity, and predictability/front-running 'a small role'. The paper also closes with an open puzzle (why the market took until the 2010s to adapt), which is not a clean-bill-of-health for passive.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Bennett-Stulz-Wang documented the decline first (1997-2017 additions)
itemVerdicts.note: Greenwood-Sammon's published text: 'Most closely related to our paper is Bennett et al. (2020), who first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017.' Verified against the primary BSW source (NBER WP 27593, July 2020, fetched fresh): 'We investigate the impact on firms of joining the S&P 500 index from 1997 to 2017. We find that the positive announcement effect on the stock price of index inclusion has disappeared...' Caveat: GS scope the priority to ADDITIONS only, and in the same paragraph credit Preston and Soe (2021) with documenting the decline 'among additions and deletions beginning in 1995' — so 'documented the decline first' should be scoped to additions and to the academic literature.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Coinbase jumped ~24% on its May 12, 2025 S&P 500 inclusion announcement
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'on May 12'. RIGHT: the ~24% move was on May 13, 2025, the first session after an after-close announcement. Daily price data (stockanalysis.com): COIN closed 207.22 on Mon 2025-05-12 (+3.96% that day, on a session when SPY rose 3.30% on the tariff-truce rally) and 256.90 on Tue 2025-05-13 = +23.97%, opening at 231.71 (gap up). SPY on 05-13 was +0.66%, so the market-adjusted one-day move is ~+23.3%. The S&P DJI press release is datelined 'NEW YORK, May 12, 2025', effective 'prior to the opening of trading on Monday, May 19'; COIN rose ~8% in extended trading on May 12. A Greenwood-Sammon-style total abnormal return (day before announcement 05-09 close 199.32 → day after effective 05-20 close 261.38, less SPY 564.34→592.85) is roughly +26%. IMPORTANT QUALIFIER the article must carry: the press release lists NO S&P MidCap 400 change, so Coinbase was a DIRECT addition (non-migration), replacing Discover Financial, which was removed for M&A. Greenwood-Sammon's own published result is that DIRECT additions still earned ~5.4% in the 2010s and that the decline is driven by migrations — so a large pop for a direct, high-idiosyncratic-risk, non-migration addition is consistent with, not a refutation of, their mechanism. The peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020 (§1 is titled 'Index tracking and the index inclusion effect 1980-2020'), so 2025 is out-of-sample and a single event is not a documented revival; I found no peer-reviewed replication, erratum, or contradicting study through 2026-08.

corrections: Replace the source URL for the published abstract. marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf is the June 2023 working-paper revision (abstract: 3.4%/7.6%/0.8%, deletions -0.6%), not the published article. Cite Crossref/Wiley 10.1111/jofi.13410 for the abstract and, for the published full text, the Harvard DASH accepted manuscript dated March 2024 (https://dash.harvard.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/647cc3b7-4803-4748-b181-e5ec8b343de7/content), which carries the published abstract verbatim and the header 'Published version https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13410'.

Do not claim the deletions finding 'flipped sign between versions.' Only the abstract wording changed. Every version's table reports a NEGATIVE 2010s deletion abnormal return: -0.603% (Dec-2022 NBER WP Table 2), -0.62% (June-2023 WP Table 2), -0.62% (published Table 1). The published body text still says 'disappeared in the 2010s, with an average abnormal return of -0.6%.' The published abstract's '0.1%' is not corroborated by any total-return cell in the paper (the nearest is the 2010s effective-date CAR of +0.13%). If the abstract's 0.1% is quoted, note that the paper's own Table 1 reports -0.62% for the same window.

If citing the Journal of Finance version, use its Table 1 (NOT 'Table 2' — in the published paper Table 2 is the characteristics regression): additions 1980s 3.42%, 1990s 7.39%, 2000s 5.16%, 2010s 0.83% (not significant); deletions 1980s -4.64%, 1990s -16.11%, 2000s -12.39%, 2010s -0.62% (not significant); deletion N per decade 39/56/85/87. The figures 7.25% / 5.14% / 0.804% / -16.1% belong to the June-2023 working paper's Table 2, and 7.59% / 5.21% / 0.799% / -16.6% to the Dec-2022 NBER WP Table 2. Tag every number with its version.

Fix the migration statistic. '~40% to >80% of additions' is a Dec-2022 NBER WP introduction figure that the paper itself later revised and that even contradicted the same WP's own body ('about 40% of additions and 0% of drops... In recent years, they both make up over 60%'). The published version says: intro — 'From the 1990s to the present day, migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%'; body — 'In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' The dramatic rise is in DELETIONS (<10% to >70%), not additions.

Correct the liquidity-provider attribution. Greenwood and Sammon explicitly rule out active mutual funds: 'active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge funds, pension fund, endowments) are the primary liquidity providers around addition events.' Retail is also ruled out. Say 'other institutions — chiefly non-13F-mutual-fund institutions such as hedge funds, pension funds and endowments — sell to the indexers,' not 'active investors provide the liquidity.'

Update the direct-addition figure to the published value: direct additions earned 5.4% in the 2010s (10.2% in the late 1990s, 8.8% in the 2000s), with migrations at -1.8% in the 2010s. 5.3% is the June-2023 working-paper number. Keep 'driven by Tesla' (verbatim in the paper, which reports Tesla's 53.35% announcement-to-effective return), but do not present the '-3 basis points' figure as an ex-Tesla version of the 5.4% direct-addition coefficient: '-3 basis points' is the ex-Tesla average inclusion effect across ALL additions in calendar 2020.

State the tracker-buying figure as a median, not a mean: Table 7 reports yearly MEDIANS. For 2020 the median addition saw trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding while 13F institutional ownership rose only 0.65%; for deletions trackers sold 8.45% while institutional ownership fell 1.42%. The whole-sample figure (mean of yearly medians) is 3.04% trackers vs 0.85% institutions.

Correct the Coinbase date. The ~24% move was on Tuesday May 13, 2025 (close 207.22 -> 256.90, +23.97%; SPY +0.66% that day, so ~+23.3% market-adjusted), following an after-close announcement datelined May 12. On May 12 itself COIN rose 3.96% while SPY rose 3.30%. Effective date was May 19, 2025.

Add the disqualifying qualifier to the Coinbase example: the S&P DJI release lists no S&P MidCap 400 change, so Coinbase was a DIRECT addition (non-migration), replacing Discover Financial, which was deleted for M&A. Greenwood and Sammon's own published result is that direct additions still earned ~5.4% in the 2010s and that the disappearance is driven by migrations plus improved liquidity provision — so a large pop for a direct, high-idiosyncratic-risk addition is consistent with their mechanism rather than evidence against it. Also state that the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020 and that a single 2025 event is not a documented revival; no replication, erratum, or contradicting peer-reviewed study exists as of August 2026.

When quoting the published abstract, quote it exactly: additions fell to 'less than 1% over the past decade' (the phrase '2010-2020' appears only in the deletions clause), and note that HBS Faculty & Research and Harvard DASH both circulate a variant abstract reading '0.3% over the past decade' — while the paper's Table 1 reports 0.83%. Prefer the table values over any abstract figure.
newContradictions: Internal contradiction inside the published paper itself: the abstract says index deletions averaged 'only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020', but Table 1 and the body text of the same document both report -0.62% / -0.6% for 2010s deletion total abnormal returns. The only ~+0.1 figure in the paper is the 2010s effective-date CAR of +0.13%.

Second internal contradiction: the HBS Faculty & Research page and Harvard DASH metadata both carry an abstract variant reading 'to 0.3% over the past decade' for additions, while the Wiley/Crossref published abstract and the March-2024 accepted PDF read 'to less than 1%' — and the paper's Table 1 reports 0.83%. Three different renderings of the same statistic.

Third internal contradiction, in the published version: the introduction says migrations 'went from about 50% of additions to over 70%', while §2.2 says 'In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions... In recent years, they both make up over 70%'. The Dec-2022 NBER WP has the same intro/body split at 40% vs 40%-to-over-60%.

Greenwood-Sammon's published paper credits Bennett, Stulz and Wang (2020) with FIRST noting the decline among additions, but in the same paragraph also credits Preston and Soe (2021) with documenting the decline among both additions and deletions beginning in 1995 — so 'BSW first' is a scoped claim about additions in the academic literature, not an unqualified priority claim.

Greenwood-Sammon (published Table 7) show active mutual funds are NOT the liquidity providers around index changes; this cuts against any narrative in which surviving active managers absorb passive demand, and points instead to hedge funds/pensions/endowments outside the 13F mutual-fund universe.
reasoning: I reached four distinct primary versions of the paper verbatim and compared them cell by cell. (1) Dec-2022 NBER WP w30748 (local gs.txt, plus gs_ivey.txt, same vintage): abstract and Table 2 read in full. (2) June-2023 revision (local gs2.txt/gs_final.txt, byte-identical to a fresh fetch of marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf): abstract, Table 2, Table 4, and §2.2 read in full. (3) The published-version text: I located and downloaded the Harvard DASH bitstream for the article record (dash.harvard.edu bitstream 647cc3b7-...), which is the March 2024 accepted manuscript carrying the header 'Published version https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13410' and the SSRN 4294297 stamp; I extracted it with pdftotext -layout and read the abstract, §1 (Table 1 with all decade cells and N), §2.2 (migrations), §3 (Table 7, liquidity provision), the intro's McLean-Pontiff sentence, the Bennett et al. priority sentence, and the conclusion. (4) The published abstract of record from Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/jofi.13410) and OpenAlex, which agree verbatim and confirm vol 80(2), 657-698, print April 2025, online 2024-12-20, and no erratum. Wiley itself returned HTTP 403, so I did not see the typeset PDF; the accepted manuscript plus two metadata deposits are my basis, and that is the one residual uncertainty — I cannot rule out that Wiley's final typeset Table 1 differs from the March-2024 accepted version, though the identical abstract strings make that unlikely. For Bennett-Stulz-Wang I fetched NBER w27593 fresh and read the abstract (1997-2017, announcement effect 'has disappeared'). For the Coinbase item I used actual daily OHLC data from stockanalysis.com's API for COIN and SPY (stooq and Yahoo were both blocked) and confirmed the S&P DJI press release dateline, effective date, and the absence of any MidCap 400 change via press.spglobal.com. Every quoted string in my output was read directly from a document or a JSON payload I fetched; I quoted nothing from a search summarizer (the one search summary that asserted '0.3%' I treated as unverified until I confirmed it independently on the HBS page and DASH raw HTML, and even then I flagged it as inconsistent with the paper's own table). What remains uncertain: (i) whether the typeset Wiley Table 1 matches the accepted manuscript; (ii) the provenance of the abstract's '0.1%' deletions figure, which no table in the paper supports.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published JF abstract: additions fell from 7.4% (1990s) to less than 1% over the past decade
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from Crossref deposit for 10.1111/jofi.13410 and confirmed independently on RePEc/EconPapers and in the accepted manuscript (Harvard DASH PDF, dated March 2024): 'The abnormal return associated with a stock being added to the S&P 500 has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1% over the past decade.' Bibliographic data also confirmed: The Journal of Finance, vol. 80, issue 2, pp. 657-698, published-print April 2025, published-online 2024-12-20. CAUTION: Harvard DASH's and HBS's repository METADATA carry a different abstract variant reading '...to 0.3% over the past decade'. That 0.3% is NOT the version-of-record wording (Crossref + RePEc + the DASH PDF's own title page all say 'less than 1%') and is not any number in Table 1. Do not quote '0.3%'.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published abstract: deletions from large negative to +0.1% average 2010-2020
itemVerdicts.note: The abstract does say this (Crossref VoR: 'with large negative abnormal returns during the 1990s but an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020'). BUT the published paper's own numbers contradict it. WRONG (as a statement of the paper's finding): deletions averaged +0.1% in 2010-2020. RIGHT: the published Table 1 reports the 2010s deletion total CAR as -0.62% (N=87, statistically insignificant), and the published body text says 'The deletion effect fell in magnitude to -12.4% in the 2000s and disappeared in the 2010s, with an average abnormal return of -0.6%.' The only 0.1%-ish figure in that row is the effective-date sub-component (+0.13%). Safest article wording: the deletion effect went to statistically indistinguishable from zero (-0.6% in Table 1); do not present '+0.1%' as the measured deletion return.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) NOTE in the claim group that the deletions figure FLIPPED SIGN between the WP and published versions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'the deletions figure flipped sign between versions.' RIGHT: the ESTIMATE never changed. June-2023 WP Table 2 Panel B: deletions 2010-2020 total = -0.0062 (-0.62%), N=87. Published (March-2024 accepted MS / JF) Table 1: deletions 2010s total = -0.62%, N=87. Identical. What changed is only the ABSTRACT's wording (WP abstract: 'only -0.6% between 2010 and 2020'; published abstract: 'an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020'). Treating this as a data revision would be an error.

These match the JUNE 2023 revision only (the PDF currently at marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf, which is 'Revised, June 2023', Table 2 Panel A: 0.0342***, 0.0725***, 0.0514***, 0.00804 with no stars). WRONG to attribute them to the Dec-2022 NBER WP w30748, whose Table 2 Panel A reads 0.0342***, 0.0759***, 0.0521***, 0.00799 (N = 196/128/210/150). And the PEER-REVIEWED version supersedes both: published Table 1 (renumbered — published Table 2 is now the characteristics-controlled regression) reports additions 1980s 3.42%***, 1990s 7.39%***, 2000s 5.16%***, 2010s 0.83% (no stars), N = 196/134/211/153. Cite the published Table 1 numbers, and do not call it 'Table 2'.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) WP Table 2 deletions: 1990s -16.1%, 2010-20 -0.62% (ns); decade cells rest on only 39-87 events
itemVerdicts.note: Deletion values verified in the June-2023 WP (Table 2 Panel B: -0.161***, -0.0062 ns) and unchanged in the published Table 1 (-16.11%***, -0.62% no stars). The Dec-2022 NBER WP instead had -0.166*** and -0.00603. Event counts: WRONG if attributed to the NBER WP (39/51/86/87). RIGHT for the June-2023 WP and the published paper: 39 (1980s), 56 (1990s), 85 (2000s), 87 (2010s). The '39-87 events' range is therefore accurate for the published version; the thin-cell caveat is fair (1980s deletions n=39, 1990s n=56).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) S&P-500-tracking funds grew from ~0 to ~7% of market cap
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published version: 'We estimate that funds tracking the S&P 500 in the form of mutual funds or ETFs have grown from essentially zero in the 1980s to approximately 7 percent of market capitalization in recent years.' Same sentence in both WP versions. Note this is share of MARKET CAP held by S&P-500 index trackers specifically, not total passive share.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Trackers buy 7-8% of shares outstanding on addition yet total institutional ownership barely moves
itemVerdicts.note: Direction confirmed, magnitudes need a year qualifier and one sign is version-dependent. Published text: 'for the average addition in 2020, index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding. However, institutional ownership only increases by 0.65% of shares outstanding'; and 'in 2020, index trackers sell an average of 8.45% of shares outstanding upon deletion, but institutional ownership overall falls by only 1.42%.' WRONG to state 7-8% as a sample-wide figure: published Table 7's full-sample mean tracker trade is 3.04% (additions) / -3.08% (deletions); 7.5-8.5% is the 2020 figure. WRONG (June-2023 WP number, superseded): institutional ownership 'falls by 0.75%' on additions. RIGHT (published): it rises 0.65% on additions.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Active investors provide the liquidity
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: 'active investors provide the liquidity.' RIGHT (published, verbatim): 'The "Active" column shows that active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge funds, pension fund, endowments) are the primary liquidity providers around addition events.' The paper also rules out retail: 'liquidity is provided, on average, by other institutions exiting their positions, rather than accommodation by other parties such as retail investors.' Attributing the accommodation to active managers/active mutual funds inverts the paper's finding.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Migrations rose from ~40% to >80% of additions
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: '~40% to over 80% of additions.' That sentence exists ONLY in the superseded Dec-2022 NBER WP ('migrations went from about 40% of additions to over 80%'), and even that version's own body text said 'about 40% of additions ... In recent years, they both make up over 60%'. RIGHT (published JF version, intro): 'From the 1990s to the present day, migrations went from about 50% of additions to over 70%.' And the published Figure 4 discussion explicitly reframes it: 'migrations have become a steady share of additions and especially deletions. In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' So in the published paper the dramatic migration rise is in DELETIONS (<10% to >70%), not additions.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s, Tesla-driven; ex-Tesla the 2020 average inclusion effect was -3bp
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed; one digit off against the published version. WRONG (June-2023 WP number): 5.3%. RIGHT (published): 'for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s. The large positive return in the last period is driven by Tesla, which, as previously discussed, had a massive return of 53.35% between its announcement and effective dates.' The ex-Tesla figure is verbatim in both versions: 'Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Authors frame the decay as arbitrage/anomaly decay (McLean-Pontiff), not as evidence passive is harmless
itemVerdicts.note: The McLean-Pontiff framing is real and verbatim: 'the decline of the index effect is much like the evidence for other anomalies: they decline once they are well recognized by the market (McLean and Pontiff, 2016).' But it is a secondary framing, not the paper's headline interpretation. The published Conclusion: 'our assessment is that the declining index effect is driven primarily by two factors: in the role of migrations from the S&P MidCap Index, as well as an overall increase in the market's ability to provide liquidity to index changes. A third factor, increased predictability of index changes, also plays a small role. Our overall conclusion is that, when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact, in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis.' Correct: the paper nowhere claims passive investing is harmless — it studies event-level price impact of index changes only and explicitly leaves aggregate-demand questions to the Koijen-Yogo / Gabaix-Koijen literature it merely cites.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Bennett-Stulz-Wang documented the decline first (1997-2017 additions)
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published version: 'Most closely related to our paper is Bennett et al. (2020), who first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017.' Also 'as originally highlighted by Bennett et al. (2020)'. Cite it as Bennett, Stulz, and Wang (2020), 'Does Joining the S&P 500 Index Hurt Firms?' — the published GS reference list still lists it as a working paper. Note the June-2023 WP inconsistently cited the same work as 'Bennett, Stulz, and Wang (2022)' in text; use the published paper's (2020).

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Coinbase jumped ~24% on its May 12, 2025 S&P 500 inclusion announcement
itemVerdicts.note: Magnitude confirmed, date attribution wrong. S&P DJI's press release is dated May 12, 2025 (COIN replaces Discover Financial Services, effective prior to the open on Monday, May 19) but was issued AFTER the close — CoinDesk's same-day story is headlined 'Coinbase (COIN) Shares Jump 8% Post-Market'. WRONG: '+24% on May 12'. RIGHT: COIN closed +3.96% on May 12 (199.32 -> 207.22) and +23.97% on May 13, 2025 (207.22 -> 256.90); SPY was +0.66% that day, so market-adjusted ~+23.3%. CNBC's contemporaneous headline: 'Coinbase jumps 24% on S&P 500 inclusion, biggest gain since post-election pop' (May 13). A Greenwood-Sammon-style total CAR (close the day before announcement, May 9, to close the day after the effective date, May 20) is COIN +31.1% vs SPY +5.1%, i.e. roughly +26% market-adjusted — larger than any decade average in their Table 1. Price data: stockanalysis.com daily OHLC for COIN and SPY.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) Whether a 2025 revival qualifies the 'disappeared' conclusion
itemVerdicts.note: Yes, and Coinbase is not the only 2025 case. The peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020 (Table 1's last row is 2010-2020); nothing in the paper speaks to 2021-2026. Two further post-sample data points I verified from daily price data: after S&P DJI's Friday-after-close announcement of September 5, 2025 (AppLovin, Robinhood Markets and Emcor Group joining the S&P 500 effective before the open on September 22), on the next session, Monday September 8, 2025, HOOD closed +15.83% and APP closed +11.59%. The article should therefore say the index effect had vanished THROUGH 2020 in the peer-reviewed evidence, and note that several large 2025 inclusions produced double-digit announcement-day moves — while flagging that these are single-name anecdotes, not a re-estimated average, and that COIN's move coincided with a crypto rally.

corrections: Do not write that the Greenwood-Sammon deletion effect turned positive at +0.1%. The published abstract says '0.1%', but the paper's own Table 1 reports the 2010s deletion CAR as -0.62% (N=87, insignificant) and the body text says '-0.6%'. Write: the deletion effect fell from -16.1% in the 1990s to a statistically insignificant -0.6% in 2010-2020.

Do not describe the deletions number as having 'flipped sign between versions'. The estimate is identical in the June-2023 working paper (-0.62%, N=87) and in the published Journal of Finance version (-0.62%, N=87); only the abstract's wording changed.

If citing the decade table, cite the PUBLISHED numbers and the PUBLISHED table number: Journal of Finance 80(2), Table 1 — additions 3.42% (1980s), 7.39% (1990s), 5.16% (2000s), 0.83% (2010s, insignificant); deletions -4.64%, -16.11%, -12.39%, -0.62% (insignificant); deletion N = 39/56/85/87. The figures 7.25%/5.14%/0.804%/-16.1% belong to the June-2023 working paper; 7.59%/5.21%/0.799%/-16.6% belong to the Dec-2022 NBER working paper. In the published version, 'Table 2' is a different table (CARs controlling for characteristics).

Replace 'migrations rose from ~40% to over 80% of additions'. That figure survives only in the superseded Dec-2022 NBER working paper. The published paper says migrations 'went from about 50% of additions to over 70%', and its Figure 4 discussion calls the additions share 'a steady share' — 'In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' The dramatic rise is in DELETIONS, not additions.

Do not say active investors provide the liquidity. The published paper states: 'active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge funds, pension fund, endowments) are the primary liquidity providers around addition events.' It also rules out retail investors. Say: non-13F/S12-filing institutions — hedge funds, pension funds, endowments.

Change '+5.3% for direct additions in the 2010s' to 5.4% (published version). The published sentence is: 'for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s.' The ex-Tesla claim is exact as written: 'Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points.'

Qualify the tracker-buying figure with a year. 7.53% of shares outstanding bought (and 8.45% sold on deletion) is the 2020 average; the full-sample mean in published Table 7 is 3.04% / -3.08%. And use the published sign for the 13F offset: institutional ownership 'only increases by 0.65%' on additions and 'falls by only 1.42%' on deletions (the June-2023 working paper's '-0.75%' on additions is superseded).

Do not present McLean-Pontiff anomaly decay as the paper's headline explanation. The published Conclusion attributes the decline primarily to (i) migrations from the S&P MidCap and (ii) an overall increase in the market's ability to provide liquidity, with predictability playing 'a small role', framed 'in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis'. McLean-Pontiff appears once, as an analogy.

Fix the Coinbase date. S&P DJI announced on May 12, 2025 after the close (effective before the open on May 19). COIN closed +3.96% on May 12 and +23.97% on May 13, 2025 (207.22 -> 256.90, vs SPY +0.66%). Write '~24% the next trading day' or 'on May 13, the session after the after-close announcement', not '+24% on May 12'.

When invoking 2025 inclusions, state explicitly that the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020 and that these are single-name anecdotes rather than a re-estimated average. Additional verified post-sample cases: after the September 5, 2025 after-close announcement, Robinhood (HOOD) closed +15.83% and AppLovin (APP) +11.59% on September 8, 2025.
Cite Bennett, Stulz, and Wang as (2020), matching the published paper's reference list; the June-2023 working paper's in-text '(2022)' is an inconsistency in that draft.

Do not quote '0.3%' as the published addition figure. Harvard DASH and HBS repository metadata carry an abstract variant reading '...to 0.3% over the past decade', but the version of record (Crossref deposit and RePEc) reads 'less than 1%', matching Table 1's 0.83%.
newContradictions: The published Journal of Finance abstract's deletion figure ('an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020') is inconsistent with the same paper's Table 1 (-0.62%) and body text ('an average abnormal return of -0.6%'). The only +0.1%-magnitude number in that row is the effective-date sub-component (+0.13%). Any article sentence built on the abstract's '0.1%' is quoting a figure the paper's own tables do not support.

Two different 'published' abstracts are in circulation: the Wiley version of record (Crossref + RePEc + the accepted-manuscript title page) reads 'to less than 1% over the past decade', while Harvard DASH and HBS repository metadata read 'to 0.3% over the past decade'. Neither 0.3% nor 0.1% appears in Table 1.

The PDF the source list points to (marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf) is NOT the published paper — as fetched on 2026-08-15 it is the 'Revised, June 2023' working paper. Its abstract still reports 3.4%/7.6%/0.8% and -0.6% even though its own Table 2 reports 7.25% for the 1990s, an internal inconsistency in that draft. The peer-reviewed text is available open-access as the March-2024 accepted manuscript in Harvard DASH.

The June-2023 working paper says institutional ownership FALLS by 0.75% of shares outstanding around 2020 additions; the published version says it INCREASES by 0.65%. A sign flip on that specific statistic did occur between versions (unlike the deletion CAR, where none did).

Post-sample market data materially qualify the 'disappeared' framing: three high-profile 2025 S&P 500 additions produced double-digit announcement-reaction moves (COIN +24.0% on 2025-05-13, HOOD +15.8% and APP +11.6% on 2025-09-08), all outside the paper's 1980-2020 sample. No peer-reviewed re-estimation covering 2021-2026 was found as of 2026-08.
reasoning: I reached four distinct primary texts and read the relevant sentences and table cells myself rather than relying on any fetch summary. (1) Crossref API record for DOI 10.1111/jofi.13410 — confirms The Journal of Finance 80(2), 657-698, published-print April 2025, published-online 2024-12-20, and gives the version-of-record abstract verbatim ('7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1%'; deletions 'an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020'). I cross-checked that abstract independently on RePEc/EconPapers, which matched word for word, so the abstract is not a single-source artifact.
