(2) The peer-reviewed text itself: Harvard DASH hosts the open-access accepted manuscript (dated March 2024, abstract identical to the VoR) as a PDF bitstream; I downloaded it and ran pdftotext -layout, then read Table 1 (the decade table, renumbered from the working paper's Table 2), Table 2 (characteristics controls), Table 7 (tracker vs 13F ownership), and the Conclusion. (3) The June-2023 working paper, freshly re-fetched from marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf — this is the URL in the article's source list, and as of today it still serves the June-2023 draft, not the published paper. (4) The Dec-2022 NBER WP w30748 text, already extracted locally, which I re-parsed from the PDF to read its Table 2. Having all three side by side is what exposed the version drift: the addition/deletion decade point estimates cited in the claim group (7.25%/5.14%/0.804%/-16.1%/-0.62%) come from the June-2023 draft, while the migration statistic ('~40% to >80%') comes only from the Dec-2022 NBER draft, and the published paper differs from both (7.39%/5.16%/0.83%; migrations 'about 50% of additions to over 70%', with the additions share described as steady at ~69% to >70% and the real rise being in deletions from <10% to >70%). The most consequential single finding is that the prompt's own premise — that the deletions figure flipped sign between versions — is false: -0.62% with N=87 appears identically in the June-2023 Table 2 and the published Table 1. What actually happened is that the abstract's wording changed to '0.1%', and that abstract number contradicts the paper's own table and body text; I searched the published text for any 0.1% deletion statistic and found only the effective-date sub-component (+0.13%), so I could not reconstruct the abstract's number from anything in the paper. I also found a second, quieter version problem: DASH's and HBS's item-level metadata carry an abstract variant saying '0.3% over the past decade', which matches neither the VoR nor Table 1 — a live trap for anyone quoting from a repository landing page instead of the article. On the liquidity-provision claim I quote the published sentence in full because the claim inverts it: active mutual funds are explicitly excluded as liquidity providers, and the paper names non-S12-filing institutions (hedge funds, pension funds, endowments). Wiley itself returned 403 to a direct fetch, so I have not read the typeset VoR pages; I treat the March-2024 accepted manuscript plus two independent renderings of the VoR abstract as sufficient, and typesetting does not normally alter table values — that is the one residual uncertainty, and I flag it rather than assert the VoR Table 1 is byte-identical. For the Coinbase check I avoided the local coin.csv (it turned out to be a bot-challenge page, not data) and Stooq (proof-of-work wall; I solved it and still got 'Access denied'), and pulled daily OHLC for COIN, SPY, HOOD and APP from stockanalysis.com's JSON API, computing the returns myself: COIN 207.22 -> 256.90 = +23.97% on 2025-05-13 against SPY +0.66%, with +3.96% on May 12 itself. I confirmed the announcement date and effective date from S&P Global's own press-release page and confirmed the after-close timing from the contemporaneous CoinDesk headline about an 8% post-market move, which is what pins the 24% to May 13 rather than May 12. I added HOOD and APP as further post-sample data points only after verifying the September 5, 2025 announcement date and September 22 effective date from S&P DJI's press release. I searched for errata, corrections or replications of jofi.13410 up to 2026-08 and found none; I also found no peer-reviewed re-estimation covering 2021-2026, so the 2025 revival evidence remains anecdotal and I labelled it as such rather than letting it overturn the paper.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) BSW JFE 2005: S&P daily beta increase on inclusion 0.067 (1976-87) vs 0.214 (1988-2000); 0.326/-0.319 is the bivariate spec
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in the published JFE version (JFE 75 (2005) 283-317, Table 1 Panel A, daily returns). Additions 1976-1987 N=196: univariate Delta-beta 0.067*** (s.e. 0.023); 1988-2000 N=259: 0.214*** (s.e. 0.032). Intro text: 'While stocks added to the S&P during 1976-1987 experience an average increase in daily S&P beta of 0.067 after inclusion, the average increase in the 1988-2000 period is 0.214.' Bivariate, 1976-2000, N=455: Delta-beta_SP500 = 0.326***, Delta-beta_nonSP500 = -0.319***. One caliber note to add: 0.326/-0.319 is the FULL 1976-2000 daily-frequency bivariate; the subperiod bivariate pairs are 0.286/-0.301 (1976-87) and 0.357/-0.332 (1988-2000), and the weekly/monthly bivariate numbers are much smaller (0.174/-0.119 weekly).

itemVerdicts.item: (b) CSW JFE 2016 univariate diff-of-diff: +0.020 (t=0.76) 1976-87, +0.199 (t=4.94) 1988-2000, -0.004 (t=-0.14) 2001-2012; bivariate spec uninformative
itemVerdicts.note: All six numbers verified verbatim in the PUBLISHED JFE 121 (2016) 624-644, Table 1 Panel A, 'Diff. of diff.' column (beta2 - beta1): 1976-1987 n=197, 0.020, t=0.763; 1988-2000 n=269, 0.199, t=4.938; 2001-2012 n=214, -0.004, t=-0.137. Identical in NBER WP 21281, so no working-paper/published drift. Abstract supports the bivariate critique verbatim: bivariate regressions 'provide little information about the economic magnitude of excess comovement, with coefficients that are sensitive to unrelated factors.' TWO CALIBER CORRECTIONS. (1) WRONG implication: that S&P beta does not rise at all after 2001. RIGHT: in the same Table 1 Panel A the raw post-inclusion change in S&P beta for 2001-2012 is +0.071 with t=2.439 (statistically significant); what is zero is the DIFFERENCE-OF-DIFFERENCES, because the change in non-S&P beta over the same window is +0.075 (t=2.496). The article must say the effect nets to zero against the counterfactual, not that betas stopped rising. (2) Table 1 is the event sample only; the matched-control samples appear in CSW's later tables, so 'univariate difference-of-differences' here means Delta-beta_S&P minus Delta-beta_non-S&P within the added stocks, not event-minus-matched-control.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Kasch-Sarkar NY Fed SR 484: no permanent value or comovement effect after pre-inclusion momentum; declines bivariate spec because regressors correlate >93%
itemVerdicts.note: Both halves verified verbatim in the primary PDF text (Staff Report 484, February 2011, revised November 2012). Footnote 25: 'we have measured the value-weighted return of non-S&P 500 stocks, following the procedure described in Table 1 of Barberis et al. (2005), and documented that the correlation between S&P 500 and non-S&P 500 stock returns exceeds 93%. The concern regarding a multiple regression with highly correlated regressors is that its parameter estimates are likely to be regression artifacts, rendering their interpretation difficult. Therefore, we do not consider specifications which include both of these highly correlated indices in one regression.' CORRECTION on the conditioning variable: WRONG = 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum'; RIGHT = after accounting for extraordinary pre-inclusion PERFORMANCE, which the abstract defines as 'large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, and positive price momentum' - momentum is one of three components, not the whole adjustment. Abstract verbatim: 'after accounting for the firms' extraordinary preinclusion performance - index inclusion has no permanent effect on value and comovement.'

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS March 2018: correlation 0.45->0.52 on inclusion, 462 stocks, 2000-2017, raw before/after with no matched control, 'exactly the design CSW demolish'
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers confirmed against the re-fetched primary PDF (Sushko & Turner, 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets,' BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, p.119 Graph 3). I checked bar-label alignment by PDF bounding box because plain text extraction reversed the order: 0.45 sits at x=102.9 under 'Before joining (from t-200 to t-1)' (x=84-110) and 0.52 at x=168.0 under 'After joining (from t+1 to t+200)' (x=153-172). Footnote 1: 'Sample based on 462 stocks joining the S&P 500 between January 2000 and September 2017'; footnote 2: 'Correlation of daily returns with the S&P 500 index.' CORRECTIONS: (1) the window is January 2000 to September 2017, not '2000-2017' loosely, and the before/after windows are +/-200 trading days around each inclusion date. (2) WRONG = 'exactly the design CSW demolish.' RIGHT = BIS does not run the bivariate regression at all; it reports a raw correlation level before vs after. CSW's central demolition target is the BIVARIATE spec, and CSW's own raw univariate S&P-beta change for 2001-2012 is positive and significant (+0.071, t=2.44) - i.e. the BIS-style uncontrolled comparison survives CSW. The applicable critique is the missing counterfactual/control (CSW's matched samples; Kasch-Sarkar's pre-inclusion run-up, which contaminates the t-200 to t-1 'before' window).

itemVerdicts.item: (e) ECB FSR Nov 2024 box: +0.005 correlation per 1pp passive ownership share (euro area, stock+time FE, index-inclusion IV, base correlation 0.50); 10pp -> +0.05
itemVerdicts.note: Core figure verified verbatim: 'Between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024, a 1 percentage point increase in the passive ownership share of a euro area stock was associated with an increase of around 0.005 in the correlation coefficient with the EURO STOXX index.' Footnote 4 verbatim: 'the average return correlation coefficient of a euro area stock with the EURO STOXX index between the first quarter of 2010 and the first quarter of 2024 is 0.50.' Box: 'Passive investing and its impact on return co-movement, market concentration and liquidity in euro area equity markets,' prepared by Daniel Dieckelmann, Emilio Siciliano and Andrzej Sowinski, FSR November 2024. CORRECTIONS: (1) WRONG = the headline coefficient comes from a spec with an index-inclusion IV; RIGHT = the 0.005 comes from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects controlling for market cap, liquidity, valuation and one autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient - the IV is a robustness check ('The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up, using index inclusion as an instrumental variable for passive ownership share'). (2) The specification includes a LAGGED DEPENDENT VARIABLE, so 0.005 is a short-run/impact coefficient, not a long-run one; the linear '10pp -> +0.05' extrapolation is the article's own arithmetic (the ECB never states it) and understates the long-run effect implied by the AR(1) term. Label it as the article's extrapolation, not an ECB finding.

itemVerdicts.item: (f) Fed's Anadu et al. Table 4: 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001.'
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in both local copies of FEDS 2018-060r1 (Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela; first draft August 27, 2018; this draft May 15, 2020), Table 4 'Impact of active-to-passive shift on index-inclusion effects and financial stability,' row 'Comovement of returns,' column 'Evidence that active-to-passive shift has exacerbated?': 'For equities, comovement effects have declined significantly since 2001.' Body text sources this to CSW: 'Chen, Singal, and Whitelaw (2016) ... do not find evidence of an upward trend in recent years. They report that adding a stock to the index had a smaller effect on its beta during the period from 2001 to 2012 than in the previous decade, even as indexing had become more common.' Cite it as the FEDS working paper 2018-060r1 (Table 4 exists there), not the 2020 Financial Analysts Journal version.

corrections: CSW 2001-2012: do not write that S&P beta stopped rising. In CSW Table 1 Panel A the raw post-inclusion S&P beta change for 2001-2012 is +0.071 (t=2.44) and is statistically significant; the non-S&P beta change is +0.075 (t=2.50). It is the DIFFERENCE-OF-DIFFERENCES that is zero (-0.004, t=-0.14). Phrase as: 'the S&P beta still rises, but by no more than the non-S&P beta rises, so the excess comovement nets to zero.'

Specify that CSW's cited diff-of-diff figures are within-event (Delta-beta_S&P minus Delta-beta_non-S&P for the added stocks, Table 1 Panel A), not event-versus-matched-control; CSW's matched-control samples are reported in separate later tables.

BSW: state that 0.326 / -0.319 is the 1976-2000 FULL-sample DAILY bivariate pair. The subperiod bivariate pairs are 0.286/-0.301 (1976-87) and 0.357/-0.332 (1988-2000), and the weekly bivariate pair is only 0.174/-0.119.

Kasch-Sarkar: replace 'after accounting for pre-inclusion momentum' with 'after accounting for extraordinary pre-inclusion performance' - the abstract defines this as large increases in earnings, appreciation in market value, AND positive price momentum. Momentum is one of three components.

BIS: replace 'exactly the design CSW demolish' with a precise statement. BIS runs no regression at all - it is a raw correlation level before vs after (t-200 to t-1 vs t+1 to t+200 trading days), so it is not the bivariate spec CSW demolish. The applicable critique is the missing control/counterfactual: CSW's matched samples and Kasch-Sarkar's point that the pre-window is contaminated by the pre-inclusion run-up. Note also that CSW's own uncontrolled univariate S&P-beta change for 2001-2012 is positive and significant, so an uncontrolled comparison like BIS's is exactly what survives CSW.

BIS: give the sample window precisely as January 2000 to September 2017, and attribute to Sushko, V. and Turner, G., 'The implications of passive investing for securities markets,' BIS Quarterly Review, March 2018, Graph 3, p.119.

ECB: the 0.005 comes from a panel regression with stock and time fixed effects controlling for market cap, liquidity, valuation and one autoregressive lag of the correlation coefficient. The index-inclusion instrumental variable is a ROBUSTNESS CHECK ('The results also hold in a two-step regression set-up'), not the headline specification. Do not present the headline estimate as IV-identified.

ECB: flag that because the specification includes a lagged dependent variable, 0.005 is a short-run coefficient; the '10pp passive rise maps to +0.05' arithmetic is the article's own linear extrapolation, which the ECB does not state and which likely understates the long-run effect. Attribute the extrapolation to the article, not to the ECB. Also give the estimation window as Q1 2010 - Q1 2024.

Anadu et al.: cite as Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2018-060r1 (Board of Governors, first draft August 2018, this draft May 15, 2020), Table 4, row 'Comovement of returns'. Table 4 is in the FEDS working paper, not the 2020 Financial Analysts Journal article.

MATERIAL OMISSION - the comovement trail must not end at CSW 2016. Add: DeCoste, J. (2025), 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership,' Global Finance Journal, Vol. 65, DOI 10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110, which uses a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, finds 'membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term,' and argues 'the previous lack of evidence for excess comovement shown in Chen, Singal, Whitelaw (2016) is due to heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members.' Presenting the CSW null as the settled last word is no longer accurate as of 2025.

Optionally add Liao, Y., Coakley, J. and Kellard, N. (2022), 'Index tracking and beta arbitrage effects in comovement,' International Review of Financial Analysis, Vol. 83, which decomposes the post-addition beta change into indexer demand and beta-arbitrageur trading and finds the overall effect is driven by pre-event LOW-beta additions while arbitrageur shorting diminishes or reverses it for high-beta additions.
newContradictions: DeCoste, J. (2025), 'Comovement and S&P 500 membership,' Global Finance Journal 65, DOI 10.1016/j.gfj.2025.101110 - peer-reviewed and published, explicitly rebuts CSW (2016). Verbatim from the publisher abstract: 'Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity approach I show that membership in the S&P 500 leads to significant positive excess comovement in the long term'; 'I show that the previous lack of evidence for excess comovement shown in Chen, Singal, Whitelaw (2016) is due to heterogeneous effects on firms who are newly included versus those that are established members.' The article's framing that the comovement effect is settled-zero post-2001 is contested in the published literature.

Liao, Coakley and Kellard (2022), International Review of Financial Analysis 83, 102330: the aggregate post-addition beta change masks two offsetting components - index-tracker demand and beta-arbitrageur trading. Pre-event low-beta additions drive the overall beta increase; arbitrageur shorting of high-beta additions 'diminishes or sometimes reverses' it. An average-effect-of-zero is therefore consistent with a real but heterogeneous indexing effect, which weakens the article's inference from the CSW null.

Internal tension the article should resolve: item (f) (Anadu et al. citing CSW that comovement effects have declined since 2001) and item (e) (ECB finding a positive, significant passive-ownership-to-correlation link over Q1 2010 - Q1 2024) are not measuring the same object. CSW/Anadu measure the INCREMENTAL event effect of index ADDITION; the ECB measures the level of a stock's correlation as a function of its PASSIVE OWNERSHIP SHARE. A declining addition effect is fully compatible with a rising ownership-share effect, and the article should say so rather than stacking them as if they point the same way. The same distinction applies to item (d): the BIS chart is an addition-event measure, not an ownership-share measure.
reasoning: I reached all six primary documents and read the relevant sentences and table cells directly. (a) Local bsw.txt is the published JFE 75 (2005) 283-317; I read Table 1 Panel A (daily) cell by cell and the introduction sentence, confirming 0.067 / 0.214 univariate and 0.326 / -0.319 bivariate (full 1976-2000 sample). (b) Local csw.txt is the published JFE 121 (2016) 624-644; I read Table 1 Panel A in full and confirmed 0.020/t=0.763, 0.199/t=4.938, -0.004/t=-0.137, and cross-checked against the NBER WP 21281 extraction (chensingal.txt) - the numbers are identical across versions, so the prompt's version-drift risk does not bite here. Reading the full Panel A rather than only the cited column is what surfaced the biggest caliber problem: the raw S&P beta change for 2001-2012 is +0.071 with t=2.44, significantly positive; only the diff-of-diff is zero. (c) Local nyfed484.txt is the NY Fed staff report cover and text; I read footnote 25 verbatim for the >93% correlation and the refusal to run the bivariate, and the abstract for the no-permanent-effect conclusion. The conditioning set is broader than 'momentum'. (d) Because no local PDF contained the BIS graph, I re-fetched the primary PDF (BIS Quarterly Review March 2018 special feature, Sushko and Turner) to the scratchpad and, since plain-text extraction printed 0.52 before 0.45 and could have inverted the bars, I ran pdftotext -bbox and matched x-coordinates: 0.45 aligns under 'Before joining', 0.52 under 'After joining'. Footnote confirms 462 stocks, January 2000 to September 2017, daily returns. (e) Local ecb_box2.txt contains the full box text; I read the 0.005 sentence, footnote 4 (base correlation 0.50) and the Chart B panel a methodology note verbatim - which is where the IV turns out to be a robustness check and where the AR(1) lag control appears, both of which the claim glosses. (f) Two independent local extractions of FEDS 2018-060r1 both give the Table 4 cell verbatim, and I read the body paragraph that sources it to CSW. Active search for post-2016 correction found DeCoste (2025, Global Finance Journal), a published fuzzy-RD paper that directly overturns the CSW null and names CSW as the target; I verified its abstract from the RePEc/IDEAS record (local decoste.html) rather than trusting a search summary, per the fabrication warning. Remaining uncertainty: I could not read the full DeCoste text (ScienceDirect returned 403), so I can characterise only its abstract, not its sample or magnitudes; and I did not verify whether the Financial Analysts Journal published version of Anadu et al. retains the same Table 4 wording, which is why I recommend citing the FEDS working paper. Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: every number checks out verbatim, but the CSW 2001-2012 result is mischaracterised in a way that overstates the null, the BIS-versus-CSW framing attributes to CSW a critique of a design CSW never run, the Kasch-Sarkar conditioning set is narrowed to momentum, the ECB estimate is described as IV-identified when the IV is a robustness check, and the trail omits the published 2025 rebuttal.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) May 6 2010 flash crash — SEC/CFTC report: >20,000 broken trades; over two-thirds of broken-trade SECURITIES were ETFs; mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing; falsification test = ETFs not based on domestic equities NOT disproportionately affected; ~2/3 of cancelled-trade shares below $1 (stub quotes)
itemVerdicts.note: All five sub-claims verified verbatim in the 30 Sept 2010 CFTC/SEC 'Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010'. p.5 and p.8: 'over 20,000 trades ... across more than 300 separate securities, including many ETFs, were executed at prices 60% or more away from their 2:40 p.m. prices' and the exchanges/FINRA 'jointly agreed to cancel (or break) all such trades.' Sec. II.2.b: 'over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca' (note the report's fuller qualifier 'listed on NYSE Arca', which the claim drops — this makes the claim weaker, not wrong). Sec. II.2.c mechanism verbatim: 'A large majority of ETF market makers with whom we spoke, and particularly those that value underlying stocks as part of their normal market making activities, paused their market making for considerable periods of time starting at about 2:45 p.m. on May 6. We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected...' Falsification test verbatim, next sentence: 'We further note that ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected.' Sec. II.2.c (stub quotes): 'Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00, and about 5% were executed at prices above $100,' preceded by 'Executions against stub quotes represented a significant proportion of broken trades on May 6.' Caliber note: the report says 'one of the reasons', not the reason. No passive/index-ownership attribution anywhere.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Aug 24 2015 — SEC research note: 1,278 LULD halts, 1,058 in 327 ETPs; 80% of ETPs zero halts; 63.3% declined <10%; SPX stale from primary-listing last-sale prices (-5.2% vs SPY -7.8%) so market-wide circuit breaker never fired; best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover
itemVerdicts.note: Counts verified verbatim in SEC Staff (Office of Analytics and Research, Division of Trading and Markets), 'Research Note: Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015', Dec 2015: 'Although most of the 1,278 LULD trading halts on August 24 occurred in ETPs, 80% of ETPs did not experience a single LULD halt. Overall, there were 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs ... and 220 LULD halts in 144 non-ETPs.' And: 'A majority of all ETPs (63.3%) declined by less than 10%'; Sec. VI gives the count as '859, 63.3% of total ETPs' and '1,226, 80% of total ETPs'. Stale-index sub-claim verified verbatim: 'The S&P 500 Index ("SPX") ... declined on August 24 by only 5.2% from its previous day's close. Until approximately 9:42, SPX remained substantially higher than the prices of the SPY (7.8% decline), E-Mini (7% decline), and the net asset value ("NAV") of SPY (8% decline)'; 'S&P DJI generally uses last sale prices from only the primary listing market to calculate its equity indexes'; 'Because the SPX did not decline by 7% (the first level trigger) on August 24, the market-wide circuit breakers ... were not triggered.' CORRECTION on the turnover sub-claim: WRONG as phrased — 'best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover' (unqualified, causal-sounding, whole-ETP-universe). RIGHT — the SEC says turnover is 'A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility'; the finding is scoped to the 114 Large- and Mid-cap US Equity ETPs (Tables VI-6/VI-7), it is an association not a prediction, and the note states its analyses 'are not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility.' The report's own logic for privileging it is that volume increases, depth-of-book and imbalances are 'after-the-fact metrics based on August 24 trading' while ADV Turnover Rate 'is based solely on control period trading volume.' Minor internal inconsistency in the SEC note itself worth knowing: Sec. VI says '315 ETPs that did experience an LULD halt' vs the executive summary's 327; and 859/1,541 total ETPs is 55.7%, not 63.3% (the 63.3% denominator is ~1,357). Quote the SEC's own figures as written and do not re-derive.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Feb 5 2018 XIV — BIS attributes spike to leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs (~$4bn AUM end-2017); XIV fell 84% and terminated; verbatim 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market.'
itemVerdicts.note: Source correctly identified: BIS Quarterly Review March 2018 box by Vladyslav Sushko and Grant Turner, 'The equity market turbulence of 5 February – the role of exchange-traded volatility products', bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1803t.htm (URL slug confirmed in the page source; note the page carries 'Updated 21 March 2018: Graph A1 has been corrected'). Verified verbatim: 'The value of one of the inverse volatility ETPs, XIV, fell 84% and the product was subsequently terminated.' And the key sentence verbatim: 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market' — CORRECTION: this sentence is in the FOOTNOTE to Graph A1, not the box's main text, and it cites forthcoming Sushko-Turner in the Banque de France Financial Stability Review; do not present it as a headline finding of the box. Second CORRECTION on caliber: WRONG — 'BIS attributes the spike to leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs' (sole cause). RIGHT — BIS says their 'systematic trading strategies ... appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February', and separately notes anticipatory bidding by other participants from ~15:30 and a dealer hedging channel into E-mini futures. Third CORRECTION: the $4bn is not all leveraged/inverse vol ETPs — verbatim 'The assets of select leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs have expanded sharply over recent years, reaching about $4 billion at end-2017' (four products shown in Graph A1). Say 'select' or 'the products shown'.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) March 2020 bond ETFs — tracking error >200bp vs 0.7bp sector average; BIS Mar 2021 reads discounts partly as run-deterrent/price-discovery; Fed May 2020 FSR passive shift 'might help reduce large redemptions... damp fire sale risks', reserving concern for leveraged/inverse ETPs; the FIMSAC 'price discovery' deck is BlackRock (EII), not SEC
itemVerdicts.note: Tracking error verified verbatim in BIS Quarterly Review March 2021, Karamfil Todorov, 'The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage' (r_qt2103d, published 1 Mar 2021): 'the tracking error of bond ETFs increased to above 200 basis points for some funds in March–April 2020, much higher than the historical average of 0.7 bp in the sector.' Run-deterrent reading verified verbatim: 'This would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes. In fact, such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode ... when some ETFs traded at a discount while redeeming baskets that were more illiquid than the holdings.' CORRECTION 1: the price-discovery half is footnote 4 only, is hedged, and is attributed to third parties — verbatim: 'In March–April 2020, ETF prices may have incorporated information in a timelier manner than NAV (SEC (2020), BlackRock (2020), Avalos and Aramonte (2020)).' The same BIS piece also says the March–April 2020 discounts/premia 'indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs' — do not present BIS as one-sidedly benign. CORRECTION 2 (material): the Fed quote's ellipsis deletes a scope limiter. WRONG: 'might help reduce large redemptions... and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' RIGHT (Fed Financial Stability Report, May 2020, box 'Institutional Activities and Market Liquidity'): 'As investors in passive mutual funds tend to be less responsive to performance than those in active funds, this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions ARISING FROM POOR PERFORMANCE and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' The leveraged/inverse reservation is confirmed as the immediately following paragraph ('some types of exchange-traded products (ETPs)—leveraged and inverse ETPs—have features that could cause strains in market liquidity'). Deck authorship CONFIRMED: 'Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020', cover 'EII Global Research / As of July, 2020'; every chart sourced 'BlackRock'/iShares; PDF metadata title 'Evaluating the Performance of Flagship iShares Fixed Income ETFs', author 'Rui, Fang'; hosted at sec.gov/spotlight/fixed-income-advisory-committee/100520-sec-conference-bond-etf-behavior-during-covid-volatility.pdf, i.e. the 5 Oct 2020 FIMSAC meeting. CORRECTION 3 (caution against over-reach): do not extend this to 'the price-discovery claim is BlackRock's, not the SEC's' generally — SEC DERA independently makes the point in 'U.S. Credit Markets: Interconnectedness and the Effects of the COVID-19 Economic Shock' (Oct 2020), which BIS cites as SEC (2020). The authorship point is specific to that FIMSAC deck.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) April 2025 tariff drawdown — BIS Sept 2025 box says RETAIL, not passive
itemVerdicts.note: Verified verbatim in BIS Quarterly Review, box 'Understanding the swift market recovery after the April 2025 tariff shock' (r_qt2509w, 15 Sept 2025), extracted from the Overview chapter 'Markets shrug off trade conflicts': 'The box also illustrates that, in contrast with past episodes, retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally.' Supporting body text: 'Even as institutional investors withdrew from equity markets, retail investors were on net "buyers of the dip", as visible from fund flows ... These dynamics were somewhat unusual compared with past stress episodes (eg the GFC), when retail investors were net sellers and institutional investors were net buyers.' The word 'passive' does not appear in the box. The box's primary attribution for the rebound is tariff backtracking through mid-May and non-tariff news thereafter, with retail flows as an amplifier ('They may have also been amplified by retail investors') — so the retail point is secondary, not the box's headline finding; state it that way.

itemVerdicts.item: Umbrella claim: no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to index/passive structure
itemVerdicts.note: Holds against the six cited primary documents, all of which I read directly. Each post-mortem's stated mechanism is ETF/ETP plumbing (market-maker pausing, stub quotes, LULD/opening-auction interaction, AP arbitrage impediments, leveraged/inverse rebalancing) or, for April 2025, retail flows — never index-fund ownership or passive flow. Two documents actively cut the other way: the flash-crash report's non-domestic-equity falsification test, and the Fed May 2020 FSR's passive-damps-fire-sales sentence. Adversarial search for a counterexample up to Aug 2026 turned up none: the FCA-commissioned survey (Allard, Farkas, Pedio, Rubio, Tonks, 8 July 2025, 'A Survey of the Consequences of Passive Investment Funds for Financial Markets') contains no mention of the flash crash, 24 Aug 2015, Feb 2018 or March 2020 as episodes; IMF GFSR Oct 2025 and ECB FSR Nov 2025 treatments of April 2025 do not attribute it to passive either. One caveat the article should own rather than hide: for (a) and (b) the official mechanism IS a structural feature of ETFs, which are predominantly index vehicles — the honest formulation is that regulators blamed the ETF trading/arbitrage layer, not index ownership or passive fund flows, and the flash-crash report's own falsification test is what separates the two. NOTE ALSO: the claim header says 'four canonical' episodes but then lists five, (a) through (e).

corrections: Restore the deleted scope limiter in the Fed May 2020 FSR quote. The Fed sentence is: 'this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions ARISING FROM POOR PERFORMANCE and, therefore, damp fire sale risks.' The article's ellipsis ('might help reduce large redemptions... and, therefore, damp fire sale risks') removes 'arising from poor performance', which is the whole basis of the Fed's claim (its premise is that passive investors are less performance-sensitive). Quote it in full.

Downgrade 'best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover' (Aug 24 2015). The SEC note says turnover is 'a pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility', scoped to the 114 Large- and Mid-cap US Equity ETPs, and the note explicitly states its analyses 'are not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility.' Write 'the only pre-event metric strongly associated with which ETPs blew up — among large and mid-cap US equity ETPs — was low secondary-market turnover.'

Downgrade 'BIS attributes the spike to leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs' (Feb 2018). BIS says their 'systematic trading strategies ... appear to have been A KEY FACTOR behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February', alongside anticipatory bidding by other participants from ~15:30 and dealer hedging into E-mini futures. Say 'a key factor', not the cause.

Flag the '$4bn' as scoped. BIS: 'The assets of SELECT leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs ... reaching about $4 billion at end-2017' — four named products in Graph A1, not the whole leveraged/inverse volatility ETP category. Add 'select' or 'the products shown'.

Note that 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market' is the FOOTNOTE to Graph A1 in the March 2018 BIS box, not a main-text conclusion. It is still BIS's own words and still usable, but do not present it as the box's headline finding.

Do not present BIS March 2021 as reading the March 2020 bond-ETF discounts benignly on balance. The same piece says the premium/discount swings and the >200bp tracking errors 'indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs.' The run-deterrent reading is hedged ('such a stabilisation mechanism was ARGUABLY in place'), and the price-discovery reading is footnote 4 only, hedged and attributed to others: 'ETF prices MAY have incorporated information in a timelier manner than NAV (SEC (2020), BlackRock (2020), Avalos and Aramonte (2020)).' Attribute the piece to Karamfil Todorov, BIS Quarterly Review, 1 March 2021.

Tighten the FIMSAC-deck point so it does not over-reach. Correct as stated for that deck: 'Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020', cover 'EII Global Research, As of July 2020', PDF metadata author 'Rui, Fang', every chart sourced to BlackRock/iShares, presented at the 5 Oct 2020 FIMSAC meeting and hosted on sec.gov. But do NOT generalise to 'the price-discovery claim is BlackRock's, not the SEC's' — SEC DERA makes the same point in 'U.S. Credit Markets: Interconnectedness and the Effects of the COVID-19 Economic Shock' (Oct 2020).
Fix the count: the passage says 'four canonical' episodes and then lists five, (a) May 2010, (b) Aug 2015, (c) Feb 2018, (d) March 2020, (e) April 2025.

Keep the flash-crash 'two-thirds' figures straight — they are two different denominators in the same report: 'over two-thirds of the SECURITIES with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca' (Sec. II.2.b) and 'Almost two-thirds of SHARES in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00' (Sec. II.2.c). Do not merge them into one statistic.

Soften 'mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing' to match the report, which says the pausing 'is ONE OF THE REASONS equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected', alongside the thin-away-from-inside order books documented in Charts 3.A/3.B.
newContradictions: Internal to the SEC Aug 24 2015 note: the executive summary and Section V say 327 ETPs experienced LULD halts, while Section VI says '315 ETPs that did experience an LULD halt' (315 + 1,226 = 1,541 total ETPs). If the article uses 327 and 80%/1,226 in the same sentence — as the SEC's own executive summary does — that is fine, but do not arithmetically combine them.

Internal to the SEC Aug 24 2015 note: 859 ETPs is stated as '63.3% of total ETPs', implying a denominator of ~1,357, whereas the 80%/1,226 figure implies 1,541. Use the SEC's percentages as printed; do not re-derive a percentage from the counts.

The BIS March 2021 piece is genuinely two-sided on March 2020 bond ETFs — it calls the discounts evidence of arbitrage impediments AND a possible run-deterring stabilisation mechanism. An article citing only the second half is cherry-picking a source that also supplies the fragility side of the ledger.

Tension worth pre-empting rather than hiding: for May 2010 and Aug 2015 the official mechanism IS a structural feature of ETFs, which are overwhelmingly index vehicles. The defensible line is 'regulators blamed the ETF trading/arbitrage layer, not index ownership or passive fund flows' — and the flash-crash report's non-domestic-equity falsification test is the evidence that separates the two. Stating flatly that no post-mortem implicates 'index/passive structure' without that distinction invites an easy rebuttal.
reasoning: I read the primary documents directly rather than relying on summaries. Reached verbatim: (1) CFTC/SEC 'Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010' (30 Sept 2010) — full extracted text, read pp.5, 8, Sec. II.2.b and II.2.c in context; all four flash-crash sub-claims confirmed word for word, including the falsification sentence 'We further note that ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected.' (2) SEC Staff 'Research Note: Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015' (Dec 2015) — executive summary bullets, Sec. V and Sec. VI including Tables VI-6 and VI-7; all counts confirmed, but the turnover finding is an 'association' scoped to 114 Large/Mid US Equity ETPs and the note disclaims causal findings, so 'best predictor' is caliber slippage. (3) BIS QR March 2018 Sushko-Turner box (r_qt1803t, URL slug confirmed from page source) — XIV -84%, ~$4bn 'select' products, and the 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies...' sentence, which sits in the Graph A1 footnote; BIS says the ETPs' strategies were 'a key factor', not the sole cause. (4) BIS QR March 2021, Todorov, 'The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage' (r_qt2103d) — the >200bp vs 0.7bp sentence, the run-deterrent passage, and footnote 4's hedged price-discovery line attributed to SEC (2020)/BlackRock (2020)/Avalos-Aramonte; the same piece calls the March-April 2020 pricing gaps evidence of arbitrage impediments. (5) Fed Financial Stability Report May 2020 — the passive/fire-sale sentence in full, which contains the qualifier 'arising from poor performance' that the article's ellipsis deletes; the leveraged/inverse reservation is the next paragraph. (6) BIS QR Sept 2025 box (r_qt2509w) — 'retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally' confirmed verbatim; 'passive' does not appear. (7) The FIMSAC deck: cover reads 'EII Global Research / As of July, 2020', PDF metadata title 'Evaluating the Performance of Flagship iShares Fixed Income ETFs' with author 'Rui, Fang', every exhibit sourced to BlackRock/iShares; web search confirmed it is hosted at sec.gov/spotlight/fixed-income-advisory-committee/100520-sec-conference-bond-etf-behavior-during-covid-volatility.pdf for the 5 Oct 2020 FIMSAC meeting. Adversarial search for counterexamples through Aug 2026 (official reports attributing any of these episodes to passive/index structure) found none; I also checked the FCA-commissioned Allard et al. survey (8 July 2025), which does not discuss these episodes at all. Remaining uncertainty: I did not extract the IOSCO COVID-19 ETF report (the local file is a saved HTML page, not a PDF) or the FSB Holistic Review, so I cannot rule out a passive attribution buried in those; from what is publicly summarised they blame open-ended fund liquidity mismatch and dealer intermediation capacity, not indexing, but I mark that as unchecked rather than confirmed. The central assertion survives; the verdict is CORRECTED only because of the Fed quote's ellipsis and four smaller caliber slips.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Published JF abstract: additions fell from 7.4% avg in the 1990s to less than 1% over 2010-2020; deletions from large negative to +0.1% avg 2010-2020
itemVerdicts.note: Crossref record for 10.1111/jofi.13410 (J. Finance 80(2), April 2025, 657-698) verbatim: 'The abnormal return associated with a stock being added to the S&P 500 has fallen from an average of 7.4% in the 1990s to less than 1% over the past decade... A similar pattern has occurred for index deletions, with large negative abnormal returns during the 1990s but an average return of only 0.1% between 2010 and 2020.' Identical wording in the Harvard DASH accepted manuscript dated March 2024 (local file v19b_gs_pub.txt lines 44-46). Two calibration notes: (i) the abstract says 'over the past decade', not literally '2010-2020', for the additions figure — only the deletions clause carries the 2010-2020 label (the sample does end in 2020, so the substance is fine); (ii) the '0.1%' deletions figure contradicts the paper's OWN Table 1, which reports the 2010s total deletion CAR as -0.62% (statistically insignificant); +0.13% is the effective-date-window return, not the total. So an article may quote the abstract's 0.1% only as the abstract's number, never as 'the paper finds deletions earned +0.1%.'

itemVerdicts.item: (b) WP Table 2: additions 1980s 3.42%, 1990s 7.25%, 2000s 5.14%, 2010-20 0.804% (ns); deletions 1990s -16.1%, 2010-20 -0.62% (ns); deletion decade cells rest on 39-87 events
itemVerdicts.note: All six numbers are verbatim correct for the SUPERSEDED working paper. In the June-2023 draft served at marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf (local v19_gs_live.txt lines 1937-1950), Table 2 Panel A 'Total' row reads 0.0411***/0.0342***/0.0725***/0.0514***/0.00804 and Panel B reads -0.0820***/-0.0464**/-0.161***/-0.124***/-0.0062, with deletion N = 267/39/56/85/87. But the PUBLISHED version's numbers differ. WRONG (as attributions to the published paper): 'Table 2', 7.25%, 5.14%, 0.804%. RIGHT (published/DASH accepted manuscript, Table 1 'S&P 500 Addition and deletion cumulative abnormal returns by year', v19b_gs_pub.txt lines 2056-2059): additions 1980s N=196 3.42%***, 1990s N=134 7.39%***, 2000s N=211 5.16%***, 2010s N=153 0.83% (no stars); deletions 1980s N=39 -4.64%**, 1990s N=56 -16.11%***, 2000s N=85 -12.39%***, 2010s N=87 -0.62% (no stars). Note the decade table is Table 1 in the published paper, Table 2 only in the 2022/2023 drafts. Addition N also changed (WP 196/137/212/155 -> published 196/134/211/153); deletion N is unchanged, so '39-87 events' for the deletion decade cells is CONFIRMED in both. Also note a third intermediate draft exists (HBS WP 23-025, revised November 2023, local v19c_hbs.txt), whose abstract reads '7.4% in the 1990s to 0.3% over the past decade... deletions... only 0.1%' while its own body text says 1.0% and -0.6% — this literature's version drift is worse than a two-way split.

itemVerdicts.item: (c1) S&P-500-tracking funds grew from ~0 to ~7% of market cap
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim in the published/accepted text (v19b_gs_pub.txt line 88) and in every draft: 'We estimate that funds tracking the S&P 500 in the form of mutual funds or ETFs have grown from essentially zero in the 1980s to approximately 7 percent of market capitalization in recent years.' The authors add that other estimates based on trading volume (Chinco and Sammon) or sell-side research 'suggest even higher levels'. This is a mutual-fund/ETF AUM measure, not total indexed ownership.

itemVerdicts.item: (c2) Trackers buy 7-8% of shares outstanding on addition yet total institutional ownership barely moves
itemVerdicts.note: Direction confirmed, numbers need fixing and the sign flipped between drafts. RIGHT (published, v19b_gs_pub.txt lines 1409-1418, Table 7): 'for the average addition in 2020, index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding. However, institutional ownership only increases by 0.65% of shares outstanding... in 2020, index trackers sell an average of 8.45% of shares outstanding upon deletion, but institutional ownership overall falls by only 1.42%.' WRONG if taken from the June-2023 draft, which said institutional ownership FALLS by 0.75% on additions and trackers sell 8.48% with ownership falling 1.07% on deletions (v19_gs_live.txt lines 1337-1343). Use +0.65% / -1.42% and 7.53% / 8.45%.

itemVerdicts.item: (c3) Active investors provide the liquidity
itemVerdicts.note: The paper says the opposite about active funds. Verbatim (v19b_gs_pub.txt lines 1421-1426): 'The "Active" column shows that active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero. This implies that non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge funds, pension fund, endowments) are the primary liquidity providers around addition events.' The framing sentence is 'liquidity is provided, on average, by other institutions exiting their positions, rather than accommodation by other parties such as retail investors.' So: other 13F institutions outside the mutual-fund universe — hedge funds, pensions, endowments — NOT active mutual funds, and NOT retail.

itemVerdicts.item: (c4) Migrations (simultaneous S&P400 exit) rose from ~40% to >80% of additions
itemVerdicts.note: No version of the paper supports either endpoint for ADDITIONS, and the migration share of additions is essentially flat. WRONG: '~40% to >80% of additions.' RIGHT (published, v19b_gs_pub.txt lines 907-909): 'Figure 4 shows that migrations have become a steady share of additions and especially deletions. In the 1990s, migrations accounted for about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions. In recent years, they both make up over 70% of index changes.' Published Table 6 (v19b_gs_pub.txt lines 2192-2196) gives migration share of ADDITIONS as 69.07% (1995-99), 59.24% (2000s), 63.40% (2010-2020) — flat to slightly down — while the share of DELETIONS runs 5.88% -> 20.00% -> 87.36%. The dramatic climb to ~87% is a deletions fact, not an additions fact. The paper's own introduction (all versions) uses a looser 'from about 50% of additions to over 70%'.

itemVerdicts.item: (c5) Direct additions still earned +5.3% in the 2010s, Tesla-driven; ex-Tesla the 2020 average inclusion effect was -3bp
itemVerdicts.note: Tesla attribution and the -3bp figure are exactly right; the 5.3% is a stale draft number. WRONG: 5.3%. RIGHT (published, v19b_gs_pub.txt line 959): 'for direct additions, the index inclusion effect was 10.2% in the late 90s, 8.8% in the 2000s, and 5.4% in the 2010s. The large positive return in the last period is driven by Tesla, which... had a massive return of 53.35% between its announcement and effective dates.' (The June-2023 draft said 10.5%/8.6%/5.3%.) Migration additions over the same decades: 6.7%, 2.7%, -1.8%. And verbatim at line 602: 'Excluding Tesla, the average inclusion effect in 2020 was -3 basis points.' CONFIRMED.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Authors frame the decay as arbitrage/anomaly decay (McLean-Pontiff), not as evidence passive is harmless; Bennett-Stulz-Wang documented the decline first (1997-2017 additions)
itemVerdicts.note: Both attributions check out; one qualifier needs adding and one priority claim needs narrowing. McLean-Pontiff framing verbatim (v19b_gs_pub.txt ~line 282): '...the decline of the index effect is much like the evidence for other anomalies: they decline once they are well recognized by the market (McLean and Pontiff, 2016).' The conclusion adds Lo (2004): 'when demand shocks become regular and repeated, competitive markets adapt over time to minimize price impact, in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis.' BSW verbatim (line 312-313): 'Most closely related to our paper is Bennett et al. (2020), who first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017.' Two corrections: (i) the published paper cites it as Bennett et al. (2020) — a working paper, 'Does Joining the S&P 500 Index Hurt Firms?' — while the 2022/2023 drafts cited (2022); (ii) BSW's priority is for ADDITIONS only — the very next sentence credits 'Preston and Soe (2021)' with documenting the decline 'among additions and deletions beginning in 1995.' Also: the paper nowhere argues about whether passive investing is harmless in general — it is silent on the index-bubble question. So 'NOT as evidence passive is harmless' is the article's own inference, defensible as a caution but not attributable to the authors as a stated position.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) NEW-WINDOW CHECK: Coinbase jumped ~24% on its May 12, 2025 S&P 500 inclusion announcement
itemVerdicts.note: The move is real and slightly understated, but the date needs one word of care. Yahoo daily bars (local v19c_coin_y2.json, fetched fresh): COIN closed 207.22 on Mon 2025-05-12 and 256.90 on Tue 2025-05-13 = +23.97% on volume of 39.1M vs 14.9M the prior day; S&P 500 rose 0.72% that day (v19c_spx.json), so the market-adjusted move is about +23.2%. WRONG if stated as an announcement-DAY move: S&P DJI announced after the close on Monday May 12 (COIN was +3.96% in regular May 12 trading, reportedly ~+8% after hours), so the ~24% is the NEXT-day reaction, May 13. RIGHT: 'announced after the close on May 12, 2025 (effective before the open May 19); COIN closed up 24% the following session.' On the paper's own total-window definition (day before announcement to day after effective) the effect is even larger: 207.22 -> 263.99 on May 19 = +27.4% raw, about +25.3% market-adjusted. Two qualifications the article must carry: the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020, so the published 'disappeared' finding says nothing about 2025; and Coinbase was a DIRECT addition, not a MidCap migration, and the paper's own published estimate for direct additions in the 2010s is already +5.4%, so a single large direct-addition pop is a data point against 'disappeared', not a refutation of the paper's mechanism. (Note also the paper's caution that individual-event returns can carry confounding news — COIN had the Deribit deal on May 8 and a data-breach disclosure on May 15, though neither falls on May 13.) No erratum or correction to 10.1111/jofi.13410 was found as of 2026-08.

corrections: Do not cite '7.25%' (1990s), '5.14%' (2000s), or '0.804%' (2010-2020) as the published paper's addition returns — those are from the superseded Dec-2022/June-2023 working paper. The published Journal of Finance version (Table 1, not Table 2) reports additions 3.42% (1980s, N=196), 7.39% (1990s, N=134), 5.16% (2000s, N=211), 0.83% (2010s, N=153, insignificant); deletions -4.64% (N=39), -16.11% (N=56), -12.39% (N=85), -0.62% (N=87, insignificant).

Relabel the decade table: it is Table 2 only in the 2022/2023 working papers; in the published paper it is Table 1 ('S&P 500 Addition and deletion cumulative abnormal returns by year'). Table 2 in the published paper is the characteristics-controlled regression.

Flag that the published abstract's '+0.1%' for 2010-2020 deletions is not reproduced in the published paper's own table, which reports a total deletion CAR of -0.62% (insignificant) for the 2010s; +0.13% is the narrow effective-date window. Quote it as the abstract's figure, never as 'the paper finds deletions earned +0.1%.'

Delete the claim that migrations 'rose from ~40% to >80% of additions.' The published text says migrations were 'about 69% of additions and less than 10% of deletions' in the 1990s and 'over 70% of index changes' recently, and calls the additions share 'a steady share.' Published Table 6 migration shares of additions: 69.07% (1995-99), 59.24% (2000s), 63.40% (2010-2020). The rise to ~87% is the DELETIONS share (5.88% -> 20.00% -> 87.36%).

Remove '(active investors provide the liquidity).' The paper states that 'active mutual funds are not the group providing liquidity, as their average net demand is roughly zero,' and concludes that 'non-S12 filing institutions (e.g., hedge funds, pension fund, endowments) are the primary liquidity providers around addition events' — with retail explicitly ruled out as well.

Update the tracker/institutional-ownership numbers to the published version: for the average 2020 addition index trackers buy 7.53% of shares outstanding while total institutional ownership only INCREASES by 0.65% (the working-paper draft said it FELL by 0.75% — sign flipped); for 2020 deletions trackers sell 8.45% while institutional ownership falls only 1.42% (draft: 8.48% and 1.07%).

Change direct additions in the 2010s from +5.3% to +5.4% (published figure; the decade series is 10.2% late-1990s, 8.8% 2000s, 5.4% 2010s), and note the published paper quantifies Tesla's announcement-to-effective return as 53.35%. The '-3 basis points' ex-Tesla 2020 average inclusion effect is verbatim correct and can stand.

Narrow the Bennett-Stulz-Wang priority claim: the published paper cites 'Bennett et al. (2020)' as having 'first noted the decline in the index inclusion effect among additions between 1997 and 2017' — additions only — and separately credits Preston and Soe (2021) with documenting the decline in both additions and deletions from 1995.

Do not attribute to Greenwood and Sammon any position on whether passive investing is harmless; the paper is silent on the index-bubble question. It frames the decay as anomaly decay once well recognized (McLean and Pontiff, 2016) and as competitive markets adapting to regular, repeated demand shocks 'in the spirit of Lo's (2004) adaptive markets hypothesis.'

Fix the Coinbase timing: S&P DJI announced after the close on Monday May 12, 2025 (effective before the open May 19). COIN closed at $207.22 on May 12 and $256.90 on May 13 — +23.97% raw, roughly +23.2% market-adjusted (S&P 500 +0.72% that day). Write it as the session after the announcement, not as an announcement-day move. If the article wants the paper's own total window, the May 12 close to May 19 close move was +27.4% raw / about +25.3% market-adjusted.

When citing Coinbase as a counterexample, state that the peer-reviewed sample ends in 2020 and that Coinbase was a direct addition rather than an S&P MidCap migration — the paper's own published estimate for direct additions in the 2010s is already +5.4%, so the case qualifies rather than overturns the 'disappeared' conclusion.

If the article links to https://marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf as the source for any number, note that the file served there (verified 2026-08-14, 2,165,718 bytes) is the June 2023 revision, not the published article; the published text is available as the March 2024 accepted manuscript in Harvard DASH.
reasoning:
I reached four distinct primary texts and read the relevant sentences and table cells directly rather than relying on summaries. (1) Crossref record for 10.1111/jofi.13410 (local v19_cr.json / v19b_crossref.json), confirming J. Finance 80(2), April 2025, 657-698 and the published abstract verbatim. (2) The Harvard DASH accepted manuscript dated March 2024 (v19b_gs_pub.txt), whose abstract matches the published abstract word for word and which therefore serves as the published text for table and body checks. (3) The June 2023 revision actually served at marcosammon.com/images/greenwood_sammon.pdf (re-downloaded and byte-matched to v19_gs_live.pdf, 2,165,718 bytes, content-length verified against the live URL). (4) The Dec 2022 NBER w30748 text (v19_gs_nber.txt), plus a fourth intermediate version I located and downloaded during this check — HBS Working Paper 23-025, revised November 2023 (v19c_hbs.pdf/txt) — which turns out to matter because its abstract already carries the 7.4% / 0.3% / 0.1% numbers while its body still says 1.0% and -0.6%.

Key findings against the claim group: the six Table-2 numbers in (b) are verbatim right for the working paper but four of them changed in the published paper, where the decade table is renumbered Table 1 and reads 3.42/7.39/5.16/0.83 for additions with N = 196/134/211/153. Deletion cells and their 39/56/85/87 event counts are unchanged, so the small-sample caveat holds. The migration claim in (c) is refuted outright: the migration share of ADDITIONS is flat at roughly 60-69% across all three eras in the published Table 6, and the 87% figure belongs to deletions. The 'active investors provide the liquidity' parenthetical is refuted by an explicit sentence in the paper saying active mutual funds are not the liquidity providers and that non-S12 institutions are. The 7% of market cap, the Tesla attribution, the -3bp ex-Tesla 2020 figure, the McLean-Pontiff framing, and the Bennett et al. priority sentence all check out verbatim.

For (e) I used market data rather than any news summary: Yahoo daily bars for COIN and ^GSPC fetched during this session (v19c_coin_y2.json, v19c_spx.json). COIN 207.22 -> 256.90 = +23.97% from May 12 to May 13, 2025, with volume 39.1M vs 14.9M; S&P 500 +0.72%. The S&P DJI press release date (May 12, 2025, effective May 19) came from a search listing the primary spglobal.com release URL; I could not extract the release PDF itself (the spglobal endpoint returned an HTML challenge page rather than the PDF), but the announcement date and effective date are corroborated by the price/volume pattern, so I treated the date as established and the move as measured.

Remaining uncertainty: the published Journal of Finance article is closed access (OpenAlex reports oa_status 'closed', no OA location), so my published-version table checks rest on the DASH accepted manuscript. That manuscript's abstract is identical to the Crossref-registered published abstract, which is strong evidence it is the same text, but I could not diff it against the Wiley typeset version. The internal conflict between the published abstract's '0.1%' for 2010-2020 deletions and the same paper's table value of -0.62% is real in the accepted manuscript and I found no erratum for the DOI as of 2026-08; I have flagged it as a caliber trap rather than resolving it.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Flash crash: >20,000 broken trades
itemVerdicts.note: SEC/CFTC Sept 30 2010 Findings, Section II.3.b: "over 20,000 trades representing 5.5 million shares were executed at prices more than 60% away from their 2:40 p.m. value. These trades were subsequently broken by the exchanges and FINRA under their clearly erroneous rules." Trades, not securities — the article gets the unit right.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Over two-thirds of broken-trade SECURITIES were ETFs
itemVerdicts.note: Section II.2 (HFT analysis): "Since over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca, we compared HFT trading activity in all securities with broken trades against those without broken trades." Note the report's phrasing is narrower than the article's: ETFs *listed on NYSE Arca*, which only strengthens the article's version.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG if stated as the mechanism. RIGHT: it is one of several. Section II.2.c: "A large majority of ETF market makers with whom we spoke... paused their market making for considerable periods of time starting at about 2:45 p.m. on May 6. We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected by the extreme price volatilities of that afternoon." The report gives a second, independent explanation as well: ETF order books are a "professional's market" with ~half of liquidity within 30bp of mid and little resting retail depth, "allowing a disproportionate number of ETF orders to hit stub-quote levels."

itemVerdicts.item: (a) Falsification test: non-domestic-equity ETFs not disproportionately affected
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, Section II.2.c: "We further note that ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected."

itemVerdicts.item: (a) ~2/3 of cancelled-trade shares executed below $1
itemVerdicts.note: Section II.3.b: "Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00, and about 5% were executed at prices above $100." Denominator is SHARES in cancelled trades, which is what the article says.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 1,278 LULD halts; 1,058 in 327 ETPs
itemVerdicts.note: SEC Research Note, Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015 (Dec 2015), Section V summary: "Although most of the 1,278 LULD trading halts on August 24 occurred in ETPs, 80% of ETPs did not experience a single LULD halt. Overall, there were 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs (many halts were repeats in the same ETP), and 220 LULD halts in 144 non-ETPs." 1,058+220=1,278 reconciles.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) 80% of ETPs had zero halts; 63.3% declined <10%
itemVerdicts.note: Section VI body: "Most ETPs (1,226, 80% of total ETPs) did not experience even a single LULD halt on August 24" and "Most ETPs (859, 63.3% of total ETPs) experienced price declines of less than 10%." Summary phrasing: "A majority of all ETPs (63.3%) declined by less than 10% -- a level that is consistent with broad market declines on August 24."

itemVerdicts.item: (b) SPX stale (primary-listing last-sale prices), -5.2% vs SPY -7.8%, so MWCB never fired
itemVerdicts.note: "The S&P 500 Index ("SPX")... declined on August 24 by only 5.2%... S&P DJI generally uses last sale prices from only the primary listing market to calculate its equity indexes. Until NYSE-listed constituents of the S&P 500 index were opened on the NYSE, the SPX disseminated by S&P DJI reflected NYSE closing prices from August 21." And: "Because the SPX did not decline by 7% (the first level trigger) on August 24, the market-wide circuit breakers, which would have implemented a 15-minute trading pause in all equities and related products, were not triggered." SPY's -7.8% is its 9:35 daily low (it opened -5.2%, closed -4.2%) — keep that framing precise.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "best predictor." RIGHT: "A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate... Large and Mid market capitalization US Equity ETPs with comparatively low secondary market turnover rates in a control period were much more likely to experience severe volatility and multiple LULD halts." It is (i) an association, not a prediction, (ii) established only within the 114 Large/Mid US Equity ETPs (Tables VI-6 and VI-7), and (iii) the note explicitly disclaims causal findings: the analyses "are not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility on August 24." That disclaimer actually strengthens the article's umbrella point and should be cited.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BIS attributes Feb 5 2018 spike to leveraged/inverse volatility ETPs; ~$4bn end-2017; XIV -84% and terminated
itemVerdicts.note: Numbers confirmed: "The assets of select leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs have expanded sharply over recent years, reaching about $4 billion at end-2017" and "The value of one of the inverse volatility ETPs, XIV, fell 84% and the product was subsequently terminated." WRONG if stated as BIS attributing the episode/selloff: RIGHT is that BIS attributes the late-afternoon VIX spike specifically, and as a key factor not the sole cause — "systematic trading strategies of the issuers of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February," preceded by "Even though the aggregate positions in these instruments are relatively small." The S&P 500's -4.2% day is described separately as a 3.8 standard deviation move; BIS traces spillovers via dealers shorting E-mini futures.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) BIS verbatim: 'Neither the size nor the complex strategies of leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs are representative of the broader ETP market.'
itemVerdicts.note: Exact string found in BIS Quarterly Review March 2018, box by Sushko & Turner (r_qt1803t). Caliber note on attribution: it is not body text — it appears in the note to Graph A1, in a sentence that continues "...; see V Sushko and G Turner, 'What risks do exchange-traded funds pose?', Bank of France, Financial Stability Review, forthcoming." Cite it as the Graph A1 note.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Bond ETF tracking error >200bp vs 0.7bp historical sector average
itemVerdicts.note: BIS Quarterly Review, March 2021, Todorov, "The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage": "the tracking error of bond ETFs increased to above 200 basis points for some funds in March–April 2020, much higher than the historical average of 0.7 bp in the sector." Same sentence continues: "These facts indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs" — cite that too, so the article isn't read as suppressing BIS's own statement that the wrapper malfunctioned.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) BIS (March 2021) reads the discounts partly as a run-deterrent / price-discovery feature
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "price-discovery." The string "price discovery" does not appear anywhere in r_qt2103d. RIGHT: BIS's words are run-deterrence / shock absorption / stabilisation. "If there is excessive selling of ETF shares in the secondary market... the ETF sponsor can include only the riskier or less liquid securities from the pool of holdings in the redemption basket... This would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes. In fact, such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode... when some ETFs traded at a discount while redeeming baskets that were more illiquid than the holdings." Also: "The decoupling of baskets from holdings weakens arbitrage forces but allows ETFs to absorb shocks on the bond market." Note the hedge "arguably." "Price discovery" is BlackRock's framing, not BIS's — conflating them would hand a source-laundering objection to a critic.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Fed May 2020 FSR: passive shift 'might help reduce large redemptions... damp fire sale risks,' concern reserved for leveraged/inverse ETPs
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: the ellipsis drops a material qualifier. RIGHT verbatim (FSR May 2020, box 'Institutional Activities and Market Liquidity,' p.33): "As investors in passive mutual funds tend to be less responsive to performance than those in active funds, this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions arising from poor performance and, therefore, damp fire sale risks." The claim is restricted to performance-driven redemptions, and the mechanism cited is passive investors' lower flow-performance sensitivity. The reservation is confirmed: "At the same time, some types of exchange-traded products (ETPs)—leveraged and inverse ETPs—have features that could cause strains in market liquidity," via end-of-day rebalancing and front-running. Footnote 9 cites Anadu, Kruttli, McCabe, Osambela and Shin, FEDS 2018-060.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) 'Bond ETFs = price discovery' FIMSAC deck is authored by BlackRock (EII), not the SEC
itemVerdicts.note: Deck cover reads "EII Global Research / As of July, 2020 / Pricing and Liquidity of Fixed Income ETFs in the Covid-19 Crisis of 2020"; bullet: "Market participants turned to fixed income ETFs for price discovery"; every chart sourced "Source: BlackRock, Bloomberg"; closing pages carry the iShares prospectus disclaimer and "©2020 BlackRock, Inc." PDF metadata: Title "Evaluating the Performance of Flagship iShares Fixed Income ETFs", Author "Rui, Fang", created 2020-10-02. Hosted at sec.gov/spotlight/fixed-income-advisory-committee/100520-sec-conference-bond-etf-behavior-during-covid-volatility.pdf, i.e. the 5 Oct 2020 FIMSAC meeting (SEC press release 2020-243 confirms that meeting covered the bond fund and ETF market). SEC hosting is not SEC authorship — the article's point stands.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) BIS Sept 2025 box: 'retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally'
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, BIS Quarterly Review 15 September 2025, box by Lombardi, Pinter and Todorov: "The box also illustrates that, in contrast with past episodes, retail investors, rather than institutional ones, bought into the rally." Supporting text: "Even as institutional investors withdrew from equity markets, retail investors were on net 'buyers of the dip', as visible from fund flows." I grepped the full box for passive/index/ETF: ZERO hits. The do-not-conflate warning is correct and well founded.

itemVerdicts.item: Umbrella: no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to index/passive structure
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as flatly stated. RIGHT: no official post-mortem attributes these episodes to the GROWTH OF INDEX/PASSIVE OWNERSHIP or to index-fund flows. Two of them do explicitly attribute disproportionate damage to the ETF wrapper's own machinery — SEC/CFTC 2010: "equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected," traced to market makers who value underlying components pausing; BIS 2021: the tracking-error blowout "indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs." An adversarial reader will call the flat version false. Separately, I grepped both SEC documents for passive/index-fund attribution: the SEC/CFTC 2010 report's only uses of "passive" refer to passive ORDER EXECUTION (liquidity provision), not passive investing; the Aug 24 2015 note contains no instance of "passive", "index fund", or "indexing" at all. I found no later official document (FSB Holistic Review Nov 2020, Fed FSRs, BIS) attributing any of these five episodes to passive/index ownership.

itemVerdicts.item: Counting: 'four canonical episodes' followed by five enumerated items (a)-(e)
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG: "four canonical episodes" with (a) 2010, (b) 2015, (c) 2018, (d) 2020, (e) 2025 listed. RIGHT: either say five, or say "four canonical episodes" for (a)-(d) and introduce April 2025 separately as a fifth, more recent case. As written the sentence miscounts its own list.

corrections: Change "the mechanism = equity-ETF market makers pausing" to "one of the reasons the SEC/CFTC report gives": the report says "We believe this is one of the reasons equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected," and offers a second explanation — ETF order books concentrate ~half of liquidity within 30bp of mid with little resting retail depth far from mid, "allowing a disproportionate number of ETF orders to hit stub-quote levels."

Change "best predictor of ETP damage was low secondary-market turnover" to the report's own caliber: "A pre-August 24 metric with a particularly strong association with volatility is secondary market turnover rate." Add that the finding is established only within the 114 Large/Mid-cap US Equity ETPs, and that the note disclaims causal findings entirely ("not intended to reach or suggest any legal conclusions or factual findings regarding the causes of the volatility on August 24") — a disclaimer that supports the article's thesis and should be quoted.

Narrow the Feb 2018 attribution: BIS says leveraged/inverse volatility ETP issuers' rebalancing "appear to have been a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February" — a key factor in the afternoon VIX spike, not the cause of the day's equity selloff, and prefaced by "Even though the aggregate positions in these instruments are relatively small." Also keep BIS's word "select" in "select leveraged and inverse volatility ETPs... about $4 billion at end-2017."
Attribute the "Neither the size nor the complex strategies..." sentence to the note to Graph A1 in the BIS March 2018 box, not to the box's body text.

Delete "price discovery" from the BIS March 2021 attribution. The phrase does not appear in the article. BIS's framing is run-deterrence and shock absorption: sponsors tilting redemption baskets toward less liquid bonds "would discourage further runs and lead to ETF discounts during run episodes," and "such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode." "Price discovery" is BlackRock's language and should stay attached to the BlackRock deck only.

Restore the dropped qualifier in the Fed May 2020 FSR quote: "this shift to passive investing might help reduce large redemptions arising from poor performance and, therefore, damp fire sale risks." The Fed's claim is limited to performance-driven redemptions and rests on passive investors' lower flow-performance sensitivity.

Add BIS's own adverse sentence when citing the >200bp tracking error, so the article is not read as cherry-picking: "These facts indicated impediments to the functioning of the arbitrage mechanism for bond ETFs."

Reword the umbrella claim from "no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to index/passive structure" to "no official post-mortem attributes any of these episodes to the growth of index/passive ownership or to index-fund flows." Two of the documents do attribute disproportionate damage to ETF wrapper mechanics (SEC/CFTC 2010: "equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected"; BIS 2021 on impeded bond-ETF arbitrage), and the flat version is refutable on its face.

Fix the count: the sentence says "four canonical episodes" but enumerates five ((a) 2010, (b) 2015, (c) 2018, (d) 2020, (e) April 2025). Either say five, or scope "four canonical" to (a)-(d) and present April 2025 separately.

Optional strengthener for the Aug 24 2015 item: state that the SEC research note contains no instance of "passive," "index fund," or "indexing," and that the SEC/CFTC 2010 report's only uses of "passive" denote passive order execution (liquidity provision), not passive investing. This is a verifiable negative that makes the umbrella claim harder to attack.
newContradictions: The article's own umbrella sentence ("no official post-mortem attributes... to index/passive structure") sits in tension with the material it then quotes: the SEC/CFTC 2010 report affirmatively finds "equity-based ETFs were disproportionately affected" and explains it by the ETF valuation/market-making mechanism, and BIS 2021 says bond-ETF arbitrage was impeded. The distinction the article needs is ownership share vs wrapper plumbing, and it must be made explicitly or the sentence is refutable.

The BIS March 2021 stabilisation reading is hedged ("arguably in place") and is a conditional mechanism about redemption-basket composition, not a measured decomposition of the March 2020 discounts. Presenting it as BIS's finding that the discounts WERE a run deterrent overstates it; "reads the discounts partly as" is acceptable only if the hedge survives into the article.

The BIS Sept 2025 box also credits the rebound mainly to "backtracking from the initial tariff shock" and, from mid-May, to "news unrelated to tariffs"; retail buying is described as possibly amplifying ("They may have also been amplified by retail investors"). If the article uses this box for anything beyond the retail-vs-institutional contrast, that hierarchy of causes should be preserved.

The SPY figures need care: -5.2% is the OPEN, -7.8% is the 9:35 daily low, and the close was -4.2%. The clean comparison to SPX's -5.2% index decline is SPY's -7.8% low (the report's own pairing), but the article should not let "SPY fell 7.8%" read as a closing move.
reasoning: I reached all six primary documents in full text and grepped them verbatim rather than relying on summaries. (1) SEC/CFTC "Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010" (Sept 30, 2010) — read Sections II.2.b, II.2.c and II.3.b in full; confirmed the >20,000 broken trades / 5.5m shares sentence, the "over two-thirds of the securities with broken trades were ETFs listed on NYSE Arca" sentence, the "Almost two-thirds of shares in cancelled trades were executed at prices of less than $1.00" sentence, and the falsification sentence "ETFs that do not derive their value from the prices of domestic equity securities were not disproportionately affected." The only slippage is caliber: the market-maker pause is "one of the reasons," and the report gives a second order-book-depth explanation. (2) SEC OAR/TM Research Note "Equity Market Volatility on August 24, 2015" (Dec 2015) — confirmed 1,278 / 1,058 / 327 / 220 / 144 (arithmetic reconciles), 80% zero-halt (1,226 ETPs), 63.3% (859 ETPs) declining <10%, the SPX staleness mechanism and the -5.2% vs -7.8% pairing, and the MWCB non-trigger. Read Tables VI-6 and VI-7 directly: the turnover finding is an association within 114 Large/Mid US Equity ETPs, and the note carries an explicit no-causal-findings disclaimer, so "best predictor" is overclaimed. (3) BIS QR March 2018 box (Sushko & Turner, r_qt1803t) — confirmed $4bn end-2017 for "select" ETPs, XIV -84% and termination, and located the "Neither the size nor the complex strategies..." sentence exactly, but it lives in the note to Graph A1, and BIS's causal language is "a key factor behind the volatility spike that occurred on the afternoon of 5 February," qualified by the small aggregate positions. (4) BIS QR March 2021 (Todorov, "The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage") — confirmed the >200bp / 0.7bp sentence verbatim; confirmed the run-deterrence/shock-absorber reading including "such a stabilisation mechanism was arguably in place during the March–April 2020 episode"; but grep for "price discovery" returned ZERO hits, so that half of the attribution is wrong and must be dropped. (5) Fed FSR May 2020 — confirmed the passage on p.33 and found the article's ellipsis silently drops "arising from poor performance"; the leveraged/inverse ETP reservation is confirmed verbatim. (6) BIS QR Sept 2025 box (Lombardi, Pinter, Todorov) — confirmed the retail-not-institutional sentence verbatim, and grep for passive/index/ETF in the box returned zero hits, so the no-conflation warning is sound.
