itemVerdicts.note: Report 1b (p.11, 'Based on Risk-Adjusted Return'): All Large-Cap Funds | S&P 500 | 75.64 | 90.50 | 94.39 | 98.16 | 96.17 (3Y/5Y/10Y/15Y/20Y). Note Report 1b has NO YTD or 1-year column, so 94.39% is unambiguously the 10-year risk-adjusted figure.

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Survivorship (Report 2): 49.95% of large-cap funds survived 15 years; 88.29% decomposes into ~50pp dead + ~38pp survived-and-lost
itemVerdicts.note: Report 2, 15-Year block: All Large-Cap Funds — Number of Funds at Start 1,033; Survivorship 49.95%; Style Consistency 54.70%. Decomposition is exact: 100 − 88.29 = 11.71pp survived AND beat; non-survivors = 50.05pp; survived-but-lagged = 49.95 − 11.71 = 38.24pp. Mechanism confirmed in Appendix B glossary, which states the denominator is 'the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period' and the numerator is 'the count of funds that have survived and beat the index' — i.e. every non-survivor is scored as not-outperforming. Sharper framing available: only 23.4% of the funds that actually survived 15 years beat the index.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) 25-year annual series (Exhibit 1): majority of large-cap funds beat the S&P 500 in only three years — 2005 (49), 2007 (45), 2009 (48); worst years 2014 (87), 2021 (85), 2011 (82); no clean secular trend
itemVerdicts.note: Substance confirmed, label wrong. I re-extracted Exhibit 1 by bounding-box (column-matched to the year axis) rather than trusting reading order: 2001-65, 2002-68, 2003-75, 2004-69, 2005-49, 2006-68, 2007-45, 2008-56, 2009-48, 2010-66, 2011-82, 2012-63, 2013-55, 2014-87, 2015-65, 2016-66, 2017-63, 2018-65, 2019-71, 2020-60, 2021-85, 2022-51, 2023-60, 2024-65, H1 2025-54. Only three bars are below 50 (2005, 2007, 2009) — correct. Three worst are 2014=87, 2021=85, 2011=82 — correct (next is 2003=75). WRONG: calling this a '25-year annual series'. RIGHT: Mid-Year 2025 Exhibit 1 shows 24 completed calendar years (2001–2024) plus a partial 'H1 2025' bar — 25 bars, not 25 annual observations. The '25-year history' phrasing belongs to the Year-End 2025 edition (2001–2025). 'No clean secular trend' is well supported: OLS slope over 2001–2024 is +0.11pp/yr (2001–2012 mean 62.8 vs 2013–2024 mean 66.1) against a passive share that roughly quadrupled — a flat-to-faintly-rising line, not a ramp. Say 'essentially flat', not 'no trend at all'.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Year-End 2025: 79% of large-cap funds underperformed in CY2025, 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history'
itemVerdicts.note: Number confirmed by two independent secondhand sources read as RAW HTML (not fetch summaries); attribution of the quoted phrase is wrong. (1) InvestmentNews, Leo Almazora, MAR 04 2026: 'the SPIVA report found that "79% of all active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500," up from 65% in 2024 and the fourth-worst showing for large-cap managers in the 25-year history of the study.' Note the quotation marks close after 'S&P 500' — the 'fourth-worst' clause is InvestmentNews's own framing, NOT quoted SPIVA text. (2) tker.co, Sam Ro, Mar 03 2026: '79% of U.S. large-cap equity fund managers underperformed the S&P 500 in 2025. It was the fourth-worst year for these managers in the report's 25-year history,' plus a direct Anu Ganti quote ending '...2025 was the worst year for large-cap active equity performance since 2021,' and '16th consecutive year in which the majority of fund managers in this category have lagged the index.' WRONG: presenting 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history' as a verbatim SPIVA quotation. RIGHT: 79% is the SPIVA figure; 'fourth-worst in 25 years' is journalists' characterization (arithmetically consistent — only 2014=87, 2021=85, 2011=82 exceed 79). Consistency checks that all pass: 16 consecutive majority-lagging years = 2010–2025, which matches 2009=48 being the last sub-50 year; 79 slots between 82 and 75. tker also reports YE2025 large-cap 3-yr 67%, 5-yr 89%, 20-yr 93%. PRIMARY UNREACHABLE — see next item. Also worth flagging for the article: MY2025 said H1 was 54% and put the industry 'on track for the best year since 2022'; the full year landed at 79%. Using both figures without noting that H2 reversal would mislead.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) primary Year-End 2025 PDF
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach spiva-us-year-end-2025.pdf by any route: direct curl with browser UA + Referer → Akamai 403; WebFetch → 403; r.jina.ai proxy → 403 (Reference #18.1968dc17...); web.archive.org id_ replay → 404 (no snapshot); Wayback CDX API → timed out; guessed CloudFront path → 404; spglobal.com/spdji/en/spiva/article/spiva-us/ → 403. Therefore I could NOT verify the YE2025 Report 1a table, the YE2025 Exhibit 1 bar values (S&P DJI does restate historical bars between editions), or whether 'fourth-worst' appears in S&P's own text. Treat all YE2025 figures as secondhand, double-sourced.

itemVerdicts.item: (e) EW vs AW gap (MY2025): 10-yr S&P 500 13.65% vs large-cap funds EW 10.85% / AW 12.46%; 20-yr gap EW −1.96pp vs AW −1.25pp
itemVerdicts.note: Report 3 (Equal-Weighted, p.16): S&P 500 6.20/15.16/19.71/16.64/13.65/14.86/10.73; All Large-Cap Funds 6.08/13.31/17.43/14.16/10.85/12.22/8.77. Report 4 (Asset-Weighted, p.18): All Large-Cap Funds 7.67/15.48/20.00/15.35/12.46/13.64/9.48. So 10-yr: index 13.65, EW 10.85, AW 12.46 — exact. 20-yr: 8.77 − 10.73 = −1.96pp (EW) and 9.48 − 10.73 = −1.25pp (AW) — exact. Caliber: these are annualized returns as of June 30, 2025, net of fees excluding loads (per the report's Fees glossary), so 'gap' is a net-of-fee return differential, not alpha.

corrections: Do not call the Mid-Year 2025 Exhibit 1 a '25-year annual series'. It is 24 completed calendar years (2001–2024) plus a partial 'H1 2025' bar — 25 bars, 24 annual observations. The '25-year history' framing belongs to the Year-End 2025 edition, which covers 2001–2025.

Do not present 'fourth-worst showing in the 25-year history' as a quotation from SPIVA. In InvestmentNews the quotation marks close after '...underperformed the S&P 500'; the 'fourth-worst' clause is the reporter's framing. Attribute it as media characterization of the SPIVA data, or drop the quotation marks. The 79% figure itself is safely double-sourced (InvestmentNews 2026-03-04; tker.co / Sam Ro 2026-03-03).

Label all Year-End 2025 numbers (79% CY2025; 3-yr 67%, 5-yr 89%, 20-yr 93%) as secondhand — the primary PDF at spglobal.com returns Akamai 403 via every route tried (direct curl, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, Wayback, guessed CDN path) and no archive snapshot exists.

If the article cites both the Mid-Year and Year-End 2025 scorecards, it must acknowledge the reversal: MY2025 reported 54% underperforming in H1 and said the industry was 'on track for the best year since 2022'; the full year finished at 79%. Presenting the two side by side without that note is misleading.

Soften 'no clean secular trend' to 'essentially flat'. The 2001–2024 annual underperformance series has an OLS slope of +0.11pp/yr (2001–2012 mean 62.8% vs 2013–2024 mean 66.1%) — a faint upward drift, not zero, though nothing resembling the passive-share ramp.

Write the survivorship decomposition with the exact figures rather than rounded ones: of the 1,033 large-cap funds alive at the start of the 15-year window, 50.05pp did not survive, 38.24pp survived but lagged, and only 11.71pp survived and beat the index. Equivalently, just 23.4% of the funds that actually survived 15 years beat the S&P 500.

When using the survivorship decomposition, note that SPIVA's convention of scoring every non-survivor as not-outperforming is exactly the choice attacked by Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley (May 4, 2026 draft, funded by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council), who evaluate exiting funds over their living period instead and find U.S. equity 20-year underperformance rates fall by roughly 16pp. The MY2025 numbers are vendor numbers computed under a contested convention.
Use the index's full name 'S&P Composite 1500', not 'S&P 1500', when citing the 93.81% All Domestic Funds 20-year figure.
When citing the EW/AW gap, state that these are annualized returns as of June 30, 2025, net of fees excluding loads — a net return differential, not alpha.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, 'How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds' (draft May 4, 2026; supported by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council) replicates SPIVA closely (they get 92.04% vs SPIVA's reported 92.66% for the 20-year average U.S. equity category) but argues three methodology choices bias it: counting all exiting funds as underperformers, equal-weighting funds regardless of AUM, and benchmarking against indices rather than investable passive funds. Adjusted, they report only 56% of ASSETS in active U.S. equity funds underperformed equivalent passive funds in 2024 (vs SPIVA's 79% of FUNDS vs the S&P Composite 1500) — a fund-count vs asset-share distinction the article must not blur. Local file: iaa_spiva.txt.

SPIVA's own MY2025 data cuts against a simple 'indexing is eating alpha' story in the smaller-cap segments: only 25.34% of All Mid-Cap and 22.33% of All Small-Cap funds underperformed YTD H1 2025, and the report notes the 2024 small-cap underperformance rate of 30% was 'the lowest annual underperformance rate across more than two decades' of SPIVA scorecards. Report 1a also shows Large-Cap Value at just 16.06% YTD and Small-Cap Value at 4.08%.

The Mid-Year and Year-End 2025 editions point in opposite directions within the same calendar year (54% at H1, 79% for the full year), which is itself evidence that these rates are driven by mega-cap concentration episodes rather than by a monotone passive-share effect.
reasoning: I verified (a), (b), (c) and (e) directly against the primary PDF, and confirmed the local copy's provenance by SHA-256 against S&P's own CloudFront-hosted file (identical, 931,922 bytes) — so no extraction-source risk. For Report 1a/1b/2/3/4 I read pdftotext -layout output where the column alignment was unambiguous. For Exhibit 1, whose reading-order text extraction scrambles the bars across vertical bands, I did NOT trust the flat text: I re-extracted word bounding boxes with pdftotext -bbox and matched each two-digit label's x-centre to the x-centre of the year-axis labels (every match within 1.1pt), producing the full 2001–2024 + H1 2025 series. That is how I confirmed exactly three sub-50 years and the three worst years, and computed the trend slope myself. The only defect found in (a)/(b)/(e) was nomenclature ('S&P 1500'); the defect in (c) is the '25-year annual series' label, which the Mid-Year edition does not support. The Year-End 2025 primary is genuinely unreachable — Akamai 403 on the spglobal path via direct curl with browser headers, via WebFetch, and via the r.jina.ai proxy; Wayback has no snapshot (404 on id_ replay) and the CDX API timed out; the CloudFront path pattern that works for Mid-Year 2025 404s for Year-End. I therefore refused to accept the WebFetch summary's quotes at face value and instead pulled the raw HTML of two independent outlets with curl and read the surrounding text myself. Both give 79% and both use 'fourth-worst ... 25-year history', but reading the raw InvestmentNews sentence shows the quotation marks close before 'fourth-worst', which is why I downgraded that phrase from SPIVA quote to media framing. Three internal consistency checks on 79% all pass (it slots fourth behind 87/85/82; 'worst since 2021' fits 2021=85; '16th consecutive year' fits 2009=48 being the last sub-50 year), which is strong circumstantial support but is not the primary document. What remains uncertain: the Year-End 2025 Report 1a table, whether S&P restated any 2001–2024 Exhibit 1 bars in that edition, and whether 'fourth-worst' appears in S&P's own prose.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 21% of active strategies survived and beat their passive counterparts over the 10 years through 2025
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim from Key Takeaways, re-extracted directly from the source PDF (pdftotext, page 2): "Just 21% of active strategies survived and beat their passive counterparts over the 10 years through 2025." Note the report's own wording in this bullet is "their passive counterparts," not "asset-weighted passive composite" — the asset-weighted phrasing appears in the 1-year bullet. Both are consistent with the Success Rate definition, so no correction needed, but do not put "asset-weighted average passive composite" inside quotation marks attached to the 21% sentence.

itemVerdicts.item: (a) 1-yr 2025: 38% all funds, 37% US stock-pickers
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim, page 2: "Just 38% survived and beat their asset-weighted average passive composite, down 4 percentage points from a year earlier" and "US stock-pickers also trended slightly lower with a 37% success rate for 2025, a 1-percentage-point drop from 2024."

itemVerdicts.item: (b) Exhibit 1 10-year success rates: Large Blend 8.1, Large Growth 3.6, Large Value 20.3, Small Growth 37.0, Foreign Large Blend 22.8, Diversified EM 29.1, Intermediate Core Bond 41.7, Corporate Bond 52.2, High-Yield 39.1
itemVerdicts.note: All nine match Exhibit 1 exactly. Re-extracted independently from the PDF with pdftotext -layout (pages 3-4) to rule out extraction corruption: US Large Blend 8.1; US Large Value 20.3; US Large Growth 3.6; US Small Growth 37.0; Foreign Large Blend 22.8; Diversified Emerging Markets 29.1; Intermediate Core Bond 41.7; Corporate Bond 52.2; High-Yield Bond 39.1. These are 10-Year columns, not 15- or 20-Year (which are much lower: Large Blend 4.3 / 6.4).

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Methodology: success = survived AND beat the asset-weighted average of actual passive funds in the category, net of fees, magnitude ignored
itemVerdicts.note: Appendix, "Success Rate": "The success rate indicates what percentage of funds that started the sample period went on to survive and generate a return in excess of the asset-weighted average passive fund return over the period... We do not consider magnitude of outperformance in defining success: A fund that just barely beat the passive alternative counts as much as a fund that significantly outperformed." Net-of-fees is verbatim on page 1: the benchmark "reflects the actual, net-of-fees performance of investable passive funds." CAVEAT the article should know: the SAME report contradicts itself twice — the next paragraph says success counts funds ranking "higher than the equal weighted average return for the passive funds in the category," and Appendix C says "count the number of funds with returns exceeding the equal-weighted average of the passive funds in the category." This is longstanding boilerplate (identical contradiction in the H2-2025 edition, mstar_h22025.txt lines 2192 and 2266). Safe to say "asset-weighted" (that is the report's own Success Rate definition and headline language), but do not present the methodology as unambiguous.

itemVerdicts.item: (c) Universe ~9,248 funds, ~$26T, ~67% of the US fund market
itemVerdicts.note: Verbatim page 1: "spans nearly 9,248 unique funds that accounted for approximately USD 26 trillion in assets, or about 67% of the US fund market, at the end of 2025." ("nearly 9,248" is Morningstar's own odd phrasing; the figure is a count of unique funds, not share classes.) Note 67% is share of US FUND assets, not of US market cap.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Passive funds survive better: 80.4% vs 62.4% at 10 years in US Large Blend
itemVerdicts.note: Exhibit 5 (US Large Blend), 10-Year row: active # at beginning 383, active survivorship 62.4%; passive # at beginning 138, passive survivorship 80.4%; active success rate 8.1%. Numbers are exactly right.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Morningstar fixes SPIVA's costless-benchmark objection
itemVerdicts.note: Supported, though Morningstar never names SPIVA anywhere in the report (grep: zero hits for "SPIVA" or "S&P Dow Jones"). Appendix C: "We believe this is a better benchmark because it reflects the performance of actual investable options and not an index. One cannot directly invest in indexes. Their performance does not account for the real costs associated with replicating their performance and packaging and distributing them in an investable format." Attribute as Morningstar's stated rationale versus "the convention of using a single, representative index," not as an explicit rebuttal of SPIVA.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) Harsher answer for US large cap: 8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14%
itemVerdicts.note: WRONG as framed: it pairs Morningstar's NARROW US Large Blend category (8.1%) against SPIVA's BROAD All Large-Cap aggregate (~14%), which bundles growth, core and value. The matched comparison reverses the sign. SPIVA's Large-Cap CORE row is the analog of Morningstar Large Blend, and there SPIVA is far HARSHER: Mid-Year 2025 Report 1a shows Large-Cap Core Funds vs S&P 500, 10-year underperformance 96.57% (= 3.43% success) — verified from a freshly downloaded PDF, not just the local extract; SPIVA Year-End 2024 shows 96.62% (= 3.38% success), as reproduced in Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley (2026). RIGHT framing: compare aggregate to aggregate. Morningstar's three US large-cap categories, weighted by starting fund counts, give 10-year success of about 10.2% (383 funds x 8.1% + 350 x 20.3% + 417 x 3.6%, all from Exhibits 5/8/11 = 11,708.5/1,150 = 10.18%), against SPIVA All Large-Cap 10-year success of 14.02% (Mid-Year 2025) or 15.66% (Year-End 2024). So Morningstar IS somewhat harsher at the aggregate level, but the gap is roughly 4pp, not the ~6pp implied, and the 8.1%-vs-14% pairing is not like-for-like. Also note the two studies use different fund universes (Morningstar Categories vs Lipper/CRSP classifications) and different hurdles (Large Blend's passive composite includes total-market funds like VTSMX, not only S&P 500 trackers), so a direct head-to-head needs a hedge in any case.

itemVerdicts.item: (d) '...partly because passive funds survive better (80.4% vs 62.4%)' as the explanation for the harsher answer
itemVerdicts.note: The causal clause is unsupported and mechanically wrong. Morningstar makes no such attribution anywhere in the report. Differential survivorship cannot explain a Morningstar-vs-SPIVA gap because SPIVA applies the identical convention — SPIVA Appendix B glossary, verbatim: "To correct for survivorship bias, we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index." Both studies already count dead active funds as failures. Separately, the operative fact for the LEVEL of 8.1% is that ACTIVE funds survive poorly (62.4%, so 37.6% are automatic failures), not that passive funds survive well; passive survivorship (80.4%) only affects the passive composite's return, and only marginally (dead passive funds' starting weights are subsumed pro rata by survivors). Either drop the causal clause or rewrite it as the active-attrition point.

itemVerdicts.item: SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025 exact 10-year All Large-Cap underperformance rate
itemVerdicts.note: Could not reach the primary document. spglobal.com is blocked at the Akamai edge from this environment (HTTP 403 on the PDF and on the SPIVA article page, via curl with browser headers, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, three CORS proxies, and the Chrome browser tool); there is no Wayback capture of spiva-us-year-end-2025.pdf; the S&P CloudFront mirror (which works for Mid-Year 2025) requires a per-file UUID I could not discover. Two web-SEARCH SUMMARIZERS returned conflicting/unverifiable 10-year figures ("fewer than one in six" and "89.93%") — per the fabrication warning I am treating both as unverified and NOT reporting either as fact. What I could verify from primary text: SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 (data as of June 30, 2025) All Large-Cap 10-year underperformance 85.98% (= 14.02% success), and SPIVA Year-End 2024 All Large-Cap 10-year 84.34% (= 15.66% success). If the article's "~14%" is meant to be the Year-End 2025 figure covering the same 2016-2025 window as Morningstar's 8.1%, it is currently sourced to the wrong vintage and must be re-checked against the Year-End 2025 PDF before publication.

corrections: Do not write "8.1% vs SPIVA's ~14%" as a like-for-like large-cap comparison. Morningstar's US Large Blend is the analog of SPIVA's Large-Cap Core, where SPIVA is far harsher: 10-year underperformance 96.57% (= 3.43% success) in SPIVA Mid-Year 2025, and 96.62% (= 3.38%) in SPIVA Year-End 2024. Compare aggregate to aggregate instead: Morningstar's three US large-cap categories, weighted by starting fund counts (383 Large Blend at 8.1%, 350 Large Value at 20.3%, 417 Large Growth at 3.6%), give about 10.2% 10-year success, versus SPIVA All Large-Cap 14.0% (Mid-Year 2025) / 15.7% (Year-End 2024).

Delete or rewrite the clause "partly because passive funds survive better (80.4% vs 62.4%)." Morningstar makes no such causal claim, and it cannot explain a gap versus SPIVA because SPIVA uses the same survivorship convention (SPIVA Appendix B: "we use the opportunity set available at the beginning of the period as the denominator. We determine the count of funds that have survived and beat the index"). If the point is worth keeping, state it as: the 8.1% is capped by active attrition — only 62.4% of the 383 US large-blend active funds that existed at the start of 2016 were still alive at the end of 2025, and every one of the other 37.6% counts as a failure by construction (passive funds in the same category survived at 80.4%).

Re-source the SPIVA comparison figure. The "~14%" matches SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 (data as of June 30, 2025), not a year-end-2025 window. If the article compares to Morningstar's "10 years through 2025," pull the corresponding row from SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025 (data as of Dec. 31, 2025) and state which SPIVA edition and which row (All Large-Cap vs Large-Cap Core) is being used.

When stating the Morningstar methodology, note that the hurdle is described inconsistently within the report itself: the "Success Rate" definition and the key takeaways say the ASSET-WEIGHTED average passive fund return, while the following paragraph and Appendix C both say the EQUAL-WEIGHTED average of the passive funds in the category (the same contradiction appears in the H2-2025 edition). Say "asset-weighted average passive composite, per Morningstar's stated definition" rather than asserting it as settled.

Say Morningstar rejects "the convention of using a single, representative index" and never names SPIVA — do not write that Morningstar is answering or rebutting SPIVA. The report contains zero mentions of SPIVA or S&P Dow Jones Indices.
Make the units explicit for the universe figures: ~9,248 unique funds, ~USD 26 trillion, and about 67% of the US FUND market (share of fund assets), not 67% of US market capitalization.
newContradictions: Cremers, Fulkerson & Riley, "How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds" (draft dated May 4, 2026; local file iaa_spiva.txt) argues in the opposite direction from the article's twist: it claims SPIVA's methodological choices "systematically understate the performance of active funds," and that after adjustment "only 56% of assets invested in active U.S. equity funds in 2024 underperformed equivalent passive funds," with the sign reversing for fixed income. Sponsorship must be disclosed if cited: "This research was supported by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council," and Cremers is an independent director at Ariel Investments. Note that this paper's central fix — benchmarking against equivalent passive FUNDS rather than an index — is exactly what Morningstar already does, so citing it alongside the Morningstar 8.1% needs care.

Morningstar's own report contains a partial counterweight the article should not omit: "Over the past 10 years, the average dollar invested in active funds outperformed the average active fund in 17 of the 20 categories examined," and "31% of active funds in the cheapest quintile of their respective categories beat their average passive peer, compared with 17% for the priciest funds" (Exhibit 1 shows US Large Blend lowest-cost quintile at 17.1% versus 8.1% overall). The 8.1% headline is an equal-weighted count across all funds regardless of size or fee; the asset-weighted return gap in US Large Blend over 10 years is 13.2% active vs 14.5% passive, i.e. 1.3pp/yr, not a wipeout.

The report's fixed-income results are volatile enough to undercut any single-year narrative: Corporate Bond had a 52.2% 10-year success rate but only 4.4% in 2025 (a 62.9pp year-over-year drop, the largest in Exhibit 2), and US Real Estate fell 51.0pp and Global Real Estate 57.9pp. If the article uses the 10-year bond numbers as evidence of anything structural, it should flag this instability.
reasoning:

I re-extracted pages 1-4 and the appendix independently with pdftotext -layout rather than relying on the pre-made .txt, so none of the numbers below rest on a possibly-garbled extraction. Local file mstar_apb_h12026.txt and mstar_h12026.txt are the same file (identical md5).

(a) and (b) check out verbatim, every figure, with no caliber slippage. The universe line in (c) is verbatim. The methodology description in (c) matches the report's "Success Rate" appendix section word for word — but I found that the SAME appendix contradicts itself two paragraphs later and again in Appendix C, both times saying the hurdle is the EQUAL-weighted passive average. I confirmed this is longstanding boilerplate, not an extraction artifact, by finding the identical contradiction in the prior H2-2025 edition. The article's "asset-weighted" claim is defensible but should not be stated as unambiguous.

(d) is where the group breaks. The survivorship numbers (80.4% passive vs 62.4% active, US Large Blend 10-year) are exactly right, from Exhibit 5. The same reversal holds in SPIVA Year-End 2024 (96.62% / 3.38%), which I read in the Cremers-Fulkerson-Riley reproduction. Second, the "partly because passive funds survive better" clause is unsupported by Morningstar and cannot explain a gap versus SPIVA, because SPIVA's Appendix B glossary — which I read verbatim — uses the identical opportunity-set denominator and the identical survived-and-beat numerator.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not reach SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2025, the vintage that actually matches Morningstar's 10-years-through-2025 window. spglobal.com is blocked at the Akamai edge from this environment across every route I tried (curl with full browser headers on www and bare domain and a Spanish-locale path, WebFetch, r.jina.ai, three CORS proxies, and the Chrome browser tool, which returned the same Access Denied page); there is no Wayback capture; the CloudFront mirror needs a per-file UUID I could not discover, though I confirmed the mirror works by successfully downloading the Mid-Year 2025 file.
